explanation:
A prostatic urethral lift uses implants to retract tissue and widen the urethra. Transurethral resection removes obstructing tissue. **TURP gave greater urinary symptom relief, while the lift better preserved ejaculation.**

**A. Lift for greater relief, resection for ejaculation** — The comparative trial favored resection on symptom scores and the lift on preservation of sexual function.
**B. Resection for greater relief, lift for ejaculation** — At two years TURP produced about six more points of improvement on the symptom score. Men undergoing the lift were less likely to experience a change in ejaculation.
**C. Lift for greater relief and flow** — Peak urinary flow as well as symptom improvement favored TURP.
**D. Resection for preservation of sexual function** — Retrograde ejaculation is common after TURP. The lift is the option to discuss when preservation of ejaculation is a priority.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 568–570, Transurethral Resection of Prostate and Prostatic urethral lift.

q: When discussing surgery for benign prostatic enlargement, what technical advantage does bipolar transurethral resection have over monopolar resection?
o: Hypotonic irrigation fluid reduces the sodium load during resection
Isotonic irrigation fluid reduces the risk of TURP syndrome
Isotonic irrigation fluid increases free-water absorption during resection
Hypotonic irrigation fluid reduces the risk of electrolyte disturbances
explanation:
Classic TURP syndrome occurs when absorbed hypotonic irrigating fluid causes volume overload and dilutional hyponatremia. **Bipolar resection permits isotonic irrigation, reducing the risk of this syndrome.**

**A. Hypotonic irrigation to reduce sodium load** — The problem is dilution of the patient’s serum sodium as hypotonic irrigant is absorbed.
**B. Isotonic irrigation lowers syndrome risk** — The bipolar circuit permits saline irrigation and avoids the large free-water load associated with classic monopolar resection.
**C. Isotonic irrigation increases free-water absorption** — Isotonic saline does not supply the same electrolyte-free water load as hypotonic irrigation.
**D. Hypotonic irrigation prevents electrolyte disturbances** — Absorption of hypotonic fluid is precisely what can lower serum sodium during a prolonged monopolar resection.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 568, Surgery and Transurethral Resection of Prostate.

q: A 71-year-old man improved after TURP but returns several years later with urinary symptoms. Which description of TURP outcomes agrees with Hazzard?
o: Symptom relief tends to increase over time, and some men require reoperation
Symptom relief tends to decrease over time, and some men require reoperation
Symptom relief tends to increase over time, and the entire prostate is removed
Symptom relief tends to decrease over time, and the entire prostate is removed
explanation:
TURP removes adenoma around the prostatic urethra and leaves the capsule and some prostate tissue in place. **Initial symptom relief is often substantial, but it can diminish over time and some men require another operation.**

**A. Increasing relief, occasional reoperation** — Reoperation is possible, but average relief decreased between early and long-term follow-up.
**B. Declining relief, occasional reoperation** — The reported symptom reduction was 87% at three months and 75% at seven years. Average reoperation rates were about 1% to 2% per year.
**C. Increasing relief, entire gland removed** — Neither description fits TURP. The procedure opens the urethral channel by resecting obstructing adenoma.
**D. Declining relief, entire gland removed** — The time course is plausible, but removing the entire prostate describes radical prostatectomy.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 568, Surgery and Transurethral Resection of Prostate.

q: A 68-year-old man has lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia and erectile dysfunction. He has no cardiovascular contraindication to PDE-5 inhibitors and takes no BPH medication. Which daily PDE-5 inhibitor does Hazzard identify as FDA-approved for male LUTS?
o: Daily tadalafil treatment
Daily sildenafil treatment
Daily vardenafil treatment
Daily avanafil treatment
explanation:
Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors can improve erectile function. **Tadalafil 5 mg once daily also has US approval for lower urinary tract symptoms associated with BPH.**

**A. Tadalafil** — Daily tadalafil can address both concerns with one medication when it is otherwise appropriate for the patient.
**B. Sildenafil** — Trials have evaluated urinary symptom scores during sildenafil treatment, but it lacks this US indication.
**C. Vardenafil** — Vardenafil was studied for urinary symptoms in younger men. The daily drug approved for male LUTS is tadalafil.
**D. Avanafil** — It belongs to the erectile-dysfunction drug class, but class membership does not confer the urinary indication.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 566–567, Table 38-7 and Phosphodiesterase Type 5 Inhibitors.

q: A patient with uncorrectable urinary retention needs prolonged catheterization after discussion of alternatives. Which combination of complications is associated with an indwelling catheter used for months to years?
o: Less chronic bacteriuria and fewer bladder stones
More chronic bacteriuria and fewer bladder stones
More chronic bacteriuria and more bladder stones
Less chronic bacteriuria and more bladder stones
explanation:
An indwelling catheter provides a surface for long-term bacterial colonization and stone formation. **Both chronic bacteriuria and bladder stones become more common.**

**A. Less chronic bacteriuria and fewer bladder stones** — Continuous drainage does not prevent colonization or stone formation.
**B. More chronic bacteriuria and fewer bladder stones** — Colonization increases, but stones also increase.
**C. More chronic bacteriuria and more bladder stones** — Both complications are recognized with catheterization lasting months to years.
**D. Less chronic bacteriuria and more bladder stones** — Stone risk rises but bacteriuria does not fall.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch. 47, pp. 715–716.

q: A 78-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage III colon cancer is being assessed for adjuvant chemotherapy. His ECOG performance status is 1, but he reports occasional falls and memory difficulties and takes eight medications. What is the main purpose of comprehensive geriatric assessment in this setting?
o: To identify aging-related problems missed by routine assessment and performance status
To convert tumor stage and histologic findings into an oncologic treatment classification
To confirm the existing performance score through a repeat assessment of exercise ability
To summarize medication burden through a review of prescriptions and drug interactions
explanation:
ECOG performance status describes global activity. **A comprehensive geriatric assessment can uncover and address risks that an ECOG score of 1 misses.**

**A. Identify overlooked vulnerabilities** — Falls raise questions about balance and home safety, memory difficulties about treatment instructions, and eight medications about interactions.
**B. Classify the cancer** — Staging and histopathology describe tumor extent and biology. They do not measure these vulnerabilities.
**C. Repeat the performance rating** — A second activity score still leaves cognition and medication use unexplored.
**D. Summarize prescriptions** — Medication reconciliation covers one domain. It cannot explain the falls and memory concerns on its own.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1387–1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: A 72-year-old woman with advanced pancreatic cancer is being considered for chemotherapy. Geriatric assessment identifies mild cognitive impairment, falls, polypharmacy, and poor nutritional status. What is the purpose of the CARG model described in Hazzard?
o: Estimate the probability of tumor response using patient and treatment variables
Estimate the risk of cancer mortality using patient and treatment variables
Estimate the risk of chemotherapy toxicity using patient and treatment variables
Estimate the probability of surgical recovery using patient and treatment variables
explanation:
The Cancer and Aging Research Group model combines patient factors, laboratory results and the planned regimen. **It estimates the risk of severe toxicity from chemotherapy.**

**A. Tumor response** — Tumor biology and drug sensitivity help predict shrinkage. CARG does not predict that endpoint.
**B. Cancer mortality** — Death from progressive cancer is a different outcome from a severe treatment complication.
**C. Chemotherapy toxicity** — Treatment intensity and measured vulnerabilities jointly influence the probability of serious adverse effects, helping the clinician discuss risk before treatment.
**D. Surgical recovery** — Recovery after an operation depends on the procedure, healing and rehabilitation. CARG was developed for chemotherapy.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: An 85-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer presents with bowel obstruction. He also has diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and chronic kidney disease. The surgical team is discussing emergency surgery and conservative treatment. Which consideration is supported by Hazzard's discussion of surgery in older adults with cancer?
o: Emergency surgery is associated with more complications and should inform the benefit-risk discussion.
Emergency surgery is associated with fewer complications because urgent intervention reduces operative risk.
Diabetes and vascular disease support faster wound healing and should reduce concern about recovery.
Reduced physiologic reserve supports shorter rehabilitation and should reduce concern about recovery.
explanation:
An emergency operation leaves little time to optimize comorbid disease. **Its higher complication risk belongs in the discussion of surgery, expected symptom relief and the patient's goals.**

**A. More complications with emergency surgery** — Obstruction may require an operation, but metastatic disease and limited reserve increase the importance of weighing its immediate burdens and likely benefit.
**B. Fewer complications with urgent intervention** — The urgency can justify operating. It does not protect the patient from postoperative complications.
**C. Faster healing with diabetes and vascular disease** — Impaired perfusion and diabetes can delay tissue repair.
**D. Shorter rehabilitation with reduced reserve** — Limited reserve makes recovery from an acute insult harder and may prolong hospitalization and rehabilitation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 376, 1388–1389.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.376, 1388

q: A 69-year-old woman with breast cancer is scheduled for mastectomy. She has well-controlled diabetes and mild peripheral vascular disease. Her family asks about wound healing. Which age-related skin changes are linked to a reduced rate of wound healing in Hazzard's perioperative table?
o: Increased re-epithelialization and increased dermal blood vessels.
Reduced re-epithelialization and increased dermal blood vessels.
Reduced re-epithelialization and reduced dermal blood vessels.
Increased re-epithelialization and reduced dermal blood vessels.
explanation:
Re-epithelialization closes a break in the skin, and dermal vessels supply the healing tissue. **Both re-epithelialization and dermal vascularity decrease with aging.**

**A. Both increase** Faster epithelial repair and a richer vascular supply would favor healing.
**B. Less re-epithelialization, more vessels** Epithelial repair does slow, but the number of dermal vessels also falls.
**C. Both decrease** Slower replacement of surface cells and reduced vascular support delay wound closure.
**D. More re-epithelialization, fewer vessels** The vascular change is in the right direction, but epithelial repair slows as well.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 27, Table 27-3, p. 375.
ref: Hazzard Ch 27 — PERIOPERATIVE CARE: EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT

q: A community-based trial in older patients with advanced cancer found an absolute reduction of 20% in treatment toxicity with comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)-guided interventions. Which description captures the approach described by Hazzard?
o: It uses routine history and examination as the assessment for age-related problems and intervention planning
It forwards an assessment report to the oncologist while retaining the usual treatment pathway
It identifies missed aging-related problems and directs interventions tailored to the findings
It centers assessment on tumor characteristics while leaving functional assessment to the usual pathway
explanation:
In GAP70+, community oncologists received a summary of age-related impairments and tailored management recommendations. **Using those findings to guide care lowered three-month grade 3–5 toxicity from 71% to 51%.**

**A. Routine history and examination** — Usual assessment can miss falls, nutritional difficulties or a need for help with daily activities.
**B. Forward a report and retain usual care** — The intervention gave oncologists specific management recommendations, beyond merely forwarding findings.
**C. Identify problems and tailor interventions** — A deficit could prompt a medication change, a fall-prevention measure or discussion of treatment intensity. The observed absolute difference was about 20 percentage points.
**D. Center assessment on the tumor** — Tumor characteristics guide drug selection but do not reveal functional risks that can be addressed during treatment.

Reference · GAP70+, Lancet 2021, pp. 1894–1904 (PMID 34741815) · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: A busy oncology clinic plans to use the geriatric assessment tool described in Hazzard, with a median completion time of 22 minutes. Which workflow matches the design of that tool?
o: Use staff interviews for most measures and patient self-report for a few items.
Use patient self-report for most measures and staff assessment for a few items.
Use oncology performance status for most measures, replacing function and nutrition domains.
Use comorbidities for most measures, replacing cognition and psychological domains.
explanation:
The geriatric assessment tool combines a patient questionnaire with a small clinician-completed component. **Patients completed most measures themselves and a health professional completed three items.**

**A. Staff interviews for most measures** — Putting most of the work on staff reverses how the tool was designed.
**B. Self-report for most measures** — The median completion time was 22 minutes and 87% completed their own portion without help. Assistance is still appropriate when needed.
**C. ECOG replaces function and nutrition** — A global activity rating omits nutritional status and cannot replace dedicated measures.
**D. Comorbidity replaces cognition and mood** — Diagnoses alone reveal little about memory, distress or ability to carry out treatment instructions.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388, Clinical Markers of Aging.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: An older woman with cancer and good ECOG performance status reports falls and forgetfulness. What does comprehensive geriatric assessment add?
o: An assessment that reduces the need to investigate falls when ECOG status is good
An assessment that concentrates on the tumor in place of function and cognition
An assessment that identifies aging-related problems missed by ECOG performance status
An assessment that postpones cognitive evaluation until ECOG performance status deteriorates
explanation:
A person can remain active enough for a good ECOG rating while falling or struggling to remember instructions. **Geriatric assessment identifies these specific and potentially actionable problems.**

**A. Less need to investigate falls** — A fall remains clinically important even when the patient is up and about most of the day.
**B. Focus on the tumor** — Tumor staging cannot explain a change in gait, medication use or cognition.
**C. Identify deficits missed by ECOG** — Assessing falls and cognition directly helps decide what support the patient needs before treatment.
**D. Wait for ECOG deterioration** — Earlier assessment may allow intervention before a fall or missed medicine disrupts treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1387–1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: A 76-year-old man with gastric cancer has a high CRASH risk score for chemotherapy toxicity. Which approach is supported by the studies described in Hazzard for reducing treatment toxicity by identifying aging-related vulnerabilities?
o: Adapt care using routine medical history and physical examination in oncology.
Adapt care using repeat assessment of the conventional oncology performance status.
Send geriatric assessment results to the oncologist for the usual care pathway.
Review geriatric assessment as a team and implement tailored interventions.
explanation:
CRASH estimates chemotherapy toxicity and distinguishes hematologic from nonhematologic risk. **A high estimate should lead the team to identify and act on the patient's specific vulnerabilities.**

**A. Routine history and examination** — A standard visit can miss falls, problems taking medicines or inadequate intake that merit intervention.
**B. Repeat performance status** — Global activity can look satisfactory despite meaningful impairment in other domains.
**C. Send results through usual care** — In GAIN the usual-care oncologist received the assessment and could act at discretion. This lacked the assigned team's implementation.
**D. Team review and tailored care** — The intervention team arranged care according to measured deficits. Grade 3 or higher toxicity occurred in 50.5% with this approach and 60.6% with usual care.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388 · GAIN, JAMA Oncology 2021, intervention and primary outcome (PMID 34591080).
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1388, CRASH assessment

q: In a randomized trial of older adults with solid tumors starting chemotherapy, a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)-guided program reduced toxicity compared with usual care. Which action distinguished the intervention arm?
o: Send the assessment findings to the oncologist for management through usual care
Review the assessment in a multidisciplinary team and implement tailored interventions
Classify patients into toxicity-risk groups and send the risk summary to the clinicians
Complete a self-reported assessment with three items completed by a health professional
explanation:
GAIN tested what happens after geriatric assessment in older adults starting chemotherapy for a solid tumor. **The multidisciplinary team reviewed the findings and implemented interventions for identified deficits.**

**A. Send findings to the oncologist** — Both groups had assessments. In usual care the oncologist received the results for consideration.
**B. Team review with implementation** — The team arranged interventions such as nutritional support or medication review when thresholds were met. The absolute reduction in severe toxicity was 10.1 percentage points.
**C. Send a risk category** — Risk classification estimates the chance of harm but does not arrange treatment of the factors contributing to it.
**D. Complete the questionnaire** — How the assessment was collected did not distinguish the two treatment groups.

Reference · GAIN, JAMA Oncology 2021, Intervention Delivery and Results (PMID 34591080) · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: A cancer center is developing a geriatric oncology program. Which combination of implementation barriers does Hazzard describe?
o: Organizational issues, limited time, scarce equipment, restrictive licensing
Organizational issues, limited space, limited staff, restrictive licensing
Organizational issues, limited time, limited staff, unclear reimbursement
Organizational issues, limited space, scarce equipment, unclear reimbursement
explanation:
Geriatric oncology requires time to assess several domains, trained staff to respond, and a way to pay for that work. **Organizational constraints, limited time and staffing, and uncertain reimbursement are recognized barriers.**

**A. Equipment and restrictive licensing** — Neither buying equipment nor changing licensing addresses the missing personnel, time and payment arrangements.
**B. Space and restrictive licensing** — Staffing is relevant, but space and licensing do not describe the documented combination of barriers.
**C. Organization, time, staff and reimbursement** — Even a brief instrument needs clinic time, familiarity with the tools and people who can implement its recommendations.
**D. Space, equipment and reimbursement** — Payment uncertainty matters. This combination omits limited clinician time and staffing.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388, CGA-Guided Interventions.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1388

q: A 68-year-old man has newly diagnosed T1c prostate cancer, PSA 6.2 ng/mL, Gleason score 6, and two positive cores out of twelve. He has controlled diabetes, mild hypertension, takes metformin and lisinopril, and has ECOG performance status 0. He is concerned about quality of life. Which strategy uses scheduled monitoring while retaining the prospect of delayed, potentially curative treatment if progression is detected?
o: Immediate radical prostatectomy with postoperative follow-up for recurrence
Active surveillance with PSA monitoring at three-month intervals
External-beam radiation with accompanying androgen-deprivation treatment
Watchful waiting with treatment deferred until symptoms develop
explanation:
Active surveillance monitors low-risk localized prostate cancer with the intention to treat while cure is still possible. **Scheduled PSA monitoring with reassessment for progression** fits this man's small-volume Gleason 6 disease.

**A. Immediate prostatectomy.** This is definitive local treatment now, not monitoring before a treatment decision.
**B. Active surveillance.** Serial PSA, examination and repeat biopsy when indicated help determine whether to offer curative treatment.
**C. Radiation plus hormones.** This begins tumor-directed therapy immediately.
**D. Watchful waiting.** The trigger is symptomatic disease, with palliation as the goal.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1414.

q: An 82-year-old man has high-risk nonmetastatic prostate cancer. He has no disease-related symptoms, and comorbidities limit his estimated life expectancy to three to four years. After discussion with him, watchful waiting is selected. Which change triggers treatment within this approach?
o: Increasing PSA velocity resulting in a PSA doubling time of less than three years
An increase in the number of positive biopsy cores or the extent of their involvement
Development of disease-related symptoms requiring treatment to relieve the resulting suffering
A primary Gleason pattern of four or five identified on a subsequent prostate biopsy
explanation:
Watchful waiting prioritizes symptom relief when competing illness limits the chance of benefit from curative treatment. **Treat when prostate cancer causes symptoms requiring relief**.

**A. Short PSA doubling time.** PSA kinetics can prompt reassessment during active surveillance, not the defining trigger here.
**B. Additional involved biopsy cores.** Biopsy progression is used in a curative-intent surveillance strategy.
**C. New disease-related symptoms.** Pain or obstructive symptoms can warrant palliative treatment consistent with the chosen approach.
**D. Higher Gleason pattern.** Histologic upgrading informs active surveillance and does not by itself define symptom-triggered care.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1414.

q: A 78-year-old man is starting androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer. Which combination of adverse effects described in Hazzard belongs in pretreatment counseling?
o: Improved memory and increased risk of osteoporosis
Memory decline and increased risk of osteoporosis
Memory decline and decreased risk of osteoporosis
Improved memory and decreased risk of osteoporosis
explanation:
Androgen deprivation lowers testosterone signaling to control prostate cancer. **Counsel about possible memory decline and increased osteoporosis risk.**

**A. Improved memory and more osteoporosis** — Bone loss is a concern, but memory may worsen during treatment.
**B. Memory decline and more osteoporosis** — Ask about cognition and assess fracture risk, particularly if falls or low bone density are already present.
**C. Memory decline and less osteoporosis** — The cognitive concern fits, but androgen deprivation can weaken bone.
**D. Improved memory and less osteoporosis** — Neither improvement is an expected consequence of androgen suppression.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1390, Hormonal therapy.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

q: A 76-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents after a fall. He has had increasing back pain for a month and difficulty walking. Examination shows L2–L3 tenderness, bilateral leg weakness (4/5), and reduced reflexes. PSA has risen to 67 ng/mL despite androgen deprivation therapy. X-rays show osteoblastic lesions in several vertebrae. Which approach to possible spinal cord compression follows Hazzard?
o: Complete assessment for a pathologic fracture before arranging definitive spinal imaging
Arrange urgent definitive spinal imaging, preferably MRI or CT myelography
Repeat the neurologic examination before arranging imaging if the weakness improves
Assess systemic cancer-treatment changes before arranging definitive spinal imaging
explanation:
Progressive back pain and new bilateral weakness in a man with vertebral metastases raise concern for malignant cord or cauda equina compression. **Arrange emergency specialist assessment and urgent whole-spine MRI, and give dexamethasone promptly for neurologic signs unless contraindicated.**

**A. Complete fracture workup first.** Plain films show vertebral metastases but can miss epidural disease or neural compression. Fracture assessment should not delay definitive imaging.
**B. Urgent MRI or a suitable alternative.** Obtain MRI as soon as possible, within 24 hours. If MRI is contraindicated, CT is used and specialist CT myelography may occasionally be needed. Imaging guides urgent radiation or surgical decisions.
**C. Wait for improvement before imaging.** Fluctuating weakness does not exclude compression. Delay risks irreversible loss of mobility or continence.
**D. Review systemic cancer treatment first.** That is important subsequently but cannot resolve the immediate threat to neural function.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1416. NICE NG234, recommendations 1.5.2, 1.5.7–1.5.8 and 1.8.1.

q: A 74-year-old man with localized prostate cancer and ulcerative colitis is discussing treatment options. Which explanation agrees with Hazzard’s prostate cancer chapter?
o: Radical prostatectomy leaves the extent of disease for clinical estimation, as radiation does
Active surveillance postpones intervention until symptoms develop, as watchful waiting does
External radiation needs caution because inflammatory bowel disease is a relative contraindication
Brachytherapy delivers radiation from beams originating outside the body, as external beam therapy does
explanation:
**Inflammatory bowel disease is a relative contraindication to external pelvic radiation** because rectal and bowel toxicity may be greater. The disease’s activity, location, radiation technique and alternatives should inform the discussion.

**A. Prostatectomy leaves only clinical staging.** Removing the prostate and relevant tissue permits pathological assessment and can refine staging.
**B. Active surveillance waits for symptoms.** Surveillance uses planned reassessment and can trigger curative treatment for progression before symptoms. Watchful waiting generally prioritizes symptom-directed care.
**C. Caution with external radiation.** Ulcerative colitis makes potential bowel injury particularly relevant.
**D. Brachytherapy uses external beams.** Brachytherapy places radioactive material within or near the prostate.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 90, p. 1414.

q: An 81-year-old man receiving androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer has osteoporosis. In addition to evaluating falls and nutrition, which approach to bone health is supported by Hazzard?
o: Consider delaying bone treatment until androgen deprivation has ended
Consider an oral bisphosphonate during androgen deprivation
Consider following pain symptoms in place of assessing bone mineral density
Consider androgen deprivation as protection against further bone loss
explanation:
Testosterone suppression accelerates bone loss. For established osteoporosis on androgen deprivation, **consider an oral bisphosphonate during therapy** after assessing suitability and renal function.

**A. Wait for treatment to end.** Fracture risk is present while testosterone remains suppressed.
**B. Oral bisphosphonate.** Treating osteoporosis complements falls prevention, nutrition and bone density assessment.
**C. Follow pain instead of bone density.** Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic until fracture, so pain is an inadequate measure.
**D. Assume hormonal protection.** Androgen deprivation adds to skeletal risk.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1417.

q: Biochemical recurrence is detected after radical prostatectomy. Which measure is useful for monitoring and deciding when to initiate treatment?
o: The passage of six months after surgery without new complaints
The PSA-doubling time assessed during follow-up after radical prostatectomy
The degree of recovery of urinary continence after surgery
The absence of local pain at a postoperative follow-up visit
explanation:
A rising PSA after prostatectomy can detect recurrent disease before symptoms appear. **PSA doubling time** quantifies the pace of biochemical recurrence and helps guide treatment timing.

**A. Six symptom-free months.** Elapsed time alone says little about how quickly recurrent disease is growing.
**B. PSA doubling time.** Serial measurements distinguish a rapid rise from a more indolent biochemical course.
**C. Urinary continence recovery.** Continence reflects postoperative function, not tumor kinetics.
**D. No local pain.** Biochemical recurrence commonly precedes local symptoms.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1416.

q: A 72-year-old man with localized prostate cancer is considering active surveillance rather than immediate treatment. He has T1c disease, PSA 4.8 ng/mL, Gleason score 6, and 3 of 12 positive biopsy cores. His hypertension is controlled and he is otherwise healthy. He worries about missing the opportunity for curative treatment. Which counseling statement accords with Hazzard?
o: Regular PSA testing and biopsies make progression before treatment a negligible concern
Surveillance uses low-intensity follow-up with an expectation of palliative rather than curative treatment
Local or metastatic progression remains a risk before treatment despite careful monitoring
Surveillance is intended for disease expected to progress to metastases despite curative treatment
explanation:
Active surveillance aims to defer treatment for low-risk prostate cancer while preserving the chance of cure. **Local or metastatic progression remains possible despite careful monitoring**, so the plan and triggers need discussion.

**A. Negligible progression risk.** Serial tests reduce uncertainty but cannot guarantee detection before significant progression.
**B. Low-intensity palliation.** That description fits watchful waiting rather than a surveillance plan with potential curative treatment.
**C. Residual risk during surveillance.** PSA, examination and periodic biopsy can detect worsening while still leaving some chance of missing a curative window.
**D. Expected metastasis despite curative therapy.** Surveillance is selected for relatively favorable disease, not disease assumed to metastasize regardless of treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1414.

q: An 85-year-old man with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease has a PSA of 12 ng/mL and an abnormal digital rectal examination. Biopsy reveals prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 7. He has been hospitalized twice this year for heart-failure exacerbations, needs help with activities of daily living, and has an estimated life expectancy of 2–3 years. He has no urinary symptoms. His care plan is to defer cancer treatment until symptomatic disease develops. Which strategy does this describe?
o: Definitive treatment by radical prostatectomy
Definitive treatment by external beam radiation
Watchful waiting with treatment for symptomatic disease
Active surveillance with delayed potentially curative treatment
explanation:
Severe competing illness and a short life expectancy favor a symptom-directed strategy when that matches the patient’s goals. **Deferring treatment until symptomatic disease is watchful waiting**.

**A. Radical prostatectomy.** Surgery would begin curative-intent local treatment immediately.
**B. External-beam radiation.** Definitive irradiation treats the localized cancer before symptoms emerge.
**C. Watchful waiting.** Treatment is reserved for symptoms that affect comfort or function.
**D. Active surveillance.** More intensive monitoring aims to detect progression early enough for delayed cure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1414.

q: A 77-year-old man has received androgen deprivation therapy for eight months. His son reports recent personality changes, irritability, and confusion fluctuating through the day. Oxybutynin was recently started for urinary urgency, and he takes diphenhydramine for sleep. He was previously cognitively well, and examination shows mild dehydration. Which interpretation of the oxybutynin–diphenhydramine combination matches Beers 2023?
o: Combined anticholinergic exposure reduces delirium risk while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases both delirium risk and fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure improves cognition while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases cognitive risk while reducing fall risk
explanation:
Oxybutynin and diphenhydramine have different uses but both block muscarinic signaling. Their anticholinergic effects add together.

**The combination increases risk of both delirium and falls.** Recent exposure is worth investigating alongside dehydration in a patient with fluctuating confusion.

**A. Less delirium and more falls.** Falls are a concern, and the added anticholinergic burden can also provoke confusion.
**B. More delirium and more falls.** Concurrent strong anticholinergics can worsen cognition and increase the chance of a fall.
**C. Better cognition and more falls.** Blocking muscarinic signaling can impair cognition, particularly in a susceptible older adult.
**D. Greater cognitive risk and fewer falls.** Cognitive risk rises, and the interaction also increases fall risk.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2066, 2070, 2074.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2070, 2074, Tables 3, 5, 7

q: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer diagnosed six months ago has worsening fatigue, reduced appetite, and mild dyspnea over a month. Chemotherapy is controlling the disease, but her ECOG performance status has declined from 1 to 2. Her daughter is concerned about quality of life. Alongside assessment of the new symptoms, which approach to palliative care is supported by Hazzard?
o: Introduce palliative care alongside the ongoing oncology treatment
Postpone palliative care until chemotherapy has been discontinued
Postpone palliative care until progression is shown on imaging
Postpone palliative care until a terminal prognosis is certified
explanation:
Palliative care can address fatigue, breathlessness, appetite and caregiver concerns during active cancer treatment. A patient can benefit even when chemotherapy is controlling the tumor.
**Introduce palliative care now alongside oncology care and evaluate the new symptoms.**

**A. Concurrent care** The team can relieve symptoms, review what the patient wants to remain able to do and coordinate support.
**B. After chemotherapy stops** Palliative input is compatible with ongoing chemotherapy.
**C. After imaging progression** Declining function and quality of life are already reasons to act despite a tumor response.
**D. After terminal certification** Certification is a US hospice issue. It is unnecessary for palliative consultation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1045, 1047.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 81-year-old man has a 2 cm breast mass. Biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma that is estrogen-receptor positive, progesterone-receptor positive, and HER2 negative. He has mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 24/30), lives independently with home-aide support, and has well-controlled diabetes and hypertension. Geriatric assessment shows mild functional limitations and good social support. Which drug does Hazzard prefer for adjuvant endocrine therapy in men?
o: Anastrozole endocrine therapy
Tamoxifen endocrine therapy
Fulvestrant endocrine therapy
LHRH agonist therapy
explanation:

q: A 72-year-old woman asks whether dietary restriction has been shown to prolong human life, as it has in some animal studies. How does Hazzard describe the human evidence?

**Human studies show improved cardiovascular measures, including blood pressure and lipid profile. A longer human lifespan has yet to be demonstrated.**

**B. Improved cardiovascular measures with uncertain longevity.** These are measurable risk factors. Knowing that they improved does not tell the woman how many years the diet might add.

q: An 85-year-old man with mild dementia has developed cataracts, hearing loss, mild heart failure, and osteoarthritis during the past year. His family asks why several problems have appeared together. Which concept in Hazzard provides a biological framework for age-related changes across organ systems?
o: Aging is understood as disease that affects several organ systems.
Aging is understood as development directly shaped by natural selection.
Aging is understood as coordinated change across multiple organ systems.
Aging is understood as increased lifespan following a beneficial intervention.
explanation:
Coordinated aging means that several tissues can lose function over the same part of life. The timing can have a shared biological basis even when each illness has its own immediate causes.

**Aging across organ systems helps explain why cataracts, hearing loss and joint disease can cluster in the same patient. In rodents, changing food intake delayed age-related changes in several quite different tissues together.**

**A. A multisystem disease.** Aging also produces changes outside disease categories, such as declining aerobic capacity. A list of diagnoses captures only part of the process.
**B. A developmental program shaped by selection.** Development builds a functioning young adult. Selection exerts much weaker pressure to preserve function at ages rarely reached in a species' natural environment.
**C. Coordinated change across organs.** The lens, inner ear and joints can all lose function during late life. Recognizing the shared timing still leaves each new symptom to be assessed on its merits.
**D. Longer lifespan after any beneficial intervention.** Treating one lethal illness can prolong life. That result alone says little about the pace of change in the patient's other organs.

q: A 78-year-old woman asks why her 82-year-old husband developed Alzheimer disease while she has cognitive impairment. She wonders whether aging and Alzheimer disease are the same process. Which explanation accords with Hazzard's definition of aging?

Aging protects against degenerative disease, with Alzheimer disease representing loss of that protection.
explanation:
Biological aging changes how well the body maintains function and increases vulnerability to illness. Alzheimer disease is a specific disorder that becomes more common in later life.

**Aging increases susceptibility to Alzheimer disease while remaining a distinct process. The woman's age and her husband's diagnosis cannot identify the cause of her own cognitive impairment.**

**A. A neurologic disease with Alzheimer stages.** Aging also affects the lens, joints, muscles and other organs. It has no Alzheimer disease staging sequence.
**B. An early form of Alzheimer disease.** The severity of a memory complaint alone cannot show that Alzheimer pathology is present. Cognitive impairment in later life requires its own assessment.
**C. Greater susceptibility to disease.** Older age raises the risk of Alzheimer disease, but people of similar ages can have different cognitive outcomes.
**D. Protection against degenerative disease.** The direction of the age association is reversed here. Vulnerability to degenerative illnesses generally increases as physiologic function declines.

q: A healthy 68-year-old retired professor takes no medications and has a family history of longevity. At a preventive visit, she asks why natural selection has not eliminated aging despite its contribution to death. Which explanation is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Selection weakens at rarely reached ages, leaving less protection against late-life loss of function
Selection favors late-life loss of function because that deterioration improves survival at ages beyond reproduction
Selection strengthens as age increases, directing maintenance of bodily function toward the later years of life
Selection shapes late-life deterioration as it shapes embryonic development, creating a program that improves function
explanation:
Natural selection acts when inherited differences change an individual's chances of surviving and reproducing. A trait expressed only at an age few animals reach has fewer opportunities to affect the next generation.

**Selection weakens at rarely reached ages, leaving less evolutionary pressure to preserve late-life function. A cataract that appears at two years, for example, affects few mice in the wild.**

**A. Weaker selection at rarely reached ages.** An inherited variant that impairs vision early can cost a mouse survival or offspring. The same impairment appearing very late has far less effect on the variant's frequency.
**B. Selection favors deterioration itself.** Late deterioration can persist because its evolutionary cost is small. No survival benefit from losing function is required.
**C. Selection strengthens with age.** Fewer members of the species survive to advanced ages in nature. That reduces the opportunity for selection to preserve function at those ages.
**D. A late-life program like embryonic development.** Embryonic development must produce a viable individual before reproduction. Weak selection in late life allows deterioration without a program that improves function.

q: A 74-year-old man asks about a commercial supplement claimed to reverse aging in humans. He presents a mouse study and a biological pathway affected by the substance. What evidence is needed to substantiate this clinical claim?
o: An animal study showing lifespan extension with the substance
Classification as a supplement exempt from drug regulatory requirements
A human clinical study of the claimed effect and safety
A human clinical study showing an improved response to vaccination
explanation:
A claim that a supplement reverses human aging concerns a broad change in health over time. To test it, the investigators must define what reversal would look like, measure it in people and document harms.

**A human clinical study must test the claimed effect and its safety. Longer survival in mice and a plausible biological pathway are reasons to investigate the supplement, but neither measures what happens to people who take it.**

**A. Longer lifespan in an animal study.** Mouse survival measures an effect in mice. It cannot predict both reversal of human aging and safety at human exposures.
**B. Classification as a supplement.** A marketing or regulatory category supplies no measurements of benefit or adverse effects in people.
**C. Human testing of the claim and safety.** The study needs outcomes that capture the proposed change in aging and a comparison that allows benefits and harms to be attributed to treatment.
**D. A better human vaccine response.** Improved response to vaccination would demonstrate an effect on one immune function. It leaves the broader claim of reversing aging untested.

**Aging promotes disease and also produces changes outside disease categories. The sisters' diagnosis counts therefore capture only part of how aging affects each of them.**

**A. Greater disease risk and other changes.** For example, aging can increase susceptibility to arthritis while also reducing muscle strength. Counting illnesses misses some of these functional changes.
**B. A disease defined by accumulated diagnoses.** Many diseases also occur in young people, and an older person can lose function without acquiring a new diagnosis. The diagnosis count cannot define aging.

q: A 76-year-old retired biologist visits your clinic and asks about the fundamental difference between aging and development, noting that both involve changes in the body over time. He's curious about why development proceeds so precisely while aging seems more variable. What is the key biological distinction?
o: Development and aging are both directed by equally strong natural selection, with aging following the same precise genetic program
Development is directly shaped by natural selection while aging occurs beyond the reach of strong selective pressure
Development is less strongly shaped by natural selection than aging, because selective pressure rises steadily after reproduction
Development proceeds without natural selection, while aging is tightly programmed to improve survival after the reproductive years
explanation:
Development turns a fertilized egg into a functioning young adult. A harmful variant that disrupts this process affects carriers early, when it can sharply reduce their chances of leaving offspring.

**Natural selection directly shapes development and exerts much weaker pressure at ages rarely reached in nature. Late-acting harmful variants can therefore persist more readily than variants that prevent normal development.**

**A. Equally strong selection throughout life.** A defect that prevents an animal from reaching reproductive age faces strong selection. One that impairs function only very late faces much less.
**B. Strong selection in development, weaker selection late.** The chance of a variant affecting reproduction depends on when its effects appear. This difference helps explain the precision of development and the variability of late decline.
**C. Selection grows stronger after reproduction.** As fewer individuals survive to a given age, selection has fewer opportunities to act on traits expressed for the first time at that age.
**D. Unselected development and programmed late decline.** Selection favors development that produces viable adults. Late-life decline can emerge as the strength of selection falls, without a program that promotes deterioration.

**C. An underlying process across systems.** Parallel changes in the kidney, lens and brain support a common influence on when disease and functional losses appear.
**D. One clinically identifiable disease.** Age-related changes include loss of physiological capacity as well as diseases. A single diagnosis cannot encompass this range.

o: A standard-dose quadrivalent vaccine, with greater efficacy than the high-dose preparation
A high-dose quadrivalent vaccine, with greater efficacy than the standard-dose preparation
A standard-dose quadrivalent vaccine, with equivalent efficacy to the high-dose preparation
A high-dose quadrivalent vaccine, with lower efficacy than the standard-dose preparation
explanation:
High-dose influenza vaccine delivers more antigen to stimulate an immune response in older adults. Vaccine efficacy here means prevention of influenza, not protection against every respiratory infection.
**High dose is the appropriate choice. In adults 65 and older, high dose improved protection against laboratory-confirmed influenza in the pivotal comparison with standard dose.**

**A. Standard dose more effective.** This reverses the direction of the efficacy comparison.
**B. High dose more effective.** High-dose trivalent vaccine reduced laboratory-confirmed influenza by 24.2% relative to standard-dose trivalent vaccine. For shared strains, high-dose quadrivalent vaccine produced antibody responses comparable to high-dose trivalent vaccine.
**C. Equivalent efficacy.** The measured advantage favored the high-dose formulation even though breakthrough infections can occur.
**D. High dose less effective.** Increasing the antigen dose improved the measured immune response in this comparison.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 165 and 1256. FDA Fluzone High-Dose Quadrivalent prescribing information, §§14.1–14.2.
Key note: Hazzard p. 1256 attributes the 24.2% efficacy advantage to the quadrivalent product. The efficacy trial compared trivalent products. Quadrivalent licensure relied on immunogenicity bridging.

q: A 68-year-old man underwent kidney transplantation five years ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone 5 mg daily. Three days ago, burning pain developed on the right chest, followed by vesicles in the T4–T6 dermatomes. Which mechanism most likely explains this presentation?
o: Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus following a new exposure.
Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus with impaired cellular immunity.
Bacterial infection superimposed on a pre-existing inflammatory dermatitis.
Drug-induced photosensitivity producing an inflammatory eruption on exposed skin.
explanation:
Shingles typically presents with pain followed by grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. In this immunosuppressed transplant recipient, **reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus as cellular immune control declines** fits the course.

**A. Primary varicella.** First infection typically causes a generalized chickenpox eruption rather than localized dermatomal pain and vesicles.
**B. Reactivation.** Cell-mediated immunity normally restrains latent VZV. Immunosuppression increases susceptibility to zoster.
**C. Bacterial superinfection.** It can complicate damaged skin but does not explain the characteristic initial pain and dermatomal vesicles.
**D. Photosensitivity.** A photosensitive eruption follows light exposure rather than a cluster of adjacent thoracic dermatomes.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1724–1725.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

q: A 75-year-old woman with well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate attends for influenza vaccination. She has no other major comorbidities and asks about research in which rapamycin improved vaccine responses in older adults. Which pathway effect does Hazzard identify in this research?
o: Activation of mTOR signaling, particularly through the TORC1 complex
Inhibition of mTOR signaling, particularly through the TORC1 complex
Activation of mTOR signaling through increased protein translation
Stimulation of TORC1 signaling through increased nutrient sensing
explanation:
TORC1 helps cells translate nutrient and growth signals into protein synthesis. Blocking this complex can also change the response of immune cells to a vaccine.

**Inhibition of TORC1 was associated with a stronger antibody response to influenza vaccination.** Older volunteers in the human trial received low-dose everolimus (RAD001), a derivative of rapamycin. This finding does not provide an indication to add an immunosuppressant for this woman's routine vaccination.

**A. Activate TORC1.** Activating the complex promotes growth signaling in the opposite direction to the intervention.
**B. Inhibit TORC1.** Everolimus suppresses signaling through this complex. The measured benefit concerned the antibody response after vaccination.
**C. Activate mTOR by increasing translation.** Enhanced protein translation is a downstream effect of active TORC1. The intervention inhibited the pathway.
**D. Stimulate nutrient sensing.** Nutrients normally activate TORC1 when resources are abundant. Greater activation does not explain the drug effect.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 60. Mannick et al., Science Translational Medicine 2014, doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.3009892.

q: Why were enhanced influenza vaccines, such as the MF59-adjuvanted vaccine, developed for older adults?
o: To counter an excessive response to standard-dose vaccination in older age
To reduce an increased immune response associated with underlying comorbidities
To improve the weaker response to standard-dose vaccination in older adults
To lower the antibody response induced by standard-dose influenza vaccination
explanation:
Aging can weaken the antibody response to standard-dose influenza vaccine and leave older adults less well protected. **MF59 is an adjuvant added to strengthen the immune response to vaccine antigens.**

**A. Counter an excessive response.** Older adults generally mount a weaker response to standard-dose vaccine than younger adults.
**B. Suppress a response caused by comorbidity.** Chronic disease increases the risk of severe influenza. It creates no general need to suppress vaccine responses.
**C. Improve the response to standard dose.** MF59 enhances the response to the vaccine antigens without increasing the amount of antigen per strain.
**D. Lower antibody production.** Enhanced formulations aim to raise antibody levels. High-dose vaccines pursue this goal by increasing the amount of antigen per strain.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1735.
ref: Hazzard Ch 108 — INFLUENZA, COVID-19, AND OTHER RESPIRATORY VIRUSES
chapterTitle: Influenza, COVID-19, and Other Respiratory Viruses

q: אישה בת 70 עם סוכרת מסוג 2 המאוזנת על metformin שואלת על clinical trials עתידיים המכוונים לתהליכי הזדקנות. היא מתעניינת ב-interventions שעשויים לשפר את תפקוד מערכת החיסון שלה ואת ה-healthspan הכולל. על בסיס המחקר הנוכחי, מה המנגנון העיקרי שבאמצעותו metformin עשוי לשפר את התגובה החיסונית במבוגרים מבוגרים?
o: הגברת שגשוג תאי T ישירות, ללא שינוי במסלולי חישת אנרגיה או בפעילות TORC1
אקטיבציה של AMP kinase המובילה לעיכוב TORC1 והפחתת דלקת
גירוי יצירת תאי גזע במח העצם כמנגנון העיקרי לשיפור התגובה החיסונית במבוגרים
הגברת הפרשת הורמון גדילה כמנגנון העיקרי לשיפור התגובה החיסונית במבוגרים
explanation:
מטפורמין היא תרופה לטיפול בסוכרת המשפיעה על חישת האנרגיה בתא. מחקר ההזדקנות בוחן אם השפעה מטבולית זו יכולה לשפר גם את תפקוד מערכת החיסון.
**מטפורמין מפעילה את האנזים AMPK, ובעקבות זאת מעכבת את TORC1. למסלול הזה יש השפעות אפשריות גם על הדלקת הכרונית הקשורה לגיל.**

**A. שגשוג ישיר של תאי T.** המנגנון הנחקר מערב חישת אנרגיה ושינוי בפעילות TORC1. פעולה ישירה על קצב החלוקה של תאי T אינה מסבירה זאת.
**B. הפעלת AMPK ועיכוב TORC1.** המסלול משפיע על בקרת הגדילה והתרגום של חלבונים. ירידה באיתות דלקתי עשויה לתרום להשפעה החיסונית. התועלת הקלינית בהתוויה זו עדיין נחקרת.
**C. גירוי ייצור תאי גזע במח העצם.** שינויים בתאי גזע אכן מתרחשים בהזדקנות, אך יצירה מוגברת שלהם אינה המנגנון המוצע למטפורמין.
**D. הגברת הפרשת הורמון גדילה.** הגברת הפרשת ההורמון אינה מסבירה את הפעלת AMPK ואת עיכוב TORC1.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 60.
label: Source: hazzard marked .pdf · 60, Ch 3

q: A 78-year-old man with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia presents with vesicular lesions involving several dermatomes over his trunk and back. He completed CLL treatment two years ago and remains in remission. His CD4+ count is 180 cells/μL. Which immune impairment is most relevant to susceptibility to herpes zoster in this presentation?
o: Impairment of humoral immunity and antibody production
Impairment of neutrophil function and directed chemotaxis
Impairment of VZV-specific T-cell-mediated immunity
Impairment of complement-system activation and function
explanation:
Control of latent varicella-zoster virus relies particularly on cellular immunity. Multidermatomal zoster and a low CD4 count point to **impaired VZV-specific T-cell-mediated immunity**.

**A. Humoral immunity.** Antibody deficiency can occur in CLL, but it is not the main mechanism controlling latent VZV.
**B. Neutrophil chemotaxis.** Neutrophils are important in other infections. A low CD4 count identifies a different immune compartment.
**C. VZV-specific T cells.** Weak cellular surveillance allows latent virus to reactivate and can accompany more extensive zoster.
**D. Complement activation.** Complement deficiency is not the characteristic immune defect in this presentation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 60, 1724.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

q: A 66-year-old woman received high-dose influenza vaccine in October. In March she asks about waning antibodies. She has diabetes and hypertension, takes an ACE inhibitor and a statin, and had no adverse vaccine reaction. Which statement accurately explains the influenza-vaccination recommendation described in Hazzard?
o: Annual vaccination is discouraged because it increases influenza-related morbidity and mortality
Annual vaccination is deferred because older adults are less affected by influenza epidemics
Annual vaccination is recommended because it decreases influenza-related morbidity and mortality
High-dose vaccination is preferred because it produces a weaker immunogenic response
explanation:
Influenza epidemics disproportionately affect older adults. Seasonal vaccination reduces illness and death even though the response to a dose can wane over time.
**Continue annual vaccination because it reduces influenza-related morbidity and mortality.**

**A. Annual vaccination increases harm.** The effect on influenza-related illness and death runs in the opposite direction.
**B. Older adults are less affected.** Older adults are especially vulnerable to severe outcomes during epidemics.
**C. Annual vaccination reduces disease burden.** The seasonal schedule is appropriate despite waning antibodies after the October dose.
**D. High dose weakens immunity.** The high-dose formulation can elicit a stronger immune response in older recipients.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 165, Influenza Vaccination.

q: A person who has never been infected with varicella-zoster virus is exposed to a herpes zoster rash. Which description correctly distinguishes primary infection from reactivation in this setting?
o: Primary infection presenting as herpes zoster after this exposure
Primary infection presenting as varicella after this exposure
Reactivation of latent virus presenting as varicella after exposure
Reactivation of latent virus presenting as herpes zoster after exposure
explanation:
Varicella and zoster are different clinical stages of VZV infection. In a person without previous infection or immunity, **a first infection after exposure can present as varicella**. Zoster requires pre-existing latent infection.

**A. Primary infection as zoster.** Shingles is reactivation, not the usual manifestation of first infection.
**B. Primary infection as varicella.** A susceptible person's first clinical illness is chickenpox.
**C. Reactivation as varicella.** Reactivation presupposes latency and typically presents as shingles.
**D. Reactivation as zoster from this exposure.** That describes a person with previous infection, not the infection-naive person in the stem.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1725.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

q: A 69-year-old woman with controlled rheumatoid arthritis takes methotrexate and prednisone 5 mg daily. She develops herpes zoster on her left shoulder and starts oral acyclovir at rash onset. The rash heals, but burning pain in the affected area continues to disrupt sleep more than 90 days after rash onset. Which diagnosis matches this course?
o: Prodromal dermatomal pain preceding the zoster eruption
Postherpetic neuralgia following the zoster eruption
Zoster sine herpete without a cutaneous eruption
Acute neuritis during the initial zoster eruption
explanation:
Zoster can injure sensory nerves, leaving burning pain in the same dermatome after the skin heals. **Pain persisting more than 90 days after rash onset is postherpetic neuralgia** in this vignette.

**A. Prodromal pain.** This precedes the eruption. Her pain persists long afterward.
**B. Postherpetic neuralgia.** The location, neuropathic quality and persistence beyond the acute illness fit.
**C. Zoster sine herpete.** This refers to zoster without a visible eruption. She had a documented rash.
**D. Acute neuritis.** This occurs during the initial episode and does not describe pain persisting beyond 90 days.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1725–1726.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

q: A 74-year-old man asks about recombinant zoster vaccine. According to Hazzard, what is the role of its adjuvant?
o: To directly inhibit viral replication within the sensory ganglia
To attenuate a live virus for replication in the recipient
To enhance the innate immune response to the vaccine antigen
To replace the antigen with prepared virus-neutralizing antibodies
explanation:
Recombinant zoster vaccine contains a varicella-zoster virus surface protein and an adjuvant called AS01B. The protein gives the immune system a specific target.
**The adjuvant stimulates the innate response, strengthening the response to the vaccine antigen.**

**A. Inhibit viral replication.** This describes an antiviral drug effect. The adjuvant does not treat virus in a sensory ganglion.
**B. Attenuate a live virus.** This recombinant vaccine presents a protein and contains no replicating vaccine virus.
**C. Enhance innate activation.** AS01B amplifies the response to the glycoprotein E antigen.
**D. Provide ready-made antibodies.** Passive immunization supplies antibodies. This vaccine induces the recipient's own response.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1728, Recombinant Zoster Vaccine.

q: גבר בן 78 ממוצא רוסי מגיע למיון עם נפילה שלישית תוך חודשיים. אשתו מדווחת שהוא הולך ונעשה חסר יציבות, מבולבל לעיתים, ועם תיאבון ירוד. בעברו: hypertension ו-COPD. מעשן 2 קופסאות ביום ושותה וודקה באופן קבוע. סימנים חיוניים: BP 160/90, HR 88, חום 36.8°C. בבדיקה פיזיקלית: שיניים במצב ירוד, בצקת בגפיים תחתונות דו-צדדית ו-tremor קל. איזה גורם תורם באופן המשמעותי ביותר לעלייה בסיכון התמותה שלו בהשוואה לבנות גילו?
o: נטייה גנטית למחלות קרדיווסקולריות
השפעות משולבות של עישון וצריכת אלכוהול
היעדר ההגנה של אסטרוגן
קצב מטבולי בסיסי גבוה יותר
explanation:
**השילוב של עישון כבד וצריכת אלכוהול** הוא גורם תמותה בר־שינוי ומוכר בדפוסים ההיסטוריים המתוארים בגברים ברוסיה. הנפילות והבלבול דורשים בירור רפואי כעת.

**א. נטייה גנטית.** אין מידע משפחתי שמכמת נטייה כזו אצל המטופל.
**ב. טבק ואלכוהול.** שתי החשיפות מעלות סיכון למחלות לב, סרטן ופגיעות נוספות, ואלכוהול מוסיף סיכון לפציעה.
**ג. אסטרוגן.** פערי תמותה המשתנים בין תקופות ואוכלוסיות אינם מוסברים על ידי הורמון אחד.
**ד. קצב חילוף חומרים.** אין בתיאור עדות שזהו הגורם המכריע.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 5, עמ׳ 85–86, השוואות היסטוריות בין המינים.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: אישה בת 82 יפנית מגיעה להערכה גריאטרית שגרתית. היא מעולם לא עישנה, שומרת על תזונה יפנית מסורתית, ונוטלת תרופות לאוסטאופורוזיס ו-hypertension קלה. בתה שואלת מדוע אמה צפויה לחיות זמן משמעותי יותר מאביה המנוח, שנפטר בגיל 74. על בסיס נתונים אפידמיולוגיים, מה מסביר בצורה הטובה ביותר את פער תוחלת החיים המגדרי המתמשך ביפן?
o: לנשים יש גישה טובה יותר לשירותי בריאות מונעים
לגברים היו היסטורית שיעורי עישון גבוהים בהרבה בעוד שנשים כמעט ולא עישנו
לנשים יש רשתות תמיכה חברתית חזקות יותר
גברים עוסקים במקצועות מסוכנים פיזית יותר
explanation:
**פערי העישון ההיסטוריים בין גברים לנשים ביפן** תרמו לפער תמותה בין המינים. תמותה ממחלות הקשורות בטבק מופיעה שנים לאחר החשיפה.

**א. גישה לרפואה מונעת.** לא הוצג הבדל בגישה המסביר את הדפוס.
**ב. חשיפה היסטורית שונה לטבק.** שיעור עישון נמוך בהרבה בנשים צמצם את נטל התמותה המיוחס לעישון באותם שנתונים.
**ג. תמיכה חברתית.** יכולה להשפיע על בריאות, אך אינה החשיפה ההיסטורית המרכזית בהשוואה.
**ד. עבודה מסוכנת.** תאונות עבודה אינן מסבירות לבדן את פער התמותה מהמחלות הכרוניות הנלוות לעישון.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 5, עמ׳ 86–87.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: אישה בת 68 מגיעה לגריאטר שלה עם אבחנה חדשה של סרטן ריאות. היא התחילה לעשן בגיל 30, בשנת 1985, והפסיקה לפני 5 שנים. בעלה, שעישן למשך אותו פרק זמן אך התחיל מוקדם יותר, נפטר מסרטן ריאות לפני שנתיים. בהתבסס על מגמות אפידמיולוגיות, איזה תופעה ממחיש המקרה שלה?
o: נשים רגישות יותר לסרטנים הקשורים לטבק
שיעור סרטן הריאות עולה באופן שווה בשני המינים
התמותה של נשים ממחלות הקשורות לעישון יורדת לאט יותר מאשר של גברים
חשיפה לעשן סביל גורמת יותר סרטן בנשים
explanation:
**הירידה בתמותה המיוחסת לטבק הופיעה מאוחר יותר בנשים** באוכלוסיות שבהן גל העישון הנשי התחיל מאוחר יותר. זוהי מגמה לפי שנתון ולא מסקנה מהשוואת שני בני זוג.

**א. רגישות נשית מוגברת.** אין צורך להניח רגישות ביולוגית שונה כדי להסביר את העיתוי.
**ב. עלייה זהה בשני המינים.** הגלים לא הגיעו לשיא באותו זמן.
**ג. ירידה מאוחרת יותר בנשים.** תקופת החביון והגמילה המאוחרת בחלק מהשנתונים משאירות תמותה מוגברת לזמן ממושך יותר.
**ד. עישון פסיבי.** המקרה מתאר עישון פעיל ממושך.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 86–87, תרשים 5-4.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: גבר שוודי בן 75 מגיע לביקור בריאות שנתי. הוא הפסיק לעשן לפני 10 שנים לאחר היסטוריה של 40 שנות עישון, ושותה אלכוהול מדי פעם. הוא שואל על תוחלת החיים שלו בהשוואה לאשתו בת אותו הגיל. בהתבסס על מגמות אפידמיולוגיות עדכניות, מה המידע שאמור להנחות את הייעוץ?
o: פער תוחלת החיים בין המינים היה יציב על 7-8 שנים במשך עשורים
הפער גדל עקב אורח חיים בריא יותר של נשים
הפער מצטמצם מאז שנות ה-1980 ועומד כיום על כ-3.5 שנים
הפער משתנה באופן בלתי צפוי ולא ניתן להעריכו
explanation:
**בשוודיה הצטמצם הפער מאז שנות השמונים, לכ־3.5 שנים בתקופה שתוארה בספר.** זהו פער ממוצע בתוחלת חיים באוכלוסייה ואינו תחזית לזוג מסוים בגיל 75.

**א. פער קבוע של 7–8 שנים.** הנתונים ההיסטוריים מצביעים על מגמת שינוי.
**ב. פער הולך וגדל.** בשוודיה נצפתה בתקופה המתוארת מגמה הפוכה.
**ג. הצטמצמות לכ־3.5 שנים.** זו התשובה המתייחסת לנקודת הזמן של הנתונים ולשינויים בדפוסי התמותה.
**ד. שינוי בלתי ניתן לתיאור.** אפשר למדוד מגמות בדיעבד, גם כשאין ודאות לגבי העתיד.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 5, עמ׳ 85–87, נתוני שוודיה בתקופת הספר.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: אישה בת 83 עם mild cognitive impairment מובאת על ידי משפחתה לסקירת תרופות. היא נוטלת 8 תרופות וחוותה 2 falls לאחרונה. בתה מזכירה שקראה שנשים חיות בדרך כלל יותר מגברים ושואלת האם המשמעות היא שאמה תצטרך תכנון טיפול ארוך טווח. איזה גורם משפיע באופן המשמעותי ביותר על ההשלכות המעשיות של יתרון האורך-חיים הנשי בטיפול גריאטרי?
o: לנשים שיעורים נמוכים יותר של מחלות כרוניות
נשים מבלות יותר שנים בבריאות לקויה למרות תוחלת חיים ארוכה יותר
לנשים יש adherence טוב יותר לתרופות
לנשים מערכת חיסון חזקה יותר
explanation:
**נשים חיות בממוצע יותר שנים עם מחלה או מוגבלות.** אצל המטופלת יש לבסס תכנון אישי על הנפילות, ריבוי התרופות, התפקוד והתמיכה הזמינה.

**א. פחות מחלות כרוניות.** הישרדות ארוכה יותר יכולה דווקא להאריך את משך החיים עם מצבים כרוניים.
**ב. שנים רבות יותר בבריאות לקויה.** תוחלת חיים אינה זהה לתוחלת חיים ללא מוגבלות, ולכן נדרשת היערכות לטיפול מתמשך.
**ג. היענות טובה יותר.** היענות אישית אינה מסבירה את פער תוחלת החיים הבריאה.
**ד. מערכת חיסון חזקה.** מנגנון יחיד זה אינו מאפשר לחזות צרכים תפקודיים.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 27, 92.

q: גבר בן 71 מגיע עם exacerbation של COPD. יש לו היסטוריה של 50 pack-year של עישון והפסיק לעשן לפני 3 שנים. אשתו, שמעולם לא עישנה, שואלת מדוע מחלות נשימה נראות שכיחות יותר בגברים מהדור שלהם. מה מסביר בצורה הטובה ביותר את הדפוס האפידמיולוגי הזה?
o: לגברים יש מערכת נשימה חלשה יותר מטבעה
דפוסי העישון ההיסטוריים מראים שגברים אימצו שימוש בטבק מוקדם יותר ובאופן מאסיבי יותר
חשיפות תעסוקתיות משפיעות רק על גברים
גברים מקבלים טיפול פחות אגרסיבי עבור תסמיני נשימה
explanation:
**גברים באותם שנתוני לידה החלו לעשן מוקדם יותר ובשיעורים גבוהים יותר.** לכן חשיפה מצטברת לטבק תרמה לעודף COPD ותמותה ממחלות נשימה.

**א. מערכת נשימה חלשה מלידה.** הבדלים ביולוגיים אינם מסבירים את השינוי לפי שנתון וחשיפה.
**ב. דפוסי עישון היסטוריים.** שנות עישון רבות יותר מעלות את הסיכון לנזק חסימתי מצטבר.
**ג. חשיפה תעסוקתית רק בגברים.** גם נשים נחשפות בעבודה, וחשיפה תעסוקתית אינה ההסבר המרכזי כאן.
**ד. טיפול פחות אינטנסיבי.** אין במידע השוואה טיפולית התומכת בהסבר זה.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 86–87, תרשים 5-4.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
