q: אישה בת 79 עם סוכרת, hypertension ואוסטאופורוזיס שואלת את הגריאטר שלה מדוע סביר שתחיה יותר מגברים בגילה למרות שיש לה מספר מחלות כרוניות. בנה מציין שגברים במשפחתם נוטים למות צעירים יותר אך עם פחות ביקורי רופא. איזה תופעה מסבירה בצורה הטובה ביותר את הפרדוקס הזה?
o: לנשים יש הגנה גנטית מפני מחלות cardiovascular
נשים משתמשות בשירותי הבריאות ביעילות רבה יותר למניעה
גברים חווים יותר אירועים חריפים מסכני חיים בעוד שנשים סובלות ממחלות כרוניות
נשים מטבוליזות תרופות ביעילות רבה יותר
explanation:
**הבדלים בדפוסי התחלואה והתמותה** מאפשרים לנשים לחיות זמן רב יותר גם כאשר נטל המחלה הכרונית שלהן משמעותי. מדובר בדפוס אוכלוסייתי.

**א. הגנה גנטית מפני מחלות לב.** גם נשים לוקות במחלות לב, וסיבות הפער מרובות.
**ב. יעילות השימוש בשירותים.** מספר ביקורים אינו מודד יעילות ואינו מסביר לבדו הבדלי תמותה.
**ג. יותר מחלות קטלניות מוקדמות בגברים.** תמותה מוקדמת יותר בגברים מתקיימת לצד שנים רבות יותר עם מחלה או מוגבלות בנשים.
**ד. מטבוליזם יעיל של תרופות.** קצב פירוק תרופות אינו הסבר כללי להבדל בין המינים.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 2, עמ׳ 27–29.

q: אישה בת 76 מגיעה לביקורת שגרתית. עישנה בין גיל 25 ל-60 והפסיקה לפני 16 שנה. היא מודאגת מסיכון לסרטן ריאות לאחר שקראה כי הוא כיום הגורם המוביל לתמותה מסרטן בקרב נשים. איזה מגמה משקפת את דאגתה?
o: עלייה בחשיפה לקרצינוגנים סביבתיים בקרב נשים
פיק מאוחר יותר של תמותה הקשורה לעישון בנשים בהשוואה לגברים
נטייה גנטית לסרטן ריאות שהופכת בולטת יותר
שיפור ביכולות האבחנה המאפשר זיהוי יותר מקרים
explanation:
**שיא התמותה הקשורה לעישון הגיע מאוחר יותר בנשים.** בדורות המתוארים נשים החלו לעשן בשיעורים גבוהים מאוחר יותר, ותמותה מסרטן ריאות מפגרת אחרי החשיפה בעשרות שנים.

**א. קרצינוגנים סביבתיים.** אין בתיאור שינוי בחשיפה סביבתית המסביר את ההבדל הבין־דורי.
**ב. שיא מאוחר בנשים.** עיתוי אימוץ העישון ועיתוי הגמילה באוכלוסייה מסבירים את ההשהיה.
**ג. נטייה גנטית חדשה.** שינוי גנטי מהיר אינו מסביר את מגמת התמותה לאורך כמה עשורים.
**ד. אבחון משופר.** אבחון משפיע על שיעורי גילוי, אך אינו מסביר לבדו את השיא המאוחר בתמותה.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 86–87, תרשים 5-4.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: גבר בן 73, מהגר מרוסיה, מגיע לחדר מיון עם acute alcohol withdrawal. אשתו מדווחת שהוא שותה בקבוק וודקה ביום ומעשן בכבדות. היא מציינת שרוב הגברים במשפחתם נפטרו לפני גיל 60. בהתבסס על נתונים אפידמיולוגיים, איזו התערבות תשפר באופן המשמעותי ביותר את תוחלת חייו?
o: שינוי אגרסיבי של גורמי סיכון קרדיווסקולריים
Comprehensive geriatric assessment לאיתור frailty
תוכנית משולבת להפסקת אלכוהול והפסקת עישון
חיזוק תמיכה סוציאלית ושירותי בריאות הנפש
explanation:
לאחר טיפול בטוח בגמילה החריפה, **טיפול משולב בתלות באלכוהול ובעישון** מכוון לשתי החשיפות המשמעותיות המתוארות.

**א. גורמי סיכון קרדיווסקולריים.** טיפול בלחץ דם ובשומנים חשוב אך אינו מטפל לבדו בנזקי האלכוהול והטבק.
**ב. הערכה גריאטרית.** מעריכה שבריריות ותפקוד, אך אינה תחליף לטיפול בהתמכרות.
**ג. טיפול משולב.** גמילה מטבק וטיפול בהפרעת שימוש באלכוהול מתייחסים לסיכוני תמותה חופפים ושונים.
**ד. תמיכה חברתית ונפשית.** יכולה לסייע בהתמדה, כחלק מטיפול ממוקד בשתי החשיפות.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 41–43. American Society of Addiction Medicine, Integrating Tobacco Use Disorder Interventions in Addiction Treatment.

q: אישה בת 69 משוודיה מגיעה לייעוץ להפסקת עישון. היא התחילה לעשן בגיל 40 ומעשנת כיום חפיסה אחת ביום. היא מציינת שעישון כיום נפוץ יותר בקרב נשים מאשר גברים בשוודיה. מה מרמז מגמה זו לגבי דפוסי תוחלת החיים בעתיד?
o: פער תוחלת החיים בין המינים ימשיך להצטמצם
פער תוחלת החיים בין המינים עשוי להתייצב או להתהפך
נשים יפתחו טיפולים טובים יותר למחלות הקשורות לעישון
גורמים גנטיים יהפכו חשובים יותר מגורמים התנהגותיים
explanation:
**התקרבות דפוסי העישון עשויה לצמצם את פער תוחלת החיים** בין נשים לגברים בשוודיה, לאחר ההשהיה שבין חשיפה לתמותה.

**א. הצטמצמות הפער.** פחות עישון בגברים לצד חשיפה גוברת בדורות מסוימים של נשים עשויים להקטין את יתרון הנשים.
**ב. התייצבות או היפוך.** אלה אינם מסקנה הכרחית משיעורי העישון. גורמי תמותה נוספים משפיעים על הכיוון.
**ג. טיפולים טובים יותר בנשים.** מגמת העישון אינה מעידה על יתרון טיפולי.
**ד. גנטיקה דומיננטית.** שינוי בדפוס תוך דורות ספורים מתאים לתרומת חשיפה התנהגותית.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 5, עמ׳ 87, נתוני העישון ההיסטוריים.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: גבר יפני בן 81 מגיע לביקורת שגרתית. הוא מעשן 2 קופסאות ביום במשך 60 שנה ואינו מעוניין להפסיק. בתו שואלת מדוע פער תוחלת החיים בין גברים לנשים ביפן לא התצמצם כמו במדינות מפותחות אחרות. מה מסביר בצורה הטובה ביותר את הדפוס המתמשך הזה?
o: לגברים יפנים יש רמות גבוהות יותר של stress תעסוקתי
מערכת הבריאות היפנית מעדיפה טיפול בנשים
נשים יפניות שמרו על שיעורי עישון נמוכים באופן עקבי בעוד הגברים נותרו מעשנים כבדים
גורמים גנטיים בולטים יותר באוכלוסייה היפנית
explanation:
**שכיחות עישון נמוכה היסטורית בקרב נשים ביפן מול חשיפה גבוהה בגברים** שמרה על פער בתמותה המיוחסת לטבק באותם דורות.

**א. לחץ בעבודה.** ייתכן שהוא תורם לבריאות, אך אין כאן מדד המקשר אותו לפער המתואר.
**ב. עדיפות לנשים בטיפול.** לא הוצגו נתונים על הטיה כזו.
**ג. הבדלי עישון בין שנתוני לידה.** שנות עישון רבות משפיעות על תמותה מסרטן וממחלת לב גם עשרות שנים לאחר תחילת החשיפה.
**ד. גנטיקה מיוחדת ליפן.** אינה מסבירה היטב את שינויי הפער המקבילים לשינוי בהתנהגות בין דורות.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, פרק 5, עמ׳ 85–87.
ref: Hazzard Ch 5 — SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND LONGEVITY
chapterTitle: Sex Differences in Health and Longevity

q: אישה בת 70 עם מספר מחלות כרוניות שואלת את הגריאטר שלה לגבי תכנון לנכות עתידית אפשרית. בעלה נפטר לפני 5 שנים והיא גרה לבד. היא חוששת מהמשמעויות הכלכליות של צורך אפשרי בטיפול ארוך-טווח. איזה היבט של דפוסי אריכות החיים בנשים משפיע באופן הישיר ביותר על צרכי תכנון הטיפול שלה?
o: לנשים יש עלויות בריאות נמוכות יותר לאורך החיים בשל תחזוקת בריאות טובה יותר
תוחלת החיים הארוכה יותר של נשים כוללת לעיתים קרובות תקופות ממושכות של ירידה תפקודית ואלמנות
נשים מסתגלות טוב יותר לסביבות של assisted living
לנשים יש רשתות תמיכה משפחתיות חזקות יותר
explanation:
**שנים רבות יותר עם ירידה תפקודית או ללא בן זוג** עשויות להגדיל את הצורך בעזרה בתשלום. יש לברר את התמיכות והמשאבים הזמינים לה בפועל.

**א. הוצאות נמוכות יותר.** תוחלת חיים ממושכת יכולה להגדיל הוצאות מצטברות על טיפול.
**ב. מוגבלות ואלמנות לאורך זמן.** אובדן סיוע של בן זוג מצטרף לצורך האפשרי בעזרה ממושכת.
**ג. הסתגלות טובה יותר לדיור מוגן.** יכולת ההסתגלות אישית ואינה הגורם הדמוגרפי המתואר.
**ד. רשת משפחתית חזקה יותר.** אין להניח כי קיימים בני משפחה זמינים לטיפול.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 27, 92.

q: גבר בן 67 מגיע להערכת סיכון קרדיווסקולרי. הוא הפסיק לעשן לפני 5 שנים לאחר הרגל של 45 שנה, ושואל מה הסיכון שלו כיום בהשוואה לגברים שמעולם לא עישנו. בהתחשב במגמות האפידמיולוגיות לגבי ההשפעות המושהות של עישון על הבריאות, מה הייעוץ המתאים ביותר?
o: הסיכון שלו חזר מיד לבסיס עם הפסקת העישון
הסיכון שלו ימשיך לרדת אך יישאר מוגבר במשך שנים רבות
הסיכון שלו שווה כעת לזה של אנשים שמעולם לא עישנו באותו גיל
היסטוריית העישון שלו אינה רלוונטית לאחר 5 שנות גמילה
explanation:
**לאחר הפסקת עישון הסיכון הקרדיווסקולרי יורד בהדרגה**, אך לאחר חשיפה ממושכת הוא עשוי להישאר מוגבר במשך שנים לעומת מי שמעולם לא עישן.

**א. חזרה מיידית לבסיס.** הירידה מתחילה לאחר הגמילה, אך נזק וסקולרי מצטבר אינו נעלם בבת אחת.
**ב. ירידה מתמשכת.** חמש שנות גמילה מועילות גם כשהסיכון השיורי עדיין מוגבר.
**ג. שוויון מלא לאחר חמש שנים.** אין מועד אחיד של השוואת סיכון, בפרט לאחר עישון כבד.
**ד. עבר עישון חסר משמעות.** שנות החשיפה ממשיכות להיות רלוונטיות להערכת הסיכון.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 38, 42. Duncan et al., JAMA 2019, Association of Smoking Cessation With Subsequent Risk of Cardiovascular Disease.

q: אישה בת 84 עם דמנציה מובאת על ידי בתה להערכה. הבת מציינת שלמרות שאמה סבלה מיותר בעיות בריאותיות לאורך החיים מאביה המנוח, אמה חיה 8 שנים יותר ממנו. היא שואלת מה המשמעות של דפוס זה לתכנון הטיפול. איזה עיקרון מרכזי צריך להנחות את הדיון?
o: לנשים עם דמנציה יש פרוגנוזה טובה יותר מאשר לגברים
הישרדות ממושכת עם מחלות כרוניות מחייבת care planning מורחב
אריכות חיים בנשים מפחיתה את הצורך בהתערבויות אגרסיביות
נשים זקוקות לתרופות שונות עבור אותן מחלות
explanation:
**יש לתכנן מראש טיפול ותמיכה לאורך שנות חיים עם מחלה כרונית.** בדמנציה התכנון כולל מטרות אישיות, מי יסייע בפעולות היומיום וצרכי המטפל העיקרי.

**א. פרוגנוזה אישית טובה יותר בנשים.** הבדל ממוצע בתוחלת חיים אינו מנבא את מסלול הדמנציה של מטופלת מסוימת.
**ב. תכנון ממושך.** הישרדות עם מוגבלות עשויה להאריך את משך הצורך בשירותים, בהשגחה ובתמיכה משפחתית.
**ג. הפחתת טיפול רק עקב אריכות חיים.** החלטות טיפול מתקבלות לפי תועלת צפויה, נטל והעדפות.
**ד. תרופות שונות לכל מחלה.** מגדר לבדו אינו קובע את בחירת התרופה או את היקף התמיכה.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 27, 92, 1078.

q: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to a geriatric evaluation and management unit after a fall at home. She has diabetes, hypertension, and mild cognitive impairment. CGA identifies 12 problems. How should the team prioritize its recommendations?
o: By how quickly the investigations for each problem can be completed
By which major recommendations are most likely to achieve desired outcomes
By the sequence in which the problems were identified during assessment
By the lead physician's specialty before addressing the remaining problems
explanation:
A comprehensive geriatric assessment may uncover more problems than a patient can address at once. **Give priority to actions most likely to achieve the patient's goals, while bringing urgent problems forward.**

**A. Fastest investigation** — A quick investigation can have little bearing on falls, independence or another outcome the patient values.
**B. Likely benefit** — Weigh the expected benefit of each recommendation, its urgency and the patient's willingness to act.
**C. Discovery order** — The order in which professionals report findings says little about their effect on the patient.
**D. Lead clinician's specialty** — A team assessment weighs needs across disciplines and builds one plan with the patient.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Development of the Treatment Plan.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: A comprehensive geriatric assessment team has implemented a care plan and is following the patient. Progress toward the agreed goals is inadequate. Which response is part of the CGA process described in Hazzard?
o: Maintain the plan and judge success by the number of documented problems
Complete follow-up and judge success by the number of recommendations delivered
Reassess the plan with the patient and monitor the effects of revisions
Expand the plan and judge success by the number of specialist referrals
explanation:
Monitoring tests whether a plan was implemented and whether the patient is reaching the agreed goals. **If progress falls short, reassess with the patient, revise the plan and follow the response.**

**A. Count documented problems** — A problem list describes findings. Its length says nothing about recovery or independence.
**B. Count recommendations** — Advice delivered may never have been feasible to carry out. Ask what actually happened.
**C. Reassess and revise** — Check implementation, barriers, clinical changes and whether the patient's priorities have changed.
**D. Count referrals** — Additional referrals can help an identified need, but their number cannot measure the patient's outcome.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Monitoring and Revising the Treatment Plan.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.130

q: A 75-year-old woman with polypharmacy and recurrent falls undergoes comprehensive geriatric assessment. The team identifies a medication as a possible cause of delirium. She also needs physical therapy for fall prevention and nutritional advice for diabetes. How should the interventions be timed?
o: Begin physical therapy and dietary changes, then review the medication after those interventions
Stop the suspected medication promptly, and implement the other measures after she stabilizes
Continue the suspected medication and add a sedative while starting the other interventions
Defer the medication change and functional interventions to a common follow-up appointment
explanation:
The order of interventions matters when one problem is causing harm now. **Address the possible medication-induced delirium promptly and introduce the longer-term interventions as she stabilizes.**

**A. Therapy and diet first** — Both may help later, but neither removes a drug that might be driving an acute cognitive change.
**B. Prompt medication action** — Review and withdraw the suspected agent appropriately while evaluating other causes of delirium and supporting safety.
**C. Add a sedative** — Sedation leaves the potential precipitant in place and can compound confusion or fall risk.
**D. Defer everything** — A shared appointment is convenient but delays management of an acute, potentially reversible problem.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 121 and 130, Polypharmacy and Development of the Treatment Plan.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: A 79-year-old man with a hip fracture receives joint orthopedic and geriatric care incorporating CGA. His family asks about the evidence for this model. Which finding is reported in the meta-analysis of eight randomized trials summarized in Hazzard?
o: More discharges to a higher level of care than before hospitalization
Fewer discharges to a higher level of care than before hospitalization
A significant increase in mortality during the hospital admission
A significant reduction in mortality during the hospital admission
explanation:
Orthogeriatric comanagement puts the surgical and geriatric teams jointly in charge of care after hip fracture. **Across eight randomized trials, fewer patients needed a higher level of care at discharge than they had needed before the fracture.**

**A. More intensive placement** — The observed difference favored return to the former level of care.
**B. Less intensive placement required** — The comparison is with the patient's own prehospital living situation. It does not imply that every patient went home.
**C. Higher inpatient mortality** — The trials did not demonstrate an increase in hospital deaths.
**D. Significantly lower inpatient mortality** — Mortality tended to be lower, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Inpatient Units and Services.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 130, 796

q: An 84-year-old woman receives several recommendations after comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA). After six weeks of monitoring, progress toward the agreed goals is below expectations. Her daughter reports reduced motivation. Which next step follows the CGA process?
o: Continue the existing plan with a longer observation period
Return care to the primary physician with the existing plan
Reassess the patient and revise the plan through team discussion
Increase the frequency of interventions within the existing plan
explanation:
Comprehensive geriatric assessment includes revising treatment when the agreed goals are slipping out of reach. **Review progress with her and the team, including whether her motivation, health or priorities have changed.**

**A. Wait longer** — Six weeks of unexpectedly slow progress gives a reason to look for barriers now.
**B. Hand back the same plan** — Primary care may provide follow-up, but the current approach already needs review.
**C. Reassess and revise** — Ask which actions she could carry out, what she wants now and whether mood or another illness is limiting recovery.
**D. Increase intensity** — More sessions will not solve a mismatch between the intervention and her goals or ability to take part.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Revising the Treatment Plan.
ref: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 130, Revising the treatment plan
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 130, Revising the treatment plan

q: A 73-year-old man with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment lives with his supportive wife and is being considered for comprehensive geriatric assessment after hospitalization for pneumonia. In the posthospital randomized trial summarized by Hazzard, which outcome improved with CGA rather than usual care?
o: Less functional decline at the 24-week assessment
Fewer acute-care visits during the postdischarge period
Fewer hospital readmissions during the follow-up period
Less depression at the 24-week assessment
explanation:
Studies of post-discharge geriatric assessment have measured service use, function and mood separately. **In this randomized trial, patients receiving the intervention were less likely to be readmitted to hospital.**

**A. Functional decline** — Functional decline at 24 weeks did not differ between the groups.
**B. Acute-care visits** — The trial did not show fewer post-discharge acute-care visits. A visit and a hospital admission are distinct outcomes.
**C. Hospital readmission** — Readmission was the outcome that improved with the intervention in this trial.
**D. Depression** — Depressive outcomes at 24 weeks did not differ. Other settings or interventions can have different effects.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 130–131, Posthospital Discharge Assessment and Management.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: A hospital uses a Mobile Acute Care of the Elderly (MACE) team for older medical and surgical inpatients. Which description matches this service?
o: A dedicated rehabilitation ward providing prolonged inpatient recovery
An interdisciplinary ward team reducing the hazards of hospitalization
A home-visiting team providing acute care instead of hospitalization
A scheduled day-clinic team providing outpatient geriatric assessment
explanation:
Mobile Acute Care of the Elderly (MACE) brings geriatric care to older patients on their existing medical or surgical wards. The team works with ward staff to reduce hazards such as immobility, educate families, and prepare for discharge.

**A. Dedicated rehabilitation ward.** Transfer to a rehabilitation unit serves patients who need ongoing recovery after an acute illness.
**B. Interdisciplinary ward team.** A geriatrician, clinical nurse specialists, and social workers can address risks at the bedside while the patient stays on the admitting ward.
**C. Acute care at home.** Hospital-at-home teams deliver acute treatment in the patient's residence.
**D. Day clinic.** Scheduled geriatric assessments serve outpatients and take place outside the inpatient ward.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 194.
ref: Hazzard Ch 14 — MODELS OF HOSPITAL AND OUTPATIENT CARE
chapterTitle: Models of Hospital and Outpatient Care

q: A 76-year-old woman with dementia, diabetes, and hypertension undergoes comprehensive geriatric assessment. Her adult son is her principal caregiver. Which approach best incorporates patient-centered care into the treatment plan?
o: Use motivational interviewing to secure agreement with goals already chosen by the team
Use motivational interviewing to identify her priorities and willingness to make changes
Use the diagnosis list to set disease-based goals before discussing the plan with her son
Use her son's preferences to set goals and judge success by adherence to instructions
explanation:
Patient-centered planning starts with what the person hopes to achieve and what changes are acceptable. **Use motivational interviewing to elicit her own priorities and readiness, involving her son as appropriate.**

**A. Obtain agreement** — Persuading her to accept predetermined goals misses the purpose of the conversation.
**B. Elicit priorities and readiness** — Questions about what matters to her and what she feels able to change help shape a feasible plan.
**C. Disease targets first** — Separate disease targets can compete. Her goals help the team decide which interventions to prioritize.
**D. Caregiver sets goals** — Her son can provide observations and practical help. Dementia alone does not remove her role in decisions.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Development of the Treatment Plan.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: An 81-year-old man is admitted to a geriatric evaluation and management unit after repeated falls and medication-related confusion. Physicians, nurses, clinical pharmacists, social workers, and therapists present their findings. What task belongs to the team-discussion phase of comprehensive geriatric assessment?
o: Determining who should assume responsibility for implementing each recommendation
Determining which problems need action and might respond to treatment
Determining whether the patient's progress might require further team review
Determining how recommendations might change after progress falls below expectations
explanation:
In the team conference, disciplines combine their findings into a shared account of the patient's needs. **During the discussion they identify problems that need action and may respond to treatment.**

**A. Assign responsibility** — The team specifies who will initiate and complete each recommendation when developing its implementation plan.
**B. Identify actionable problems** — Repeated falls and medication-related confusion can generate coordinated priorities after the team compares observations.
**C. Review progress** — The patient's response becomes apparent during monitoring after action has begun.
**D. Revise recommendations** — Revision follows a reassessment when progress differs from expectations.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 129–130, Discussion Among Team and Development of the Treatment Plan.

q: A 77-year-old woman receives CGA recommendations for medication changes, physical therapy, and home safety. Which account of the purpose and resource implications of monitoring matches Hazzard?
o: Monitoring tracks implementation; longer, more intensive follow-up reduces consultation resource use
Monitoring tracks assessment completion; longer, more intensive follow-up leaves resource use unchanged
Monitoring tracks implementation and progress; longer, more intensive follow-up increases resource use
Monitoring tracks the final diagnosis; shorter, less intensive follow-up increases consultation resource use
explanation:
Follow-up has two jobs after comprehensive geriatric assessment. **Check that the recommendations were carried out and that they are helping. More frequent or prolonged follow-up requires more team resources.**

**A. Intensive follow-up saves resources** — Tracking implementation is appropriate, but additional contact increases the workload of the consultation.
**B. Track completion of assessment** — An assessment can be complete even when physical therapy never started or the home modification was impractical.
**C. Track implementation and progress** — Check both the action taken and the change in the patient's function or symptoms.
**D. Track only the final diagnosis** — A diagnosis cannot show whether the recommendations were implemented. Shorter, less intensive contact generally uses fewer resources.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 130, Monitoring.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: A healthy 72-year-old man takes lisinopril for hypertension and exercises regularly. He asks whether supplements advertised as targeting aging pathways will help him live longer. What should guide your advice?
o: Recommend the supplement on the strength of its proposed biological mechanism
Defer supplement use pending rigorous clinical data and FDA review
Recommend the supplement on the strength of its over-the-counter availability
Recommend the supplement on the strength of claims from an unregulated clinic
explanation:
An aging-pathway effect in a laboratory cannot show whether a person lives longer or experiences harm. **Defer using this supplement for longevity until rigorous human evidence shows meaningful benefit and acceptable risk.** In the United States, dietary supplements generally are sold without FDA premarket approval for efficacy.

**A. Recommend from the mechanism.** A plausible pathway does not quantify survival benefit, adverse effects or interactions with lisinopril.
**B. Wait for clinical data and FDA review.** Waiting for outcome evidence is appropriate. A new drug seeking authorization for a therapeutic indication faces an approval process distinct from the rules for ordinary dietary supplements.
**C. Recommend because it is over the counter.** Availability establishes neither lifespan benefit nor safety in this patient.
**D. Rely on clinic claims.** Testimonials and marketing do not compare clinical outcomes or harms against an appropriate control.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 602–603. FDA, Information for Consumers on Using Dietary Supplements.
Key note: FDA does not approve ordinary dietary supplements for safety and efficacy before sale. The relevant reason to defer is lack of demonstrated clinical benefit, not an expected premarket supplement approval.

q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension, and osteoarthritis wishes to join a trial of an intervention intended to slow biological aging. Which biomarker property is needed to detect a response to the intervention?
o: Association with chronological age despite unchanged biomarker values
Sensitivity of biomarker values to change with intervention
Association with one age-related disease despite unchanged values
Stability of biomarker values despite an effective intervention
explanation:
A biomarker intended to monitor treatment must move detectably when the biological process changes. **Sensitivity to intervention-related change** is necessary before it can measure response.

**A. Correlation with chronological age.** It may distinguish younger from older people without changing during treatment.
**B. Responsive values.** A measurable change permits comparison over the course of an intervention. Clinical significance still requires validation.
**C. Association with a single disease.** Disease association is different from responsiveness and is narrow for a general aging marker.
**D. Unchanged despite benefit.** A marker insensitive to effective treatment cannot track the response.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.

q: A clinician is considering a biomarker of aging that is associated with mortality in an observational study. What is needed before interpreting a treatment-induced change in this biomarker as evidence of clinical benefit?
o: An observational assessment of its association with mortality
An assessment within an intervention with demonstrated clinical benefit
An analytical assessment of laboratory accuracy and reproducibility
A combined assessment of several biomarkers in one blood sample
explanation:
A prognostic biomarker identifies risk. To interpret a change in it as treatment benefit, **study the biomarker during an intervention that improves clinical outcomes** and examine how the changes relate.

**A. An observational assessment of its association with mortality.** An association with mortality can reflect illness burden without indicating how treatment changes outcomes.
**B. An assessment within an intervention with demonstrated clinical benefit.** Intervention evidence tests whether moving the marker tracks a meaningful benefit. Confirmation may be needed across interventions and settings.
**C. An analytical assessment of laboratory accuracy and reproducibility.** Laboratory reproducibility establishes measurement quality, not clinical surrogacy.
**D. A combined assessment of several biomarkers in one blood sample.** Combining several markers does not prove that changing them improves health.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 602.

q: A 70-year-old woman receives a result showing peripheral white-cell telomere length below the average for her age. Which limitation is important when interpreting this result in an individual?
o: The telomere measurement is calibrated primarily from DNA methylation patterns
Substantial variability limits the clinical applications of the telomere measurement
Telomeres lengthen with age and provide a measure of reversed aging
Uniformity between individuals permits precise estimation of biological age from telomeres
explanation:
Leukocyte telomeres generally shorten with age, but lengths vary considerably between people. **Substantial variability limits interpretation of an individual below-average result**.

**A. Calibrated from methylation.** Methylation patterns underlie epigenetic clocks, not direct measurement of telomere length.
**B. Substantial variability.** An individual's length overlaps broadly across age groups and cannot precisely assign biological age.
**C. Progressive lengthening.** The usual association with aging is shortening, not reliable lengthening or reversal.
**D. Uniform precise age determination.** The wide distribution prevents the proposed precision.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 602

q: An older patient asks to start caloric restriction after hearing that CALERIE slowed the advancement of physiologic age. What principle should guide interpretation before an individual recommendation?
o: Treat the biomarker change as evidence that dementia is prevented
Assess effectiveness and safety beyond the change in the aging measure
Treat the biomarker change as evidence of suitability in malnutrition
Use the biomarker change in place of an assessment of treatment risks
explanation:
A change in a physiological aging measure is a surrogate finding. **Assess clinical effectiveness and safety before recommending caloric restriction to an individual**, particularly when nutritional reserve may be limited.

**A. Prevents dementia.** Slower change in an aging measure is not a demonstrated cognitive outcome.
**B. Assess benefit and risk.** Ask whether people function better or avoid disease and whether restriction causes harm in the relevant population.
**C. Suitable in malnutrition.** Further energy restriction could worsen weight and muscle loss. A biomarker result cannot answer that safety question.
**D. Replace risk assessment.** Favorable laboratory changes can coexist with clinical harms.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.

q: A 69-year-old woman with coronary disease asks why LDL cholesterol can serve as a treatment-development biomarker whereas developing biomarkers for aging interventions remains difficult. Which explanation matches Hazzard?
o: An established single aging pathway makes the main difference the duration of trials
LDL has a causal atherosclerotic role; no single longevity pathway is identified
Validated aging surrogate endpoints make the main difference the cost of clinical trials
Aging biomarkers need no linkage between treatment-related changes and health outcomes
explanation:
A treatment biomarker is easier to interpret when the biological factor has a causal role in disease. **LDL contributes causally to atherosclerosis, whereas no single pathway explains human longevity**.

**A. One known longevity pathway.** Aging reflects interacting processes and cannot be reduced to one established pathway.
**B. Causal LDL versus complex longevity.** LDL has a defined disease relationship. An aging marker must earn an analogous link to meaningful outcomes.
**C. Validated aging endpoints already exist.** Validation of treatment surrogates is itself a major challenge beyond trial expense.
**D. No outcome link needed.** Treatment-related biomarker change must be linked to altered health risk before substituting for an outcome.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 602

q: An aging study uses a DNA methylation clock. According to Hazzard, what relationship underlies the age estimate?
o: Correlation of plasma protein concentrations with chronological age
Correlation of cellular telomere length with chronological age
Correlation of DNA methylation patterns with chronological age
Correlation of organ volumes on imaging with chronological age
explanation:
A DNA methylation clock estimates age from chemical marks on DNA that change over the lifespan. Researchers calibrate the clock against known chronological ages, then use the methylation pattern in a new sample to estimate the donor’s age.

**A. Plasma protein concentrations.** Age-related changes in circulating proteins can inform a proteomic clock, which measures a different set of molecules.
**B. Telomere length.** Shortening at chromosome ends can reflect a cell’s history of division. Length is a separate marker of aging.
**C. DNA methylation patterns.** The clock combines measurements at sites whose methylation varies predictably with chronological age. The biological mechanism behind that association remains uncertain.
**D. Organ volumes.** Imaging measures anatomical changes such as tissue loss. It cannot measure methylation at individual DNA sites.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 41.

q: A 73-year-old woman with age-related diseases is considering a study using a panel of aging biomarkers. Researchers want to establish that an intervention-related biomarker change reflects a health-outcome change. Which finding most directly supports that link under the Hazzard criteria?
o: An association between the biomarker level at baseline and chronological age measured at the same assessment
An association between biomarker change and outcome-risk change, with evidence of mediation during an effective intervention
An association between the biomarker level at baseline and subsequent mortality assessed during the follow-up period
An association between the biomarker level at baseline and the presence of multiple age-related health conditions
explanation:
An intervention surrogate must reflect what treatment changes about health, beyond predicting risk at baseline. **Link biomarker change to change in outcome risk and show mediation of an effective treatment's benefit**.

**A. Baseline age correlation.** It shows a cross-sectional relationship, not response to therapy.
**B. Change and mediation.** Track the marker and a meaningful outcome under treatment, then assess whether the marker accounts for treatment-related benefit.
**C. Baseline mortality prediction.** Prediction identifies risk without proving that modifying the marker changes it.
**D. Baseline multimorbidity association.** Association with several diseases is relevant for aging biology but does not demonstrate mediation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 602

q: An 80-year-old man with several chronic diseases asks whether an aging biomarker could measure the effect of treatment. Which relationship is required for a biomarker used to evaluate outcomes in a geroscience trial?
o: A relationship between the biomarker and laboratory availability.
A relationship between the biomarker and treatment cost.
A relationship between biomarker change and clinical change.
A relationship between the biomarker and clinic-visit frequency.
explanation:
A geroscience outcome biomarker should reflect meaningful changes in function or health. **Changes in the marker must relate to clinical changes** for it to inform treatment evaluation.

**A. A relationship between the biomarker and laboratory availability.** A widely available test can be easy to use yet clinically uninformative.
**B. A relationship between the biomarker and treatment cost.** Cost affects feasibility rather than validity as an outcome measure.
**C. A relationship between biomarker change and clinical change.** Linking changes in the marker to patient outcomes gives its movement a clinical interpretation.
**D. A relationship between the biomarker and clinic-visit frequency.** Visit frequency changes sampling opportunities and does not validate the measurement.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 601.

q: Researchers develop a blood biomarker associated with future mortality and propose using treatment-related changes in it to assess benefits of interventions targeting aging. Which study design provides the prerequisite setting for evaluating this use?
o: An observational study comparing age groups and correlations with chronological age
An intervention study using an accepted outcome and proven effective treatment
An observational study replicating the association with long-term mortality in another cohort
A laboratory study combining aging-pathway markers and examining their interrelationships
explanation:
To test whether a biomarker can stand in for a clinical outcome, investigators need an intervention with a known outcome benefit. **Study an effective treatment against an accepted clinical outcome** and assess how biomarker change relates to that benefit.

**A. Compare age groups.** Cross-sectional age differences do not test a treatment effect.
**B. Effective treatment and accepted outcome.** This design allows investigators to assess change and potential mediation.
**C. Replicate mortality prediction.** A second observational association still cannot show whether treatment-induced change tracks benefit.
**D. Combine laboratory markers.** Correlations within a panel do not supply a clinical intervention or endpoint.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 602.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 602, Biomarkers of aging

q: A 78-year-old woman living alone has unintentionally lost 8 lb over six months. Her appetite has declined and food no longer tastes the same. She takes lisinopril, metformin, sertraline, and omeprazole; BMI is 20 kg/m2. Which approach incorporates the nutritional screening and medication review described in Hazzard?
o: Obtain metabolic and thyroid tests in place of assessing weight change and food intake
Perform MNA and review medications affecting taste or appetite
Arrange endoscopy in place of assessing nutritional status and medication effects
Prescribe calorie supplements and postpone nutritional assessment for three months
explanation:
Unintentional weight loss can reveal inadequate intake before an older adult looks malnourished. Changes in appetite and taste make a medication history part of the assessment.
**Use the Mini Nutritional Assessment and review medicines that may impair taste or appetite.**

**A. Laboratory tests alone.** Metabolic and thyroid tests may help identify an illness but leave actual intake and weight trajectory unmeasured.
**B. Nutritional screen and medication review.** This documents nutritional risk while addressing a potentially reversible contributor.
**C. Proceed directly to endoscopy.** Endoscopy may follow specific clinical findings. It does not assess nutritional risk or medication effects.
**D. Supplements and delayed assessment.** Delaying evaluation overlooks continued weight loss and treatable causes of poor intake.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 166, Nutrition and Table 11-3.

q: An inactive 82-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, and osteoarthritis spends most of the day watching television. He asks whether joint pain, fear of falling, and his age make it too late to start exercising. Which counseling statement is supported by Hazzard?
o: Joint pain generally makes prolonged reduction of daily activity preferable
Starting at an advanced age generally offers little prospect of benefit
Benefits generally outweigh risks, with guidance tailored to his limitations
Fall risk generally makes rest preferable until baseline risk has fallen
explanation:
Physical activity helps older adults preserve strength and mobility. Joint symptoms and fear of falling influence how the person should start and which activities are feasible.
**The benefits generally outweigh the risks. Start at a tolerable level and tailor activity to his pain and balance.**

**A. Reduce daily activity.** Persistent inactivity worsens conditioning and can make daily tasks harder.
**B. Little benefit at advanced age.** Older adults can still gain strength, maintain function and improve mood.
**C. Individualized exercise.** Low-impact activity at a manageable intensity can be paired with balance and strength work.
**D. Rest until fall risk subsides.** Prolonged rest may erode mobility. Fall risk calls for adapted guidance and a safe setting.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 166, Physical Activity and Table 11-3.

q: A 69-year-old woman at high cardiovascular risk wants to improve a diet rich in processed foods. Which change fits the Mediterranean-style pattern described in Hazzard?
o: Favor processed meats and hydrogenated fats over fish and nuts
Favor olive oil, nuts, and fish while reducing processed meat
Favor animal fats while reducing oils derived from plant sources
Favor foods containing trans fats while reducing olive oil and fish
explanation:
A Mediterranean-style eating pattern changes both the type of fat and the foods supplying it. **Favor olive oil, nuts and fish while reducing processed meats.**

**A. Processed meat and hydrogenated fats** — These displace the whole foods and unsaturated fats emphasized in this pattern.
**B. Olive oil, nuts and fish** — They provide unsaturated fats, and lowering intake of processed meat is consistent with the overall pattern.
**C. Animal fats in place of plant oils** — This reverses the suggested substitution.
**D. Trans fats in place of olive oil and fish** — Partially hydrogenated fats can adversely affect the lipid profile.

q: A 75-year-old man reports altered food taste, reduced appetite, and weight loss beginning after changes to several medications. His mood is stable, he eats with family, and oral examination reveals no problem. Which area of evaluation most directly addresses the timing and taste change?
o: Evaluate depression and its effects on appetite and food intake
Evaluate medication effects on food taste and appetite
Evaluate chewing difficulty and its effects on food intake
Evaluate mealtime isolation and its effects on food intake
explanation:
Medications can change taste or suppress appetite, reducing food intake. The timing of symptoms after a prescription change can identify where to start the evaluation.
**Review the newly started or adjusted medicines and ask how the taste change affected eating.**

**A. Depression.** Mood symptoms can affect intake, but his mood is stable and the onset follows medication changes.
**B. Medication effects.** The temporal relationship and altered taste support reviewing each recent change.
**C. Chewing difficulty.** An oral examination and chewing history matter, but the described symptom is taste change.
**D. Isolation during meals.** He already eats with family. Isolation is a weaker explanation for this new temporal pattern.

q: An 85-year-old woman attends with her daughter, who reports increasing social isolation since the patient's husband died six months ago. The patient rarely leaves home and mainly eats frozen meals by herself in front of the television. She has lost interest in cooking and preparing meals. Her weight is stable, but the quality of her diet appears poor. Which intervention addresses the social contribution to her eating difficulties?
o: Arrange private meals in a quiet room and defer her return to eating with company.
Wait for documented weight loss before arranging social meals and offering additional dietary support.
Address social isolation and encourage community meal participation to provide company while she eats.
Use a restricted uniform menu to simplify food selection while keeping meals separate from social activities.
explanation:
Bereavement and eating alone can reduce both interest in food and dietary variety before the scale changes. **Offer a community meal where she can eat with others.**

**A. Private meals** — She is already eating alone. Further separation leaves the identified barrier in place.
**B. Wait for weight loss** — Stable weight can coexist with a poor-quality diet. The history already gives a reason to intervene.
**C. Community meals** — Eating with company can restore the social cue and pleasure that she lost after bereavement.
**D. Separate meals with a uniform menu** — A fixed menu restricts choice and does not address isolation.

q: A 71-year-old man with well-controlled heart failure, diabetes, and hypertension follows a longstanding diet restricting salt, fat, and sugar. He says the food tastes like cardboard, eats very little, and is losing weight. Which dietary approach is consistent with the source’s strategies to improve oral intake?
o: Tighten the dietary restrictions and continue foods he finds unappealing
Relax unnecessary restrictions and offer foods matching his preferences
Reduce meal frequency and retain the same restrictive diet
Remove preferred foods and encourage adaptation to the restricted menu
explanation:
A restrictive diet can make food so unappealing that energy intake becomes inadequate. **Reassess each restriction and offer preferred foods while monitoring the conditions that justified the diet.**

**A. Tighten restrictions** — He already eats little because the food is unpalatable. Further restriction could deepen the deficit.
**B. Relax unnecessary restrictions** — A dietitian can retain essential limits and restore flavor and choice where the nutritional cost exceeds the expected benefit.
**C. Reduce meal frequency** — Fewer opportunities to eat can worsen low intake and leave the taste problem untouched.
**D. Remove preferred foods** — This gives him still less incentive to eat.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 427, Table 30-11 and measures to enhance oral intake.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION
