q: גבר בן 78 עם דמנציה וסקולרית, מחלת כליה כרונית בשלב 3b (eGFR 35), ושבר ירך לאחרונה, משוחרר מאשפוז שיקומי. ה-MoCA שלו הוא 16/30. בתו רוצה שישוב הביתה אליה; בנו מתעקש על מעבר לבית אבות. המטופל אומר 'אני רוצה ללכת הביתה עם מרי [הבת]' אך אינו מסוגל להסביר כיצד תעזור לו או מה בדיוק הוא צריך. הפיזיותרפיסט מציין שהוא זקוק להשגחה בכל העברות ונפל פעמיים במהלך הטיפול. הוא נוטל warfarin בגלל פרפור פרוזדורים והחסיר מספר מנות במהלך האשפוז. איזה גורם תומך בצורה החזקה ביותר בצורך באפוטרופסות?
o: קבלת ציון MoCA התואם דמנציה בדרגת חומרה בינונית
חוסר יכולת לנהל בבטחה טיפול תרופתי נוגד קרישה
מחלוקת בין בני המשפחה לגבי מקום המגורים המתאים
חוסר יכולת להסביר צורכי טיפול למרות הבעת העדפה
explanation:
יכולת החלטה נבחנת ביחס להחלטה המסוימת, לאחר הסבר מותאם ובחינת חלופות מגבילות פחות. הבעת רצון לבדה אינה מוכיחה הבנה. **חוסר יכולת להסביר צורכי טיפול למרות הבעת העדפה**.

**א. קבלת ציון MoCA התואם דמנציה בדרגת חומרה בינונית.** ציון סקר אינו קובע לבדו כשירות משפטית.
**ב. חוסר יכולת לנהל בבטחה טיפול תרופתי נוגד קרישה.** קושי בניהול תרופות מעיד על צורך בעזרה מעשית.
**ג. מחלוקת בין בני המשפחה לגבי מקום המגורים המתאים.** מחלוקת משפחתית אינה הוכחה לאי־יכולת.
**ד. חוסר יכולת להסביר צורכי טיפול למרות הבעת העדפה.** חוסר הבנה של צרכיו לאחר הסבר מצדיק הערכה מעמיקה של הצורך בהגנה.

אסמכתא · חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, סעיפים 33 ו־33א, עמ׳ 44 עד 45.

q: מטופלת מאושפזת בישראל מוגדרת חסרת ישע. בבירור עולה חשד שהאדם האחראי עליה פוגע בה. איזה צעד מתחייב לפי נוהל משרד הבריאות?
o: מסירת הודעה מיידית לפקיד סעד או למשטרה על החשד
דחיית ההודעה עד לפגישה משותפת עם המטפל ועם המשפחה
המתנה לאימות סופי של האירוע לפני העברת הודעה לגורם חיצוני
הסתפקות במעקב מחלקתי ובתיעוד במקום מסירת הודעה חיצונית
explanation:
חשד מבוסס לעבירה כלפי חסרת ישע בידי האחראי עליה מחייב הודעה לצד שמירה על בטיחותה. **מסירת הודעה מיידית לפקיד סעד או למשטרה על החשד**.

**א. מסירת הודעה מיידית לפקיד סעד או למשטרה על החשד.** מוסרים את המידע לעו״ס שמונה לפי חוק או למשטרה.
**ב. דחיית ההודעה עד לפגישה משותפת עם המטפל ועם המשפחה.** פגישה עם המשפחה אינה תנאי לדיווח.
**ג. המתנה לאימות סופי של האירוע לפני העברת הודעה לגורם חיצוני.** אין צורך בוודאות חקירתית כדי לדווח על חשד סביר.
**ד. הסתפקות במעקב מחלקתי ובתיעוד במקום מסירת הודעה חיצונית.** תיעוד ומעקב נדרשים אך אינם מחליפים הודעה.

אסמכתא · משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, סעיף 8.5, עמ׳ 6.
ref: משרד הבריאות, חוזר המנהל הכללי 22/03: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות

sourceChecked.source: משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, סעיף 8.5

q: מטופל באשפוז ממושך מופנה להערכת צורך באפוטרופוס. הצוות מכין את התעודה הרפואית הנדרשת בהליך המתואר בחוזר משרד הבריאות. מי צריך לערוך את התעודה?
o: רופא כללי המכיר את המשפחה ללא מומחיות
עובד סוציאלי המכיר את המשפחה ואת מצבה
רופא מומחה מאחד התחומים המנויים בחוזר
בן משפחה המכיר את המטופל ומלווה אותו
explanation:
תעודה לצורך הליך מינוי באשפוז ממושך היא חוות דעת רפואית על יכולתו וצורכי האדם. **מומחה בגריאטריה, בפסיכיאטריה, בנוירולוגיה, ברפואת המשפחה או ברפואה פנימית** רשאי לערוך אותה. רצוי לבחור מומחיות המתאימה למצב הרפואי שהוביל לבקשה.

**א. רופא כללי המכיר את המשפחה ללא מומחיות.** היכרות עם המשפחה אינה ממלאת את דרישת המומחיות.
**ב. עובד סוציאלי המכיר את המשפחה ואת מצבה.** דוח סוציאלי משלים את התמונה אך אינו תעודת מומחה רפואי.
**ג. רופא מומחה מאחד התחומים המנויים בחוזר.** רופא בעל המומחיות המתאימה מבצע את ההערכה ומתעד את מסקנתו.
**ד. בן משפחה המכיר את המטופל ומלווה אותו.** קרוב יכול למסור מידע על התפקוד אך אינו עורך חוות דעת רפואית.

אסמכתא · חוזר מינוי אפוטרופוס באשפוז ממושך, סעיף 9.3.1, עמ׳ 4.
ref: משרד הבריאות, חוזר מנהל רפואה 10/2006: מינוי אפוטרופוס על גופו של אדם ו/או רכושו במסגרת אשפוז ממושך

q: לפי סעיף 2 לחוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, איזה מצב מהווה חריג לברירת המחדל של כשרות אדם לפעולות משפטיות?
o: כאשר נרשמה אבחנה קוגניטיבית בתיק הרפואי
כאשר הכשרות נשללה בחוק או בפסק דין
כאשר בני המשפחה חולקים על ההחלטה שקיבל
כאשר הפעולה חורגת מהעדפותיו הקודמות
explanation:
**אדם כשר לפעולות משפטיות אלא אם הכשרות נשללה או הוגבלה בחוק או בפסק דין.** זוהי חזקת הכשרות המשפטית.

**א. אבחנה קוגניטיבית.** ממצא רפואי אינו כשלעצמו שלילה משפטית של כשרות.
**ב. חוק או פסק דין.** זהו החריג המפורש, ויש לבדוק מה היקף ההגבלה.
**ג. מחלוקת במשפחה.** אינה שוללת את יכולת האדם לפעול.
**ד. שינוי בהעדפות.** אדם רשאי לשנות עמדה ללא אובדן כשרותו.

אסמכתא · חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, סעיף 2.

q: מטופל מבוגר שוקל טיפול רפואי בעל אופי חדשני במסגרת מחקר. בשיחה על הסכמה מדעת, איזה פרט מחייב סעיף 13 לציין, נוסף לתועלת, לסיכונים ולחלופות?
o: את צורכי השלמת הנתונים כתחליף לתיאור החדשנות
את עובדת היות הטיפול המוצע בעל אופי חדשני
את תמיכת המשפחה כתחליף לתיאור החדשנות
את העדפת החוקר כתחליף לתיאור החדשנות
explanation:
**יש לציין במפורש שהטיפול המוצע בעל אופי חדשני.** מידע זה מסייע להבין את מידת אי־הוודאות ולהבחין בין מחקר לטיפול המקובל.

**א. הצורך בנתונים.** מטרות המחקר אינן תחליף לגילוי על חדשנות הטיפול.
**ב. אופיו החדשני של הטיפול.** זהו רכיב מידע נפרד בסעיף 13(ב).
**ג. תמיכת המשפחה.** אינה מספקת למטופל את המידע המדעי והקליני החסר.
**ד. העדפת החוקר.** אינה תחליף להסבר ולבחירה חופשית.

אסמכתא · חוק זכויות החולה, סעיף 13(ב)(5).

q: בת 86 בישראל נוהגת למרות ליקוי ראייה קבוע והפרעה קוגניטיבית. הרופא מעריך שמצבה עלול לסכן אותה או אחרים בנהיגה. מה הפעולה המתאימה לפי חוזר מנכ״ל 6/2023?
o: לדווח למרב״ד ולהמליץ להפסיק נהיגה עד הבדיקה
להמתין להסכמת בני המשפחה לפני מסירת הדיווח למרב״ד
למסור תיעוד למשפחה ולהעביר אליה את ההחלטה על דיווח
להימנע מדיווח למרב״ד בשל חובת שמירת הסודיות הרפואית
explanation:
רופא המטפל באדם ומעריך שמחלתו עלולה לסכן אותו או את זולתו בנהיגה חייב לפעול לפי חובת הדיווח ולתת הדרכה בטיחותית. **לדווח למרב״ד ולהמליץ להפסיק נהיגה עד הבדיקה**.

**א. לדווח למרב״ד ולהמליץ להפסיק נהיגה עד הבדיקה.** מדווחים למרב״ד ומתעדים שהומלץ להימנע מנהיגה עד הבדיקה.
**ב. להמתין להסכמת בני המשפחה לפני מסירת הדיווח למרב״ד.** הסכמה משפחתית אינה תנאי לחובת הרופא.
**ג. למסור תיעוד למשפחה ולהעביר אליה את ההחלטה על דיווח.** אי אפשר להעביר את אחריות הדיווח למשפחה.
**ד. להימנע מדיווח למרב״ד בשל חובת שמירת הסודיות הרפואית.** חובת הסודיות כפופה לחובת דיווח הקבועה בדין.

אסמכתא · משרד הבריאות, חוזר מנכ״ל 6/2023, הגדרה מחדש של חובת ההודעה על נהגים עם מצבי בריאות העלולים לסכן את עצמם וזולתם, עמ׳ 2–3.
ref: משרד הבריאות, חוזר המנהל הכללי 6/2023: הגדרה מחדש של חובת ההודעה על נהגים עם מצבי בריאות העלולים לסכן את עצמם וזולתם

q: גבר בן 77 מתקשה להבין עסקה כספית מסוכנת אך ממשיך לקבל החלטות רפואיות. לאחר בחינת חלופות נקבע שיש צורך באפוטרופוס לעניין הכספי. איזה עיקרון ינחה את היקף המינוי לפי חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות?
o: התאמת היקף המינוי לכלל האבחנות הרפואיות של האדם
התאמת היקף המינוי לצורך בניהול מרוכז של ענייני האדם
התאמת העניינים והתקופה לצורך שנקבע ולמטרת המינוי
התאמת היקף המינוי להעדפת המשפחה לקבל סמכות רחבה
explanation:
גם כשהוחלט שנדרש אפוטרופוס, בית המשפט מגביל את סמכותו לעניינים ולזמן הנחוצים. **התאמת העניינים והתקופה לצורך שנקבע ולמטרת המינוי**.

**א. התאמת היקף המינוי לכלל האבחנות הרפואיות של האדם.** רשימת האבחנות אינה קובעת באילו החלטות חסרה יכולת.
**ב. התאמת היקף המינוי לצורך בניהול מרוכז של ענייני האדם.** ריכוז ניהולי אינו הצדקה להרחבת סמכות.
**ג. התאמת העניינים והתקופה לצורך שנקבע ולמטרת המינוי.** המידתיות נבחנת בנפרד לגבי תחום המינוי ומשך המינוי.
**ד. התאמת היקף המינוי להעדפת המשפחה לקבל סמכות רחבה.** למשפחה אין זכות לקבל סמכות רחבה רק משום שהיא מעדיפה זאת.

אסמכתא · חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, סעיף 33א, עמ׳ 46.

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has lost weight because of missed meals and low intake. Nutritional assessment finds that dietary restrictions are making intake difficult; he has no swallowing problem. Which plan is appropriate?
o: Increase dietary restrictions and concentrate food into one large meal
Reduce dietary restrictions and provide assistance with small meals
Increase dietary restrictions and reduce the number of daily meals
Reduce food variety and avoid snacks between regular meals
explanation:
Memory impairment can cause missed meals even when the patient can swallow safely. **Simplify unnecessary restrictions and arrange help with frequent small meals.**

**A. More restrictions and one large meal** — A single missed meal could remove most daily intake, and tighter rules make eating harder.
**B. Fewer restrictions and assisted small meals** — Cues and help address forgetfulness, while smaller, more frequent meals offer repeated chances to eat.
**C. More restrictions and fewer meals** — Both changes aggravate the barriers already identified.
**D. Narrow variety and avoid snacks** — Preferred foods and snacks can add energy when ordinary meals are inadequate.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 427, Table 30-11 and nonpharmacologic strategies.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: An older woman with falls takes antihypertensive medication and zolpidem for sleep. Which principle applies to zolpidem in her falls assessment?
o: Increase its dosage to prevent falls attributed to fragmented sleep
Review its ongoing need during the falls risk assessment
Exclude it from review because the fall occurred after sleep
Prioritize it as treatment for falls before nonpharmacologic sleep care
explanation:
Zolpidem is a centrally acting Z-drug used for insomnia. **Review whether she still needs it** and consider behavioral treatment for sleep.

**A. Increase the dose** — Greater sedative exposure could compound impaired balance or alertness during nighttime mobility.
**B. Review the continuing indication** — Clarify when she takes it, whether it helps and whether a supervised reduction or alternative is appropriate.
**C. Ignore the drug after sleep** — A fall on getting out of bed can occur while a nighttime hypnotic still impairs alertness.
**D. Use zolpidem to treat falls** — A hypnotic treats sleep complaints and carries fall risk. It has no established role in preventing falls.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 639.

q: A 79-year-old man with heart failure and cognitive impairment struggles with a complex medication regimen after discharge. Review identifies nonessential drugs and administration times that can be combined. Which structural change follows Hazzard's prescribing principles?
o: Add separate administration times to create more reminders
Retain nonessential medications to preserve familiar habits
Remove nonessential medications and combine administration times
Separate administration times to practice independent management
explanation:
Simplifying a regimen reduces the number of decisions a person must make each day while retaining effective treatment.

**Remove nonessential drugs and combine compatible administration times.** Cognitive impairment makes extra medication-taking steps particularly burdensome after discharge.

**A. Add administration times.** Each extra time creates another opportunity to forget or repeat a dose.
**B. Keep nonessential drugs.** Familiarity cannot supply a therapeutic indication and keeping them adds avoidable complexity.
**C. Remove drugs and combine times.** Eliminating unnecessary treatment and aligning compatible doses reduces the work of following the plan.
**D. Separate times for practice.** This makes daily treatment harder for someone already struggling with it.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 313–314.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An 81-year-old woman has lost about 8 lb and feels fatigued over recent months. She lives with her daughter, who works full time, and spends most days alone watching television and eating microwave meals. BMI is 19.5 and albumin 3.1 g/dL; PHQ-2 is negative, and the Berkman-Syme social network index indicates marked isolation. Which plan directly addresses mealtime isolation as part of nutritional care?
o: Provide oral nutritional supplements to consume alone at home.
Arrange delivered meals to consume alone at home.
Provide an appetite stimulant while maintaining solitary meals.
Arrange shared lunches through a senior-center meal program.
explanation:
A meal program can address food access, companionship or both. **Shared lunches at a senior center directly address her marked mealtime isolation.**

**A. Drink supplements alone** — They may add energy, but they do not bring another person to the table.
**B. Have meals delivered to eat alone** — Delivery helps with shopping and preparation. In this version of the plan, social isolation continues.
**C. Take an appetite stimulant** — Drug treatment leaves the social barrier in place and can introduce serious adverse effects.
**D. Attend shared lunches** — This provides a meal and people to eat with. Follow intake, weight and the remaining causes of weight loss.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 409–410 and 427, determinants of intake and feeding assistance.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: A sedentary 77-year-old woman with osteoarthritis wants to begin exercising. Her medical condition has been assessed and is stable. Which principle should guide the initial program?
o: Start at full workload and reduce it when marked pain develops
Choose a fixed workload and maintain it after capacity improves
Start at low workload and progress with capacity and response
Choose vigorous sessions and avoid pauses for recovery during exercise
explanation:
An exercise prescription should start from the workload a person can perform safely and recover from. Once that workload becomes easy, gradual progression provides the challenge needed for further improvement.

**Start at a low workload, check technique and symptoms, and increase the dose as capacity and recovery permit.**

**A. Start at full workload.** A sedentary beginner has little training reserve. Marked pain is a late signal that the opening dose was too high.
**B. Keep a fixed workload.** A workload that was challenging at the outset may become routine as fitness improves and will then offer less stimulus.
**C. Start low and progress.** Short, manageable sessions allow the patient to learn the movements and assess the next-day response before increasing effort.
**D. Vigorous sessions without pauses.** Older beginners often need recovery both between bouts and between sessions. Removing rest can turn an appropriate activity into excessive stress.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 824–825.

q: An 86-year-old man with moderate dementia, heart failure (EF 40%), and stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24; Cockcroft-Gault CrCl 22 mL/min) physically resists care and has thrown a cup at another resident. He takes donepezil 10 mg, carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily, and furosemide 20 mg daily. After assessing contributors and trying nonpharmacologic measures, dangerous aggression persists. If the risk-benefit assessment favors risperidone, which prescribing approach matches Hazzard?
o: Start low, monitor adverse effects, and titrate to the effective dose
Start at a high dose, then reduce treatment when behavioral control is established
Start several psychotropic drugs together, then identify the most useful combination
Continue treatment without a stop plan, using sedation as the principal target
explanation:
Risperidone can reduce aggression in some patients with dementia. Orthostasis, sedation and dose-related parkinsonism can compromise mobility, particularly in a frail patient with severe renal impairment.

**If a trial is justified, start low, titrate cautiously and monitor the target aggression and adverse effects.**

**A. Low starting dose** Use the minimum effective dose and reassess tolerability as exposure increases.
**B. High starting dose** Early hypotension or sedation may cause harm before benefit can be evaluated.
**C. Several drugs together** Concurrent changes obscure both the effective drug and the cause of an adverse effect.
**D. Sedation as target** Reduced alertness can conceal aggression while impairing function. Define the behavioral goal and plan reassessment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 927–928, Tables 60-7 and 60-8
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: A 75-year-old woman with documented cognitive decline still bathes and dresses independently. The clinician is distinguishing mild cognitive impairment from early dementia. Which financial-management finding, if caused by her cognitive decline, indicates loss of the independence required for MCI?
o: Managing finances independently but taking longer than before
Needing help with finances because of repeated errors
Managing finances independently but less efficiently than before
Managing finances independently but making more errors than before
explanation:
The boundary between mild cognitive impairment and dementia is loss of independence due to cognition. Complex tasks such as paying bills often change while basic self-care is still intact.

**Repeated financial errors that require someone else's help** cross that functional boundary.

**A. Taking longer.** Extra time to complete the bills independently is compatible with MCI.
**B. Needing help after errors.** Another person now has to participate for the task to be completed safely or correctly.
**C. Working less efficiently.** Reduced efficiency alone leaves independence intact.
**D. More errors while still independent.** Occasional errors can occur in MCI. The decisive change here is the need for another person's assistance.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 895–896, Table 59-2.
ref: Hazzard Ch 59 — DEMENTIA INCLUDING ALZHEIMER DISEASE

q: An 83-year-old man with advanced COPD, FEV1 30% predicted, coronary disease, and frailty with CFS 6 is hospitalized with pneumonia. After 48 hours of antibiotics, he remains on 4 L of oxygen with little improvement. He has no advance directive. His daughter asks the team to do everything. Which approach best begins a goals-of-care discussion?
o: Recommend a DNR order from the disease severity before exploring his values
Recommend comfort-focused care before establishing what outcomes he values
Explore what doing everything means to the patient and family
Defer discussion of values while continuing the current treatment plan
explanation:
A goals-of-care discussion translates a broad request into outcomes a person values. Severe illness makes discussion timely but does not specify a treatment preference.
**Ask what “doing everything” means to the patient and his daughter before recommending individual interventions.**

**A. Recommend DNR from disease severity** COPD, frailty and pneumonia help estimate the likely outcome of resuscitation. They do not reveal whether he would want it.
**B. Recommend comfort care first** Comfort may be his overriding goal, but his priorities and acceptable tradeoffs have yet to be explored.
**C. Explore the request** Ask him directly if he can participate, invite his daughter to explain her concerns, and relate the available treatments to their likely outcomes.
**D. Defer while treating** Continuing antibiotics and oxygen is compatible with discussing what to do if his breathing worsens.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 72, pp. 1098 and 1102–1103.

q: An older woman with recurrent falls takes amitriptyline for neuropathic pain. Which adverse-effect profile supports reassessing this medicine under the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Anticholinergic effects with sedation and orthostatic hypotension
Anticholinergic effects with alertness and improved postural stability
Sedative effects with protection against orthostatic blood-pressure changes
Antidepressant effects with alertness and improved postural stability
explanation:
Amitriptyline can relieve neuropathic pain but has substantial anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects. **Sedation and orthostatic hypotension add to its anticholinergic burden.**

**A. Anticholinergic, sedating and hypotensive** — Together these effects can impair attention and stability during the transition to standing.
**B. Anticholinergic but alert and stable** — Its anticholinergic activity is real. The proposed improvement in alertness and stability is inconsistent with its sedating effects.
**C. Sedating but protects standing pressure** — The sedation is plausible, while the claimed protection is reversed. The drug can produce orthostatic hypotension.
**D. Antidepressant and stabilizing** — An antidepressant indication describes therapeutic use and does not eliminate this tricyclic drug's adverse effects.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 2, p. 2059.

q: An 80-year-old man with mild Alzheimer dementia lives with his 82-year-old wife, who has severe arthritis. He has wandered outside twice this week. She manages their instrumental activities and appears exhausted. She says, "I promised we would never go to a nursing home." Which approach to discussing long-term services follows Hazzard?
o: Choose a home service from her stated preference before assessing their support needs
Choose a nursing facility from the dementia diagnosis before discussing service options
Explore their preferences and match available services to their assessed support needs
Choose a placement service from his wandering history before discussing their preferences
explanation:
Choosing long-term services begins with the older person's preferences, functional needs, caregiver capacity and available local programs. Wandering and exhaustion make the safety assessment urgent.
**Explore what each partner wants and match an available service plan to the supervision and assistance they actually need.**

**A. Choose from her preference alone.** Her wish to remain together matters, but it leaves unanswered who can supervise him and give her time away.
**B. Choose a facility from the diagnosis.** Mild dementia alone cannot determine his level of assistance or whether remaining home is feasible.
**C. Assess preferences and support together.** Ask how he wanders, when she needs help, who can take over, and whether available services cover those times.
**D. Choose placement from wandering alone.** Repeated wandering calls for a concrete supervision plan and a discussion of feasible settings with both partners.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 237–241, Spectrum of Care and Table 17-1.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
chapterTitle: COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE

q: A 78-year-old woman takes nitrofurantoin daily for long-term suppression of recurrent urinary tract infections. Her creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min. According to the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, which recommendation addresses the long-term suppression?
o: Stop long-term suppression and reassess the prevention plan
Continue long-term suppression with periodic renal-function monitoring
Reduce the daily dose and continue long-term suppression
Give the dose in the evening and continue long-term suppression
explanation:
Nitrofurantoin can cause pulmonary, hepatic, or peripheral nerve toxicity, particularly with prolonged exposure.

**Stop long-term suppression and reassess prevention.** Her creatinine clearance of 42 mL/min is above the separate renal cutoff, but duration is sufficient reason to reconsider.

**A. Stop suppression.** Removing prolonged exposure addresses toxicity risk while allowing a fresh review of recurrent infection prevention.
**B. Continue and monitor kidney function.** Renal monitoring cannot remove the pulmonary, hepatic, and neurologic risks of ongoing suppression.
**C. Reduce the daily dose.** A lower daily dose still leaves her on prolonged suppressive treatment.
**D. Give it at night.** Changing the hour of dosing does not shorten exposure.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, p. 2057.

q: An 85-year-old man develops delirium with inattention and disorganized thinking over one day. He has no fever, head trauma, focal neurologic deficit, or suspected seizure. The initial assessment has not found a cause, but medication review remains incomplete: his daughter provides a partial list including an unidentified sleep preparation. What should be completed next?
o: Obtain brain CT as the next component of the initial evaluation
Perform lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid testing next
Complete review of prescribed and nonprescription medications
Obtain EEG as the next component of the initial evaluation
explanation:
Medication reconciliation includes prescribed, as-needed and nonprescription products. A sleep preparation with unknown ingredients is a specific unresolved clue.
**Identify the sleep product, actual doses and recent changes before advancing to low-yield investigations.**

**A. Obtain brain CT as the next component of the initial evaluation.** Imaging becomes relevant with focal signs, trauma or persistent unexplained delirium after initial assessment.
**B. Perform lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid testing next.** There is no fever or other clue to meningeal or encephalitic infection.
**C. Complete review of prescribed and nonprescription medications.** The daughter can help identify the drug or obtain its container and dosing history.
**D. Obtain EEG as the next component of the initial evaluation.** EEG is useful especially when nonconvulsive seizures are suspected. The history here points to an unfinished medication review.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 885
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.885

q: A 74-year-old woman with diabetes and HbA1c 7.2% reports dizziness and near-falls. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glipizide 5 mg daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily, and recently began tramadol 50 mg three times daily for osteoarthritis pain. Pre-lunch glucose values are 68–75 mg/dL. When reviewing glipizide because of concern about hypoglycemia, which statement follows Hazzard?
o: Withdraw glipizide because sulfonylureas should be avoided when hypoglycemia is a concern
Continue glipizide because pancreatic insulin release is not part of its mechanism of action
Continue glipizide because hypoglycemia is not an adverse effect of its drug class
Substitute glyburide because its longer half-life lowers hypoglycemia risk in older people
explanation:
Sulfonylureas lower glucose by stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion. In a patient with low pre-lunch readings and near-falls, even a shorter-acting member can be hazardous.

**Withdraw glipizide when recurrent low values make hypoglycemia a concern.** Follow glucose and assess the other contributors to dizziness and falls separately.

**A. Withdraw glipizide.** Removing the secretagogue reduces a specific medication-related risk.
**B. Continue because insulin release is unrelated.** Beta-cell insulin release is the defining action of sulfonylureas.
**C. Continue because the class does not cause lows.** Hypoglycemia is a major limitation of this class in older adults.
**D. Switch to longer-acting glyburide.** Its longer half-life increases the likelihood that hypoglycemia will be prolonged.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp1577, 1579.

q: אישה הוגדרה כחולה הנוטה למות שאינה בעלת כשרות. אין הנחיות מקדימות, ייפוי כוח או החלטת ועדה, ובני המשפחה חלוקים בנוגע להזנה מלאכותית. איזה מידע רלוונטי לרופא האחראי בבירור רצונה לפי סעיף 5?
o: העדפת הבן לפי מיקומו בסדר הלידה במשפחה
העדפת רוב בני המשפחה לפי הצבעה ביניהם
הצהרה מפורשת של אדם קרוב על רצונה שלה
העדפת בן המשפחה שמבקר בתדירות הגבוהה ביותר
explanation:
האדם הקרוב נשאל מה החולה עצמה רצתה. בוחנים את עדותו במסגרת הדרך הקבועה לבירור הרצון. **הצהרה מפורשת של אדם קרוב על רצונה שלה**.

**א. העדפת הבן לפי מיקומו בסדר הלידה במשפחה.** לבכור אין עדיפות ראייתית מעצם הבכורה.
**ב. העדפת רוב בני המשפחה לפי הצבעה ביניהם.** רוב קולות משקף את עמדות המצביעים.
**ג. הצהרה מפורשת של אדם קרוב על רצונה שלה.** הצהרה מפורשת על רצונה רלוונטית להכרעת הרופא.
**ד. העדפת בן המשפחה שמבקר בתדירות הגבוהה ביותר.** ביקורים תכופים עשויים לבסס היכרות אך אינם נותנים קול מכריע.

אסמכתא · חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס״ו-2005, עמ׳ 6.

q: A 79-year-old man awaiting a below-knee amputation asks about returning to mobility with a prosthesis. Which functional assessment supports rehabilitation planning according to Hazzard?
o: Assess potential from arm strength and chronological age
Assess previous walking, medical status, and ability to learn
Assess potential from kidney disease stage and chronological age
Assess potential from diabetes duration and the prosthesis type
explanation:
Walking with a prosthesis requires physical reserve and learning new skills, including transfers, balance and care of the residual limb. Earlier walking ability provides a starting point for setting a realistic mobility goal.

**Assess how he walked before the illness, whether his medical and cardiopulmonary status can support prosthetic walking, and whether he can learn the technique.**

**A. Arm strength and age.** Arm strength matters for transfers and early use of an aid. It cannot by itself predict a return to walking, and age is no substitute for assessment.
**B. Previous walking, medical status and learning.** Together these identify his starting function, capacity for the energy demands of walking and ability to master the prosthesis.
**C. Kidney disease stage and age.** Comorbid illness affects reserve and healing, but these two descriptors say little about his previous mobility or ability to learn.
**D. Diabetes duration and prosthesis type.** Diabetes may affect healing and sensation. Choose the prosthetic components after assessing functional potential.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 830–831.

q: An 84-year-old man with renal impairment, reduced fluid intake, and mild dementia develops delirium. He takes morphine and gabapentin and now has hypotension and worsening kidney function. Which approach addresses potentially treatable contributors?
o: Review medication while evaluating acute illness and fluid status
Reduce one medication and defer other evaluation pending the response
Start sedation and defer evaluation of the physical changes
Attribute the change to dementia and repeat cognitive testing later
explanation:
Delirium can result from several simultaneous insults. As renal function declines, gabapentin and active morphine metabolites can accumulate and increase sedation. **Assess the hypotension and fluid status promptly while reviewing both medicines and looking for acute illness.**

**A. Evaluate the patient and the medicines together.** Check perfusion, oxygenation, renal function, actual doses and timing. Reduced intake and worsening kidney function can amplify drug effects even without a recent prescription change.
**B. Reduce one drug and wait.** A dose adjustment may help, but hypotension requires evaluation now. A response to one change would not rule out infection or volume depletion.
**C. Sedate first.** Additional sedation can worsen or obscure depressed arousal while the circulatory problem persists.
**D. Attribute the change to dementia.** Mild dementia increases vulnerability to delirium. It does not account for the abrupt cognitive change with hypotension and renal deterioration.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 881–882, 885. NEURONTIN and morphine sulfate prescribing information, section 12.3 (renal impairment).

q: A 79-year-old woman is brought by her daughter for routine follow-up. She has fallen twice in the past month and seems more forgetful. She lives alone and manages her finances, but recently burned a pot while cooking. She takes donepezil 10 mg daily, amitriptyline 50 mg at night for neuropathic pain, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Blood pressure is 128/78 sitting and 108/65 after three minutes standing. Her Mini-Cog score is 2/5. Which approach to amitriptyline addresses the medication concern identified in Beers 2023?
o: Retain amitriptyline because it has little effect on standing blood pressure
Review amitriptyline for discontinuation because of anticholinergic and orthostatic effects
Increase amitriptyline because stronger anticholinergic activity supports cognitive function
Replace amitriptyline with imipramine to avoid the strongly anticholinergic antidepressant group
explanation:
Amitriptyline blocks muscarinic receptors, causes sedation, and can lower blood pressure on standing. These effects matter in a patient with falls and new difficulty managing at home.

**Review amitriptyline for discontinuation.** Her fall history and documented postural pressure drop make the risk especially relevant.

**A. Retain it as blood-pressure neutral.** Amitriptyline can worsen postural hypotension and dizziness.
**B. Review discontinuation.** Removing a possible contributor to impaired thinking and orthostasis can clarify how much function is reversible.
**C. Increase for cognition.** Stronger anticholinergic exposure can worsen cognitive impairment.
**D. Replace with imipramine.** Imipramine is also a strongly anticholinergic tricyclic and shares the concerns prompting review.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, p. 2059.

q: בישראל, חולה שנקבע לגביו שהוא נוטה למות כבר קיבל החלטה על היקף הטיפול הרצוי לו. במהלך האשפוז משתנים מצבו הנשימתי ורצונו ביחס לטיפול. מה נדרש מהרופא האחראי לפי החוק?
o: להותיר את התוכנית הקודמת עד שיסתיים האשפוז הנוכחי
להעריך את השינוי ולחזור ולהחליט על דרך הטיפול
להסתמך על ההחלטה הראשונה עד לביקורת במרפאה
להעביר את ההחלטה לצוות הבא בלי הערכה מחודשת
explanation:
**הרופא האחראי חוזר ומעריך את דרך הטיפול** כשמשתנים המצב הרפואי או רצון החולה. יש לתעד את הממצאים, את כשירות החולה ואת ההחלטה המעודכנת.

**א. המתנה לסוף האשפוז.** החמרה נשימתית עשויה לדרוש שינוי טיפול באותו יום.
**ב. הערכה והחלטה מחודשת.** משלבות את המצב העדכני עם המטרות והרצון העכשוויים.
**ג. המתנה למרפאה.** משאירה תוכנית שכבר אינה מתאימה.
**ד. העברה לצוות הבא.** העברת משמרת מחייבת מסירה מסודרת ואינה תחליף להערכה הנדרשת כעת.

אסמכתא · חוק החולה הנוטה למות, סעיפים 8–12.
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: A woman taking metformin is hospitalized with a severe acute illness that reduces tissue perfusion. Which risk explains avoiding metformin in this setting?
o: Lactic acidosis in the setting of reduced tissue perfusion
Excess insulin in the setting of pancreatic stimulation
Metabolic alkalosis in the setting of increased acid loss
Fluid overload in the setting of increased sodium retention
explanation:
In severe systemic illness, inadequate perfusion promotes lactate accumulation. Metformin poses a rare but important lactic acidosis risk in that setting.

**Withhold metformin because tissue hypoperfusion can precipitate lactic acidosis.** Reassess perfusion and renal function as the patient recovers.

**A. Lactic acidosis.** Poor blood flow and possible impaired drug clearance turn a usually well-tolerated drug into a safety concern.
**B. Excess insulin from pancreatic stimulation.** This mechanism fits insulin secretagogues and does not explain the metformin precaution.
**C. Alkalosis from acid loss.** The feared disturbance is an acidosis associated with lactate.
**D. Fluid overload from sodium retention.** This is characteristic of thiazolidinediones and does not explain avoiding metformin.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p1576.

q: An 82-year-old man recently returned from rehabilitation after a hip fracture. His daughter reports that he sleeps 14 hours daily, eats little, and no longer reads the newspaper. Medicines added during admission were oxycodone 5 mg every six hours as needed, quetiapine 25 mg at night for sleep, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and docusate 100 mg twice daily. Before the fracture he was independent in all instrumental activities of daily living; his current IADL score is 3/8. Which approach to the quetiapine insomnia prescription follows Hazzard?
o: Continue quetiapine because trials establish its routine benefit for insomnia
Increase quetiapine because sedation establishes its safety for older adults
Review quetiapine for discontinuation because routine insomnia use is discouraged
Replace quetiapine with diphenhydramine as the primary treatment for chronic insomnia
explanation:
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic with sedating effects. In a patient sleeping 14 hours a day after it was added solely for sleep, **review it for discontinuation** and assess other causes of new functional decline.

**A. Continue for routine insomnia benefit** Evidence for routine insomnia treatment is limited, particularly without a separate psychiatric indication.
**B. Increase because it sedates** More sedation could worsen alertness and function, especially with concurrent oxycodone.
**C. Review for discontinuation** Removing an unnecessary sedating drug addresses a plausible contributor to hypersomnolence.
**D. Replace with diphenhydramine** Its anticholinergic effects and residual sedation make it unsuitable as primary insomnia therapy.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 661.

q: A 91-year-old woman with vascular dementia and chronic kidney disease develops acute confusion in assisted living. Evaluation finds no urinary symptoms, fever, or hemodynamic instability. Urinalysis shows pyuria and a few bacteria, and nitrofurantoin was started for suspected UTI. Which approach follows the source’s advice about nonspecific symptoms without localizing evidence of UTI?
o: Continue nitrofurantoin and add medication for agitation
Replace nitrofurantoin with a broader-spectrum antibiotic
Stop nitrofurantoin, monitor, and evaluate other causes
Continue nitrofurantoin while awaiting a urine culture
explanation:
Bacteriuria and pyuria are common in older residents and can coexist with delirium for unrelated reasons. Without urinary symptoms, fever or instability, **stop empiric nitrofurantoin, monitor and investigate other causes of confusion**.

**A. Continue and add an agitation drug.** This treats neither a demonstrated urinary syndrome nor the cause of delirium.
**B. Broaden antibiotic therapy.** The problem is a lack of a clinical indication, not inadequate antibiotic breadth.
**C. Stop, monitor and evaluate.** Assess medications, hydration, metabolic disturbances and other illnesses and reassess if new signs appear.
**D. Continue pending culture.** A positive culture can also represent asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 885, 1703.

q: A 78-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes two hours to finish his morning routine, has difficulty fastening buttons, and walks with a shuffling gait. His MMSE is 24 and he pauses before answering. He also reports constipation and blurred vision. His drugs are carbidopa–levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily, ropinirole 2 mg three times daily, trihexyphenidyl 2 mg twice daily, and trazodone 50 mg at night. Which change addresses the antimuscarinic exposure that Hazzard advises avoiding at his age?
o: Increase levodopa while continuing trihexyphenidyl
Add rivastigmine while continuing trihexyphenidyl
Discontinue trihexyphenidyl during medication review
Increase ropinirole while continuing trihexyphenidyl
explanation:
Trihexyphenidyl blocks muscarinic receptors and can lessen tremor. In an older patient its central effects can impair thinking, while peripheral effects can aggravate constipation and blurred vision.

**Discontinue trihexyphenidyl during medication review.** At age 78, the antimuscarinic burden is a modifiable contributor worth addressing before adding another drug.

**A. Increase levodopa.** More levodopa may help slow movements but leaves the antimuscarinic exposure in place.
**B. Add rivastigmine.** It increases available acetylcholine while trihexyphenidyl continues to block its action at muscarinic receptors.
**C. Discontinue trihexyphenidyl.** Removing the offending drug allows cognition, bowel symptoms and tremor to be reassessed.
**D. Increase ropinirole.** This maintains trihexyphenidyl and adds exposure to an agonist that can itself cause hallucinations and confusion.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 946–948.
ref: Hazzard Ch 61 — PARKINSON DISEASE AND RELATED DISORDERS

q: An 86-year-old woman with heart failure and congestion is receiving a loop diuretic. After treatment adjustment her congestion improves and creatinine rises slightly. Which monitoring principle follows Hazzard?
o: Reduce diuresis for the creatinine rise despite persistent congestion
Assess volume status and electrolytes alongside the creatinine change
Use the creatinine change as the measure of fluid removal
Add metolazone to reduce the need for electrolyte monitoring
explanation:
A loop diuretic removes sodium and water from the congested circulation. **Interpret a small creatinine rise alongside congestion, perfusion and electrolytes** before deciding how much more fluid to remove.

**A. Reduce treatment for creatinine alone** Persistent venous congestion can itself impair kidney function, so a modest rise alone cannot determine the next dose.
**B. Reassess volume and electrolytes** Weight, edema, breathlessness, blood pressure, urine output and potassium help distinguish effective decongestion from volume depletion.
**C. Use creatinine to measure fluid removal** Creatinine reflects filtration and changes in concentration. It does not measure liters removed.
**D. Add metolazone to simplify monitoring** Additional distal sodium blockade increases the risk of brisk water loss, hyponatremia and hypokalemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1182.

q: A medication review after a fall identifies zolpidem use for sleep in an older adult. How do the 2023 Beers Criteria characterize the balance of benefit and harm for Z-drugs?
o: Substantial sleep improvement with fewer delirium and fall events than benzodiazepines
Substantial sleep improvement with less cognitive impairment than benzodiazepines
Minimal sleep improvement with adverse events similar to benzodiazepines
Minimal sleep improvement with increased risk attributed chiefly to benzodiazepines
explanation:
Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic acting at benzodiazepine receptors. **It provides little improvement in sleep latency or duration and carries risks similar to benzodiazepines in older adults.**

**A. Substantial improvement and fewer falls** — Sleep improves only slightly, and falls, fractures and delirium remain concerns with Z-drugs.
**B. Substantial improvement and less cognitive impairment** — Cognitive adverse effects, including delirium, remain possible despite the different chemical class.
**C. Minimal improvement with similar adverse events** — A small sleep benefit comes at the cost of risks that matter particularly after a fall.
**D. Minimal improvement with risk mainly from benzodiazepines** — Zolpidem itself contributes to adverse events, including falls, fractures and emergency visits.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 2, p. 2060.

q: An older woman with hypernatremia and water deficit cannot drink safely. She also has intravascular volume depletion that threatens cardiovascular stability. What sequence of fluid treatment matches Hazzard?
o: Replace free water intravenously before restoring intravascular volume
Give oral water replacement before restoring intravascular volume
Withhold fluid replacement until the serum sodium has normalized
Restore intravascular volume with saline before using hypotonic fluid
explanation:
Hypernatremia reflects a deficit of water relative to solute, but threatened circulation takes priority. **Restore intravascular volume with isotonic saline, then correct the free-water deficit with hypotonic fluid.**

**A. Replace free water intravenously before restoring intravascular volume.** Free water alone distributes throughout total body water and is inefficient for immediate circulatory resuscitation.
**B. Give oral water replacement before restoring intravascular volume.** She cannot drink safely, and drinking would not provide prompt volume resuscitation.
**C. Withhold fluid replacement until the serum sodium has normalized.** Withholding fluid permits shock and hypernatremia to worsen.
**D. Restore intravascular volume with saline before using hypotonic fluid.** Treat perfusion first, then replace free water at a rate guided by duration, ongoing losses and serial sodium.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 588.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS

q: A 79-year-old woman with mild dementia and pneumonia develops delirium after receiving diphenhydramine for sleep. What should the medication assessment consider?
o: A medication effect that protects against confusion during infection
A medication contribution alongside the effects of the infection
A medication effect that excludes infection as a contributor
A medication effect that establishes progression of dementia
explanation:
Pneumonia can precipitate delirium, especially in a patient with impaired cognitive reserve. An anticholinergic given during the same illness can lower the threshold further.
**Consider the diphenhydramine and infection together, and remove the unnecessary sleep drug.**

**A. A medication effect that protects against confusion during infection.** Diphenhydramine can impair attention and offers no protection against delirium.
**B. A medication contribution alongside the effects of the infection.** The new exposure adds a modifiable insult to an already vulnerable patient.
**C. A medication effect that excludes infection as a contributor.** A drug contribution does not make the simultaneous infection irrelevant.
**D. A medication effect that establishes progression of dementia.** An acute change after two insults is insufficient to diagnose progression of dementia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 881–883, Table 58-2

q: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops confusion and visual hallucinations after amantadine is added. Which benefit-risk pairing explains why the treatment should be reassessed?
o: Reduced dyskinesia with a tendency to block dopaminergic activity
Reduced dyskinesia with a tendency to improve visual hallucinations
Reduced dyskinesia with a risk of confusion and hallucinations
Reduced dyskinesia with a tendency to decrease ankle edema
explanation:
Amantadine can lessen levodopa-induced involuntary movements through its antiglutamatergic action. Older adults may find its effects on cognition and perception harder to tolerate than the movements themselves.

**Amantadine can reduce dyskinesia and also cause confusion and visual hallucinations.** Their appearance soon after it was added is a reason to reassess its benefit.

**A. Dopamine blockade.** Amantadine promotes dopamine release and reduces its uptake. Dopamine-receptor blockade is the wrong mechanism.
**B. Improved hallucinations.** Amantadine can provoke visual hallucinations in a susceptible patient.
**C. Reduced dyskinesia with mental adverse effects.** The motor benefit and the change in mental state can both be effects of the same drug.
**D. Reduced ankle edema.** Ankle edema is another adverse effect of amantadine, alongside livedo reticularis.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 944.
ref: Hazzard Ch 61 — PARKINSON DISEASE AND RELATED DISORDERS

q: An 88-year-old woman with advanced COPD is seen in palliative care. She uses continuous oxygen and a wheelchair and needs assistance with all activities of daily living. Because of treatment burden, she asks to stop her medications, including prednisone taken daily for two years. What approach applies if chronic prednisone is discontinued?
o: Stop prednisone and monitor for recurrent respiratory symptoms
Stop prednisone and restart it if fatigue develops
Taper prednisone gradually to allow adrenal-axis recovery
Stop prednisone and reserve replacement for a future illness
explanation:
Daily prednisone can suppress endogenous ACTH and cortisol production for months. **If her goals and respiratory status allow withdrawal after two years, taper gradually and reassess as the dose approaches physiologic replacement.**

**A. Stop and watch breathing** — Monitoring COPD alone misses hypotension, weakness and gastrointestinal symptoms from cortisol deficiency.
**B. Stop and restart for fatigue** — Fatigue is nonspecific and an adrenal crisis may develop before a trial of oral prednisone is practical.
**C. Taper gradually** — A tailored taper reduces the risk of symptomatic deficiency while the adrenal axis recovers and allows respiratory symptoms to guide comfort care.
**D. Reserve steroids for future illness** — Basal cortisol can already be inadequate during withdrawal even before a new stressor occurs.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532. ESE/Endocrine Society glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency guideline (2024), recommendations 2.2–2.8.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: During medication review for an older adult with recurrent hypoglycemia, which glucose-lowering drug class does Hazzard advise avoiding when hypoglycemia is a concern?
o: Treatment with DPP-4 inhibitors.
Treatment with sulfonylurea drugs.
Treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
Treatment with GLP-1 agonists.
explanation:
The risk of hypoglycemia depends partly on whether a drug keeps raising insulin as glucose falls. Sulfonylureas stimulate endogenous insulin and can outlast the protective effect of a meal.

**Avoid sulfonylureas when recurrent hypoglycemia is a concern.** Glyburide is especially problematic because its effect can persist.

**A. DPP-4 inhibitors.** Their glucose-dependent incretin effect makes hypoglycemia uncommon in monotherapy.
**B. Sulfonylureas.** Insulin release continues despite poor or irregular intake, leaving the patient vulnerable to a low.
**C. SGLT2 inhibitors.** They increase urinary glucose excretion. Volume depletion and genital infection are different concerns.
**D. GLP-1 receptor agonists.** Their insulin effect is glucose dependent. Gastrointestinal symptoms and weight loss are more characteristic.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp1577–1580, Table 99-11.

q: An 85-year-old woman living independently has stopped hosting family meals and needs help with shopping, cooking, and medication management. Cognitive testing shows recall and clock-drawing difficulties. Examination and laboratory results are normal, and MRI shows mild atrophy. Donepezil has been started. Which additional approach directly evaluates her daily care needs and home safety?
o: Use medication-dose escalation in place of evaluating daily task performance
Arrange an in-home occupational therapy assessment to guide practical support
Use the cognitive screening score in place of evaluating daily task performance
Use the degree of MRI atrophy in place of evaluating daily task performance
explanation:
Cognitive testing estimates impairment, while observing an activity reveals which step fails and what support makes it safe. This patient has difficulty with complex tasks in her usual environment.

**Arrange occupational therapy assessment in the home.**

**A. Increase medication** A prescription change cannot show whether she can handle her medicines or prepare a meal safely.
**B. Home assessment** Observation of task performance and the home layout guides adaptations and supervision.
**C. Cognitive score** It describes test performance without measuring how she manages her own kitchen and medications.
**D. MRI atrophy** Anatomic change offers little practical guidance on where help is needed in the home.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 924–925, Table 60-5
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: An 87-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 22/30) and hypertension is seen in the emergency department after a fall at his assisted-living facility. His daughter reports two other falls during the past month. He takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, donepezil 10 mg daily, and trazodone 50 mg at bedtime. Blood pressure is 138/82 sitting and 118/70 after three minutes standing. Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min. Which approach to his insomnia treatment is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Review trazodone and introduce a behavioral insomnia treatment plan
Increase trazodone because it improves orthostatic blood-pressure control
Replace trazodone with diphenhydramine as primary treatment for chronic insomnia
Retain trazodone because sustained benefit is established in nondepressed patients
explanation:
Trazodone is a sedating antidepressant that can cause orthostatic hypotension. **Review trazodone and begin behavioral insomnia care** in this patient with recurrent falls and a systolic drop of 20 mm Hg on standing.

**A. Medication review and behavioral treatment** This addresses a plausible fall contributor while treating insomnia.
**B. Increase trazodone** The drug may worsen postural hypotension and morning drowsiness.
**C. Switch to diphenhydramine** Its cognitive and sedative adverse effects are particularly undesirable with preexisting impairment.
**D. Continue for established sustained benefit** Evidence of lasting benefit for insomnia in nondepressed patients is limited.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 659, 661–662.

q: A patient with Parkinson disease develops motor worsening after starting metoclopramide. Which mechanism-and-risk pairing explains the Beers recommendation to avoid it?
o: Dopamine-receptor blockade with a risk of worsening parkinsonian symptoms
Dopamine-receptor activation with a risk of worsening parkinsonian symptoms
Dopamine-receptor blockade with an expected improvement in parkinsonian symptoms
Dopamine-receptor activation with an expected improvement in parkinsonian symptoms
explanation:
Metoclopramide relieves nausea partly through dopamine D2 receptor blockade. Blockade in motor pathways can aggravate the movement disorder already present in Parkinson disease.

**Dopamine-receptor blockade can worsen parkinsonian symptoms.** New rigidity or slowing after starting this antiemetic is a reason to review its use.

**A. Blockade with worsening.** Antagonism reduces dopamine signaling in the basal ganglia and can worsen movement.
**B. Activation with worsening.** Metoclopramide is a receptor antagonist. It does not stimulate dopamine receptors.
**C. Blockade with improvement.** Parkinsonian slowness and rigidity can worsen when central dopamine signaling is blocked.
**D. Activation with improvement.** This pairing describes the intended motor effect of a dopamine agonist, a different drug class.

Reference · American Geriatrics Society 2023 Beers Criteria, Table 3, p. 2067.

q: גבר בן 84 עם heart failure (EF 35%) ו-CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22) מגיע לקליניקה. אשתו מדווחת שהוא מבולבל יותר בימים האחרונים וישן במהלך היום. התרופות כוללות furosemide 80mg BID, spironolactone 25mg daily, metoprolol 50mg BID, ו-gabapentin 300mg TID לנוירופתיה. תוצאות מעבדה: K+ 5.8, Na+ 134, BUN 78, Cr 3.2. איזו התאמה תרופתית היא המתאימה ביותר?
o: הפסקת spironolactone
הפחתת gabapentin ל-300mg daily
החלפת furosemide ב-bumetanide
הפחתת metoprolol ל-25mg BID
explanation:
Gabapentin is cleared by the kidneys and can accumulate in advanced kidney disease. Spironolactone can independently raise potassium to dangerous levels.

**Reduce gabapentin from 300 mg three times daily to 300 mg daily to address possible drug-related somnolence.** The potassium of 5.8 also requires urgent assessment and a decision about holding spironolactone.

**A. Stop spironolactone.** Hyperkalemia with severe renal impairment makes withholding this potassium-sparing drug clinically defensible while the patient is assessed.
**B. Reduce gabapentin.** Reducing exposure can relieve sedation or confusion. The individual regimen should be checked against renal function.
**C. Switch loop diuretics.** Changing furosemide to bumetanide leaves the excessive gabapentin exposure unaddressed.
**D. Halve metoprolol.** No symptomatic bradycardia or hypotension is described to justify this change as the response to somnolence.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 6, pp. 2072–2073. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Heart Failure Guideline, §7.3.3.
Key note: The AGS criteria also advise avoiding spironolactone below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. Heart failure guidance calls for discontinuation if potassium cannot be kept below 5.5 mEq/L. Gabapentin reduction alone leaves an urgent competing problem.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING
retiredReason: Two defensible answers by Hazzard pp. 1181-1182; a look-alike question teaches the opposite.

q: A 91-year-old woman with moderate dementia has increasing agitation and refuses medication. She has round-the-clock caregivers, an MMSE score of 14/30, and needs assistance with all activities of daily living. Her family requests risperidone. Her daughter, the healthcare proxy, says, "We want her comfortable without hastening her death." Which approach follows the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Begin risperidone before behavioral approaches, relying on continuous supervision for safety.
Discuss stroke and mortality risks and assess nonpharmacologic approaches before prescribing.
Substitute scheduled lorazepam before behavioral approaches, relying on its cognitive safety.
Begin risperidone without a risk discussion, relying on comfort as sufficient justification.
explanation:
In dementia, antipsychotics can increase stroke, cognitive decline and mortality. **Discuss these risks, assess reversible distress and try appropriate nonpharmacologic approaches.** For dementia-related agitation, reserve a limited trial for behavior threatening substantial harm when safer measures have failed or are not feasible. Refusal of medication alone does not meet that threshold.

**A. Start risperidone under supervision.** Caregivers can monitor behavior, but supervision does not prevent drug-related stroke or death.
**B. Discuss risks and behavioral care.** Involve the woman as far as possible and discuss comfort goals with her proxy. Define the target behavior, likely benefit, risks and a plan for reassessment.
**C. Scheduled lorazepam.** Benzodiazepines can worsen confusion and increase falls, so there is no assurance of cognitive safety.
**D. Prescribe solely for comfort.** Comfort is a priority but does not demonstrate that risperidone's expected benefit outweighs its harms in the absence of dangerous behavior.

Reference · AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 2, p. 2060, and dementia/cognitive impairment criterion in Table 3, p. 2066.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp.2059, 2066, Tables 2–3

q: An 82-year-old man develops hyponatremia after starting sertraline. Sodium is 124 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and the urine is concentrated. He is euvolemic without edema, orthostasis, or signs of heart failure. Renal function is stable, and thyroid and adrenal function are normal. Which mechanism best fits?
o: Hypervolemic hyponatremia due to heart failure
Euvolemic hyponatremia due to drug-associated SIADH
Hypovolemic hyponatremia due to fluid losses
Hypervolemic hyponatremia due to nephrotic syndrome
explanation:
In hypo-osmolar hyponatremia, healthy kidneys should excrete dilute urine. **Drug-associated SIADH** fits euvolemia, concentrated urine and recent sertraline exposure after adrenal and thyroid disease have been excluded.

**A. Heart failure.** This generally produces hypervolemic hyponatremia with clinical evidence of congestion.
**B. Euvolemic SIADH.** Persistent antidiuretic activity retains water despite low serum osmolality. Sertraline is a plausible contributor.
**C. Volume loss.** Orthostasis or other signs of depletion would support this mechanism and are absent here.
**D. Nephrotic syndrome.** Edema and evidence of heavy urinary protein loss would be expected in that hypervolemic setting.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS

q: A 76-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension is brought by her daughter because she leaves the stove on and forgets medications. MMSE is 24/30 with memory and orientation deficits. HbA1c is 9.2%. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, glyburide 10 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 20 mg daily. BP is 142/84 and Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance is 48 mL/min. Which paired approach best reflects Hazzard’s concerns about drug choice and treatment intensity?
o: Retain glyburide for its short half-life; consider less intensive glycemic targets
Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment
Avoid glyburide for its hypoglycemia risk; consider less intensive glycemic targets
Retain glyburide for its short half-life; intensify treatment because of cognitive impairment
explanation:
Diabetes self-management requires memory and planning. A long-acting secretagogue adds risk when a patient misses meals, doubles a dose or fails to recognize a low.

**Avoid glyburide and choose an individualized, potentially less intensive target.** An A1C of 9.2% still merits attention, but the route to better control should be safe and workable with support.

**A. Retain glyburide and relax the target.** A less stringent target may fit, but glyburide has a long half-life and can cause prolonged hypoglycemia.
**B. Avoid glyburide and intensify because of cognitive impairment.** The drug concern is right. Cognitive impairment increases the burden and risk of intensive treatment.
**C. Avoid glyburide and individualize the target.** This addresses both the pharmacologic risk and the ability to carry out treatment safely.
**D. Retain glyburide and intensify.** Both premises undermine safety when medication errors are already apparent.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp1568, 1571, 1579.

q: An 88-year-old man is found after lying for a prolonged period in a cold environment. His core temperature is 30°C, with a pulse and spontaneous breathing. After initial stabilization, which approach to hypothermia is supported by Hazzard?
o: Passive rewarming in a warm room, volume replacement, and ECG monitoring
External rewarming with an electric blanket, volume replacement, and ECG monitoring
Active rewarming of the body core, volume replacement, and ECG monitoring
External rewarming in a warm bath, volume replacement, and ECG monitoring
explanation:
At 30°C, accidental hypothermia can cause arrhythmias and circulatory failure despite a pulse. **Actively rewarm the patient, monitor the ECG and core temperature, and replace volume as indicated.** Blood pressure, rhythm and response to warming guide the method. A pulse alone cannot confirm circulatory stability.

**A. Passive warming only.** Insulation prevents further loss, but a warm room alone may be inadequate at 30°C.
**B. Active external warming.** Controlled heat applied to the trunk, such as forced-air warming, can be appropriate when circulation is stable. Monitor the response rather than assuming a blanket is sufficient.
**C. Active core rewarming.** Restore core temperature under monitoring. Escalate to internal or extracorporeal techniques for instability, arrest or failure to rewarm as clinically indicated.
**D. Warm bath.** Peripheral vasodilation can worsen hypotension, and a bath makes safe monitoring and resuscitation difficult.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 583–584. ERC Guidelines 2025, Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Figure 5.
Key note: Hazzard calls for active core rewarming below 32°C. Contemporary guidance allows monitored active external trunk warming with stable circulation. A temperature of 30°C alone does not mandate an invasive technique.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS

q: A 77-year-old woman with COPD and knee osteoarthritis has persistent knee pain despite acetaminophen. She has fallen twice this month and attributes this to knee pain. She takes tiotropium, albuterol, calcium, and vitamin D, has an MMSE score of 28/30, uses a walker, and has creatinine clearance of 38 mL/min. Which pharmacologic step follows Hazzard’s approach before oral NSAIDs or opioid escalation?
o: Apply topical diclofenac to the painful knee joints
Begin oral tramadol for the persistent knee pain
Begin oral celecoxib for the persistent knee pain
Begin oral hydrocodone with acetaminophen for knee pain
explanation:
Knee OA is accessible to a topical anti-inflammatory, while recurrent falls and reduced renal clearance make systemic escalation consequential. **Apply diclofenac locally and reassess pain and walking.**

**A. Topical diclofenac** — It addresses the painful joints with lower systemic exposure. The falls still deserve assessment beyond their presumed relationship to pain.
**B. Tramadol** — Dizziness and somnolence can compound falls, and opioid exposure adds respiratory risk in someone with COPD.
**C. Celecoxib** — COX-2 selectivity does not protect renal perfusion. Oral exposure is avoidable while a local option remains.
**D. Hydrocodone with acetaminophen** — This adds a stronger opioid before a topical trial, together with sedation, respiratory risk and another source of acetaminophen.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 787–788, Topical NSAIDs and Narcotic analgesics. ACR/Arthritis Foundation OA guideline.

q: An 83-year-old nursing-home resident with dementia becomes restless during bathing and personal care, then returns to baseline after reassurance without a new change in attention. He is stable, has no dysuria, new urinary symptom, flank pain, or fever, and has no catheter. A urine sample that was sent shows pyuria and nitrites. What is the appropriate approach?
o: Start ciprofloxacin because the nitrites justify attributing the behavioral episode to infection
Start nitrofurantoin because the pyuria justifies attributing the behavioral episode to infection
Assess other causes and monitor without antibiotics based on the urine findings
Repeat urinalysis daily and base antibiotic treatment on subsequent changes in pyuria
explanation:
Behavioral distress during personal care can have situational causes. This resident settles with reassurance and has no new inattention, urinary symptoms or systemic illness. **Assess discomfort and other triggers and observe without antibiotics.**

**A. Ciprofloxacin for nitrites.** Nitrites suggest bacteria in urine but do not identify a symptomatic infection.
**B. Nitrofurantoin for pyuria.** Urinary white cells can accompany colonization.
**C. Assess and monitor.** The timing with bathing and return to baseline support looking for pain, fear or environmental distress.
**D. Daily urine tests.** Changing pyuria does not substitute for new clinical signs or symptoms.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1704–1705.

q: A 79-year-old woman is diagnosed with major depression after evaluation of weight loss and withdrawal from social activities. She wishes to consider psychotherapy before starting medication. Which statement matches Hazzard?
o: Psychotherapy may be delivered as open-ended work without defined goals
Structured psychotherapy may improve mood and develop coping skills
Psychotherapy may be selected with no need to define treatment processes
The same psychotherapy may be continued without reviewing a lack of improvement
explanation:
Psychotherapy for late-life depression can use cognitive, behavioral or interpersonal techniques to address problems the patient identifies. Effective treatment has agreed goals and a way to judge progress.
**Offer structured psychotherapy to improve mood and help her develop coping skills.**

**A. Open-ended treatment without goals.** Depression trials used time-limited approaches with explicit goals. A goal such as resuming a valued social activity makes progress observable.
**B. Structured psychotherapy.** An older adult who prefers this option can benefit. Discuss the approach, availability, target symptoms and follow-up.
**C. Leave the process undefined.** Explain what sessions involve and how she and the therapist will assess change.
**D. Continue unchanged despite no improvement.** Reassess after roughly one to two months without improvement and consider another modality or treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1014

q: A patient with HFpEF receives a diuretic for congestion. Creatinine rises, but congestion persists, urine output is adequate, and blood pressure and perfusion remain stable without signs of hypovolemia. Which principle should guide ongoing treatment?
o: Adjust diuresis to congestion and hemodynamic status
Hold the diuretic and begin correction of presumed volume depletion
Increase the diuretic and add metolazone immediately
Hold the diuretic until creatinine returns to baseline
explanation:
In HFpEF both residual congestion and excessive volume removal can harm the kidneys. **Use clinical congestion and perfusion to guide the diuretic** when urine output and pressure remain adequate.

**A. Titrate to hemodynamics** This patient remains congested without evidence of depletion. Follow the creatinine trend, electrolytes and response during adjustment.
**B. Treat presumed depletion** Giving fluid solely for a creatinine rise may worsen the elevated filling pressure.
**C. Escalate immediately to combination treatment** First judge response to the loop dose and route. Metolazone carries additional electrolyte risk.
**D. Wait for baseline creatinine** Withholding decongestion until a laboratory value normalizes can prolong venous congestion.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1182, 1186.

q: אישה בת 90 בישראל עם מחלת ריאות חסימתית קשה אושפזה בשל דלקת ריאות. הרופא האחראי קבע שהיא חולה הנוטה למות. לאחר ייצובה נמצאה בעלת כשרות לקבל החלטות, והיא יכולה להשתתף בשיחה על הנשמה אם מצבה יחמיר. היא ובנה קיבלו מידע על אפשרות זו. בעבר אמרה לרופא המשפחה שאינה רוצה להיות מחוברת למכונות, ואילו בנה מבקש שיעשו הכול. על מה יש לבסס את בירור רצונה כעת לפי חוק החולה הנוטה למות?
o: העדפת בנה לאחר ששמע על התועלת והסיכונים של הנשמה
רצונה המפורש לאחר שקיבלה מידע על אפשרות ההנשמה
דבריה הישנים על מכונות כפי שתועדו אצל רופא המשפחה
הערכת הצוות את איכות חייה על סמך הגיל ומחלת הרקע
explanation:
חולה כשירה יכולה להכריע כעת אם היא רוצה בהנשמה. מסבירים את מטרתה, הסיכון, התוצאות הצפויות והחלופות ושומעים את רצונה. **רצונה המפורש לאחר שקיבלה מידע על אפשרות ההנשמה**.

**א. העדפת בנה לאחר ששמע על התועלת והסיכונים של הנשמה.** הבן יכול לתמוך ואינו בוחר במקומה.
**ב. רצונה המפורש לאחר שקיבלה מידע על אפשרות ההנשמה.** בחירתה הנוכחית לאחר הסבר קודמת לעמדות אחרים.
**ג. דבריה הישנים על מכונות כפי שתועדו אצל רופא המשפחה.** אמירה כללית מהעבר אינה גוברת על רצון מפורש ומושכל בהווה.
**ד. הערכת הצוות את איכות חייה על סמך הגיל ומחלת הרקע.** גיל ומחלת רקע אינם מדד לערך שהיא מייחסת לאיכות חייה.

אסמכתא · חוק החולה הנוטה למות, סעיף 5(א), עמ׳ 5; סעיף 15(א), עמ׳ 10.
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: An older woman starts trazodone for sleep and subsequently develops morning drowsiness and dizziness on standing. Which paired effects described by Hazzard support concern that trazodone is contributing to her symptoms?
o: Increased daytime alertness together with increased standing blood pressure
Increased daytime alertness together with reduced standing blood pressure
Increased daytime sleepiness together with reduced standing blood pressure
Increased daytime sleepiness together with increased standing blood pressure
explanation:
Trazodone can leave an older patient sleepy the next morning and impair blood-pressure maintenance on standing. **Daytime somnolence with orthostatic hypotension** explains both complaints.

**A. Greater alertness and higher standing pressure** Both directions conflict with the symptoms.
**B. Greater alertness and lower standing pressure** A pressure drop fits the dizziness, but morning drowsiness indicates reduced alertness.
**C. Sleepiness and lower standing pressure** Residual sedation and orthostasis together fit the timing and symptoms.
**D. Sleepiness and higher standing pressure** Sedation fits, but a pressure fall is the characteristic postural effect.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 661.

q: Medications are being considered for a woman with neuropathic pain and a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Which recommendation matches the renal-adjustment table in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Use pregabalin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction
Avoid duloxetine because of the degree of kidney impairment
Use gabapentin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction
Use extended-release tramadol at the usual prescribed dose
explanation:
The renal threshold depends on the specific analgesic. **At a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min, avoid duloxetine.**

**A. Use pregabalin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction** Pregabalin needs dose reduction below 60 mL/min because CNS effects increase.
**B. Avoid duloxetine because of the degree of kidney impairment** Duloxetine is on the avoid list below 30 mL/min, in part because gastrointestinal adverse effects increase.
**C. Use gabapentin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction** Gabapentin also needs renal adjustment below 60 mL/min.
**D. Use extended-release tramadol at the usual prescribed dose** Below 30 mL/min avoid extended-release tramadol. Immediate-release tramadol, if used, needs a reduced dose.

Reference · AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 6, p. 2073.

q: An 86-year-old man is grieving the death of his wife. He describes persistent hopelessness, loss of the ability to enjoy things and suicidal thoughts. Which clinical concern is particularly raised by this combination?
o: A major depressive episode with suicide risk
A normal grief response with adaptation to loss
An emotional change of normal older adulthood
A functional decline caused by progressing dementia
explanation:
Bereavement can coexist with major depression. **Persistent hopelessness, loss of pleasure and suicidal thoughts raise concern for a major depressive episode and require suicide-risk assessment**.

**A. Major depression.** The combination extends beyond transient waves of grief and warrants prompt evaluation.
**B. Normal adaptation.** Pervasive anhedonia and suicidal thoughts need separate assessment.
**C. Normal aging.** Depression is not an expected consequence of age.
**D. Dementia.** No cognitive course is given to explain the mood syndrome.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1024.
ref: Hazzard Ch 66 — GENERAL TOPICS IN GERIATRIC PSYCHIATRY

q: אישה בת 84 עם דמנציה קלה (MMSE 22) המתגוררת בבית עם בתה מובאת לחדר מיון לאחר fall. היא נוטלת donepezil 10 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, ו-aspirin 81 mg ביום. בתה מדווחת על קושי הולך וגובר בניהול כספים ותרופות במשך 3 חודשים, וכעת דורשת השגחה על כל ה-IADLs. בבדיקה גופנית: חבורות באזור הירך, סימנים חיוניים תקינים, ללא ממצאים נוירולוגיים פוקאליים. X-ray ירך תקין. Creatinine clearance הוא 42 mL/min. איזו התערבות תפחית ביעילות הרבה ביותר את הסיכון ל-falls עתידיים ולירידה תפקודית?
o: הפניה למוסד שיקומי אשפוזי
הרשמה לתכנית PACE
התחלת memantine 5 mg ביום
מרשם ל-hip protectors ו-vitamin D
explanation:
נפילה לצד דמנציה ותלות גוברת בניהול הבית מצדיקה בירור של גורמי הסיכון ושל העזרה הזמינה. בארה״ב PACE מרכזת הערכה רפואית, פיזיותרפיה, ריפוי בעיסוק ותמיכה בבית למי שעומד בתנאי הקבלה. התועלת האפשרית כאן היא טיפול משולב בגורמי הסיכון. יתרון על כל החלופות במניעת נפילות לא הוכח.
**בדיקת התאמה ל־PACE מאפשרת לבנות תוכנית משולבת למניעת נפילות ולשימור תפקוד. יש לברר זכאות ובטיחות בבית לפני הרשמה.**

**א. שיקום באשפוז.** לא תואר שבר או צורך בטיפול שיקומי בעוצמה המחייבת אשפוז.
**ב. PACE.** הצוות יכול לבדוק הליכה, סביבת בית, ניהול תרופות והעזרה שהבת יכולה לספק לאורך זמן.
**ג. ממנטין.** טיפול תרופתי בקוגניציה אינו בודק את ההליכה או את הסכנות בבית.
**ד. מגיני ירך וויטמין D.** צעדים אלה אינם מספקים השגחה על התרופות או התאמה של התרגול והבית לסיכון האישי.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 238–239, 243–244, טבלאות 17-1 ו־17-2. Medicare, PACE, Who can get PACE?
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
