**B. Rate control plus anticoagulation** — In the population described, outcomes were similar or better with this approach, and antiarrhythmic toxicity was avoided.
**C. Catheter ablation is generally required** — Mild symptoms alone do not require ablation. AF duration, comorbidities, preferences and the goals of rhythm control matter.
**D. Anticoagulation replaces rate control** — Anticoagulants prevent embolism. They do not slow ventricular conduction or relieve tachycardia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1194 and 1200–1201. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline, §8.1.

q: A 75-year-old man survives a witnessed ventricular-fibrillation arrest at his gym. CPR begins immediately and circulation returns after two shocks. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Angiography shows 40% mid-LAD stenosis without intervention; echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 42% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. He is extubated on day 3 and is neurologically intact. Evaluation identifies no transient or reversible cause. Which conclusion about ICD therapy follows from Hazzard?
o: Evaluate ICD implantation for secondary prevention after the VF arrest
Defer ICD consideration because the ejection fraction exceeds primary-prevention cutoffs
Defer ICD consideration because chronological age weighs against implantation
Defer ICD consideration because inducible ventricular tachycardia has not been demonstrated
explanation:
An ICD can terminate recurrent ventricular fibrillation after a patient survives an arrest. **Assess ICD implantation for secondary prevention** because no transient or reversible trigger explains his VF.

**A. Evaluate ICD implantation** — The prior arrest identifies a risk of recurrence. Discuss expected survival, recovery and his goals.
**B. Defer because EF is 42%** — Low-EF cutoffs identify primary-prevention candidates. They do not exclude a survivor of unexplained VF.
**C. Defer because he is 75** — Chronological age alone does not outweigh a documented arrest and meaningful neurologic recovery.
**D. Require inducible VT** — He has already had spontaneous VF. Electrophysiologic induction is part of other risk-assessment pathways.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1206–1207. AHA/ACC/HRS ventricular arrhythmia guideline, §7.1.1.

q: An 83-year-old woman taking digoxin and furosemide develops hypokalemia and new arrhythmias. Which relationship between these findings is important to recognize?
o: Hypokalemia reduces the cardiotoxic effects of digoxin
Hypokalemia improves cardiac tolerability of digoxin therapy
Hypokalemia potentiates the cardiotoxic effects of digoxin
Hypokalemia indicates a need to increase digoxin exposure
explanation:
Potassium and digoxin interact at the sodium–potassium ATPase. **Hypokalemia makes the myocardium more susceptible to digoxin toxicity**, so loop-induced potassium loss matters when a new arrhythmia occurs.

**A. Reduces cardiotoxicity** Low potassium increases susceptibility to adverse electrophysiologic effects.
**B. Improves tolerability** A potassium deficit can make a previously tolerated digoxin exposure hazardous.
**C. Potentiates cardiotoxicity** Review the ECG, electrolytes, renal function and digoxin exposure urgently, and correct the electrolyte disturbance appropriately.
**D. Increase digoxin exposure** Increasing the dose can worsen the arrhythmia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1183.

q: A 77-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, and a left ventricular ejection fraction below 40% has recurrent activity-limiting episodes despite high-dose metoprolol. Between episodes his heart rate and blood pressure are low. He receives anticoagulation. Which next strategy best fits the source?
o: Add regular diltiazem to improve control of the ventricular rate
Start regular flecainide to maintain sinus rhythm between episodes
Increase metoprolol further to improve control of the ventricular rate
Assess suitability for restoring sinus rhythm because symptoms persist
explanation:
Rate control can leave a patient symptomatic during paroxysms even when the resting pulse is already slow. **Evaluate rhythm control** because activity-limiting attacks persist and further AV nodal blockade risks hypotension or bradycardia.

**A. Add diltiazem** — His ejection fraction is below 40%, and additional negative inotropy and AV nodal slowing are undesirable.
**B. Start flecainide** — Ischemic heart disease and reduced EF make this class Ic antiarrhythmic unsuitable because of proarrhythmia.
**C. Increase metoprolol** — Low heart rate and blood pressure between episodes limit further titration.
**D. Assess restoration of sinus rhythm** — Discuss rhythm-control drugs compatible with his heart disease or catheter ablation and continue stroke prevention according to risk.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1201, Rate Control, Rhythm Control and Table 77-6.

q: An 84-year-old man with symptomatic carotid stenosis is being assessed for intervention. Which comparison between carotid endarterectomy and transfemoral carotid artery stenting is described by Hazzard?
o: More myocardial infarction with endarterectomy and more stroke with transfemoral stenting
More stroke with endarterectomy and more myocardial infarction with transfemoral stenting
Less myocardial infarction with endarterectomy and less stroke with transfemoral stenting
Less cranial nerve injury with endarterectomy and less stroke with transfemoral stenting
explanation:
Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque through a neck incision. Transfemoral stenting traverses the aortic arch and crosses the plaque. **Myocardial infarction is more frequent with endarterectomy, while perioperative stroke is more frequent with transfemoral stenting**, especially at this age.

**A. More infarction with surgery and more stroke with stenting** — The operation adds cardiac stress. Catheter manipulation can dislodge emboli from arch or carotid plaque.
**B. More stroke with surgery and more infarction with stenting** — These comparisons reverse the observed directions of the two procedural risks.
**C. Less infarction with surgery and less stroke with stenting** — Neither advantage applies. The patient's cardiac reserve and embolic risk both matter.
**D. Less cranial nerve injury with surgery and less stroke with stenting** — Surgical dissection near the carotid can injure cranial nerves, often transiently. Older stent recipients have a higher procedural stroke risk.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1214, carotid interventions and complications.

q: A 78-year-old woman is under surveillance for an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm. According to Hazzard, which finding is the main determinant of rupture risk and the timing of intervention?
o: The serum lipid level measured at the latest follow-up assessment
The fasting glucose level measured at the latest follow-up assessment
The systemic blood pressure measured at the latest clinic assessment
The abdominal aneurysm diameter measured on the latest surveillance imaging
explanation:
An abdominal aortic aneurysm enlarges as its wall loses structural strength. For an asymptomatic woman, **the aneurysm's maximum diameter on imaging** is the principal measure used to estimate rupture risk and plan elective repair.

**A. Latest lipid level** — Lipid lowering reduces atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk. Serum lipids cannot measure how large the aneurysm has become.
**B. Latest fasting glucose** — Glucose helps guide diabetes care. It gives no anatomical estimate of aneurysm size or expansion.
**C. Latest clinic blood pressure** — Control sustained hypertension because it adds vascular risk. A single reading cannot replace serial aortic measurements.
**D. Aneurysm diameter** — Rupture risk rises with diameter. Discuss repair at a smaller diameter in women than in men, and reassess sooner for new symptoms or rapid enlargement.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1214–1215, abdominal aortic aneurysm.

q: An 81-year-old man with a 4.8-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm undergoes annual ultrasound surveillance. Which recommendation agrees with Hazzard’s surveillance and medical-management principles for a small aneurysm?
o: Consider doxycycline treatment to slow expansion of the small aneurysm
Reduce aerobic activity to decrease the risk of aneurysm rupture
Repeat imaging if symptoms potentially related to the aneurysm develop
Prefer MRI surveillance as the recommended first-line method for the aneurysm
explanation:
Surveillance follows the enlargement of an asymptomatic aneurysm so repair can be timed before rupture. **New symptoms potentially caused by the aneurysm warrant prompt reassessment and imaging**, even when the next annual ultrasound is months away.

**A. Doxycycline** — A trial in small aneurysms found no meaningful slowing of expansion. Antibiotic treatment has no role for this indication.
**B. Reduce aerobic activity** — Walking and other tolerated aerobic activities are appropriate during surveillance. Inactivity sacrifices cardiovascular and functional benefits.
**C. Repeat imaging for new symptoms** — New abdominal or back pain may mark expansion or rupture. Assess urgency immediately, especially with sudden severe pain or hemodynamic instability.
**D. Prefer MRI as first-line surveillance** — Ultrasound is preferred when it gives adequate measurements. CT or MRI can clarify anatomy when ultrasound is inadequate or repair is being planned.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1215–1216, AAA surveillance and Table 78-2.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1215, AAA surveillance

q: A 79-year-old woman has peripheral arterial disease (ABI 0.45), stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22), and a recent fall with hip fracture. Claudication now limits walking to 50 feet, and duplex shows 80% superficial femoral artery stenosis. She takes clopidogrel 75 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, and metoprolol 25 mg twice daily. When planning exercise within her safe capabilities, which walking approach is described for claudication?
o: End walking at the onset of pain and avoid walking beyond that point
Use supervised walking beyond pain onset within safe tolerance
Replace walking with prolonged rest to protect the leg musculature
Continue walking beyond safe tolerance to maximize training intensity
explanation:
Claudication occurs when working muscle requires more oxygen than a narrowed artery supplies. **Use supervised interval walking beyond pain onset within safe tolerance**, adjusted for her fracture recovery and fall risk.

**A. Stop at the first discomfort every time** — In stable claudication, the first ache signals a training threshold. Stopping there on every bout omits the exercise stimulus that improves endurance.
**B. Walk beyond onset under supervision** — Agree on a safe pace and weight-bearing limits, walk into tolerable claudication, rest until it subsides, then repeat. Progress the dose as function permits.
**C. Prolonged rest** — Rest relieves an individual episode. Continuous inactivity deconditions the muscles and reduces walking capacity.
**D. Exceed safe tolerance** — Severe pain, unsteadiness or a fracture-related limit calls for a pause or modification. A training prescription must protect balance and recovery.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1210–1211, exercise therapy for claudication.

q: An 86-year-old nursing-home resident with moderate vascular dementia, hypertension, and a 4.2-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm stable for two years requires help with all activities of daily living; BIMS is 8/15. During a goals-of-care meeting, the team confirms his previously expressed preference for comfort-focused care. After an individualized discussion, aneurysm repair would not be pursued and surveillance results would not change his care. Which approach applies Hazzard’s goals-based principle?
o: Continue annual surveillance to preserve the existing disease-monitoring schedule
Discontinue surveillance that would not advance the agreed goals
Increase surveillance frequency to compensate for his cognitive impairment
Arrange preventive repair to replace the agreed comfort-focused strategy
explanation:
Surveillance has value when a result could change care in a way the patient would welcome. Here the team has established that repair would be declined and that a scan would not change the comfort plan.
**Stop routine aneurysm surveillance and continue care directed toward comfort.**

**A. Continue annual imaging** An unchanged schedule gives no clinical benefit when enlargement would trigger no action consistent with his wishes.
**B. Discontinue surveillance** This spares him the burden of tests that cannot advance his goals. New symptoms can still be addressed on their own merits.
**C. Increase surveillance** A cognitive score describes an impairment. It supplies no reason to intensify a test whose result would have no effect on care.
**D. Arrange repair** Preventive surgery would reverse the agreed decision and expose him to burdens he previously wished to avoid.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 72, p. 1103.

q: An older man with postoperative delirium endangers himself and interrupts essential care despite nonpharmacologic measures. A short antipsychotic trial is being considered. What is its intended role in this setting?
o: Reduce mortality attributable to postoperative delirium
Control agitation that threatens safety and essential care
Shorten delirium duration by treating its underlying cause
Shorten the hospital stay by correcting the confusion
explanation:
For severe agitation, a short antipsychotic trial can be considered after supportive measures fail. Its purpose is immediate safety while separate treatment addresses the cause.
**Control behavior that threatens the patient or interrupts essential care.**

**A. Reduce mortality attributable to postoperative delirium.** Trials do not support prescribing an antipsychotic to reduce mortality from delirium.
**B. Control agitation that threatens safety and essential care.** Safe access to necessary treatment is the immediate behavioral goal.
**C. Shorten delirium duration by treating its underlying cause.** An antipsychotic does not reverse the precipitating illness or consistently shorten the syndrome.
**D. Shorten the hospital stay by correcting the confusion.** Length of stay is not a reliable pharmacologic treatment effect.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 888–889

q: An 82-year-old woman undergoing preoperative evaluation has an elevated Clinical Frailty Scale score. How should this information be used?
o: As a global measure replacing cardiac and pulmonary surgical-risk assessment
As a measure with uniform predictive performance across surgical outcomes
As a research measure adding little to clinical surgical-risk assessment
As additional information on mortality and nonhome discharge risk
explanation:
The Clinical Frailty Scale grades overall fitness and frailty. **A higher score adds information about mortality and the likelihood of discharge somewhere other than home.**

**A. Replace cardiac and pulmonary assessment** Frailty complements the appraisal of organ-specific disease and procedural risk.
**B. Uniform prediction of every outcome** Different measures perform better for different outcomes. The phenotype is linked to delirium and the Edmonton scale to complications.
**C. Little clinical contribution** The Clinical Frailty Scale offers prognostic information for patient and family discussions, including discharge planning.
**D. Additional mortality and discharge information** Greater frailty signals less reserve to tolerate the operation and resume independent living.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 27, p. 373, Table 27-2.
ref: Hazzard Ch 27 — PERIOPERATIVE CARE: EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT

q: A 75-year-old man taking clopidogrel before surgery asks why it belongs in the bleeding-risk assessment. Which explanation is consistent with Hazzard?
o: It increases platelet adhesion and thereby reduces bleeding risk
It improves platelet aggregation and thereby reduces bleeding risk
It inhibits platelet function and contributes to bleeding risk
It stabilizes platelet function and makes medication review unnecessary
explanation:
Clopidogrel blocks platelet P2Y12 signaling and inhibits aggregation. **Impaired platelet function increases perioperative bleeding risk**, making its indication and timing important in preoperative review.

**A. Increases adhesion.** Clopidogrel inhibits platelet activation rather than improving hemostatic adhesion.
**B. Improves aggregation.** P2Y12 blockade reduces ADP-mediated aggregation.
**C. Inhibits platelets.** Bleeding risk must be balanced against the thrombotic risk of interrupting treatment.
**D. No review needed.** Its antiplatelet action is precisely why perioperative medication review matters.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1515.

q: An 80-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease and intermittent claudication remains limited in walking despite supervised exercise. She takes an antiplatelet agent and a statin, has no heart failure, and is not currently scheduled for a vascular intervention. Which additional recommendation is supported by Hazzard?
o: Add cilostazol to improve walking distance limited by claudication.
Reduce painful walking to protect the limb muscles from injury.
Prioritize antiplatelet therapy over exercise for greater walking improvement.
Obtain invasive angiography as the initial study of vascular anatomy.
explanation:
Cilostazol inhibits phosphodiesterase III, producing vasodilation and inhibiting platelet aggregation. In persistent intermittent claudication without heart failure, **adding cilostazol can improve walking distance** alongside exercise and cardiovascular prevention.

**A. Add cilostazol** — It treats exertional leg symptoms. Check for heart failure of any severity before prescribing, because heart failure is a contraindication.
**B. Reduce painful walking** — Structured bouts into tolerable exertional discomfort improve walking. Avoiding all discomfort can limit training benefit.
**C. Prioritize antiplatelet treatment for walking distance** — Antiplatelet therapy reduces vascular events. Structured exercise has a greater effect on walking capacity.
**D. Start with invasive angiography** — Physiologic testing and noninvasive imaging usually precede invasive imaging. Catheter angiography is generally reserved for situations where the result will guide intervention.

Reference · 2024 ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, §§3.2, 5.7 and 6. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1211

q: An 83-year-old man is being evaluated for a suspected prosthetic device infection. He is clinically stable, has no sepsis, and cultures can safely be obtained. According to Hazzard, what should guide antibiotic treatment?
o: Obtain cultures and base treatment on their results
Begin empirical treatment before collecting specimens for culture
Begin prolonged suppressive treatment before identifying the organism
Defer culture collection until antibiotic treatment is completed
explanation:
An implant infection often involves bacteria attached to foreign material. In a stable patient **obtain appropriate cultures before antibiotics and use the results to select treatment**.

**A. Obtain cultures first** — Identifying the organism and its susceptibilities guides drug choice and helps decide whether implant retention is feasible.
**B. Give empirical treatment before specimens** — Early antibiotics can reduce diagnostic yield. Sepsis or instability would change the urgency, but neither is present here.
**C. Begin prolonged suppression immediately** — Suppression is a management choice after assessing the organism, implant stability, function and prospects for surgery.
**D. Wait until antibiotics are finished to collect cultures** — This loses the best initial opportunity to recover the organism from relevant specimens.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1673–1674, Table 104-1 and Figure 104-3.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION

q: A 76-year-old woman treated for hypertension reports dizziness on standing. Which measurement principle is important before changing treatment?
o: Use seated blood pressure to assess the response to standing
Use a high office reading to justify intensifying medication
Obtain supine and standing readings to detect a postural decrease
Use diastolic blood pressure in place of standing measurements
explanation:
Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in pressure after standing that can cause dizziness or a fall. **Compare supine pressure with standing readings during the first three minutes** and record whether the symptoms recur.

**A. Use seated pressure** — A seated value alone cannot show the size of the fall from lying to standing.
**B. Intensify for a high office reading** — The office pressure may coexist with low upright pressure. Escalation before checking posture could worsen symptoms.
**C. Obtain supine and standing readings** — A fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes supports orthostatic hypotension.
**D. Substitute diastolic pressure** — Either component can fall on standing. A diastolic value in one position cannot answer the postural question.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1222–1223.

q: An 85-year-old man is under surveillance for an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm. According to Hazzard, which anatomical measurement is the major determinant of rupture risk and the timing of intervention?
o: The degree of cerebral atrophy documented on brain imaging
The degree of cardiac chamber enlargement documented on echocardiography
The degree of limb arterial stenosis documented on Doppler imaging
The current diameter of the aneurysm documented on imaging
explanation:
Elective aneurysm repair trades an immediate procedural risk for protection against future rupture. **The current maximal aortic aneurysm diameter** is the principal anatomical predictor in this comparison.

**A. Cerebral atrophy** — Brain imaging may contribute to a separate neurologic assessment. It gives no measurement of the aneurysmal aortic wall.
**B. Cardiac chamber enlargement** — Cardiac disease can influence fitness for repair. Chamber size does not measure the likelihood that this aneurysm will rupture.
**C. Limb arterial stenosis** — This measures impaired limb inflow. Coexisting peripheral artery disease does not substitute for measuring the aorta.
**D. Current aneurysm diameter** — Compare serial diameters to assess growth. In men, 5.5 cm is the usual elective repair threshold for an unruptured infrarenal aneurysm, with symptoms and rapid growth prompting earlier assessment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1215–1216. 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, §6.5.5.3.

q: A 78-year-old woman develops acute confusion, visual hallucinations, and nighttime agitation after femoral endarterectomy. The CAM is positive and there are no focal neurologic findings. She takes gabapentin 300 mg three times daily for neuropathic pain. Creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, previously 1.2; sodium is 138 mmol/L and glucose 95 mg/dL. Which medication-review approach is appropriate while the team investigates delirium?
o: Increase gabapentin before reviewing its cognitive adverse effects
Review gabapentin for reduction or withdrawal and reassess analgesia
Add a sleep medication before reviewing existing psychoactive drugs
Add a cognitive enhancer before reviewing existing psychoactive drugs
explanation:
Gabapentin can cause central adverse effects, especially when renal clearance falls. Reassess both analgesic benefit and cognitive effects as kidney function changes.
**Review reducing or safely withdrawing gabapentin and reassess pain while evaluating other postoperative causes.**

**A. Increase gabapentin before reviewing its cognitive adverse effects.** Increasing it with a rising creatinine can worsen drug accumulation.
**B. Review gabapentin for reduction or withdrawal and reassess analgesia.** A renal-dose review addresses the new risk while checking that pain remains controlled.
**C. Add a sleep medication before reviewing existing psychoactive drugs.** An additional hypnotic could worsen confusion and leave the existing exposure unchanged.
**D. Add a cognitive enhancer before reviewing existing psychoactive drugs.** A cognitive enhancer does not correct an acute drug effect or impaired clearance.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 885. AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 6, p. 2073

q: An 81-year-old man with carotid stenosis and significant heart disease is being assessed for intervention. Which consideration explains why transfemoral carotid stenting does not simply remove the procedural risks in this age group?
o: A higher perioperative stroke risk with endarterectomy than with transfemoral stenting
A lower perioperative stroke risk with transfemoral stenting among octogenarians
A higher perioperative stroke risk with transfemoral stenting among older patients
A lower perioperative myocardial infarction risk with endarterectomy than with stenting
explanation:
Transfemoral carotid stenting avoids a neck operation but requires navigating the aortic arch and crossing a diseased carotid. In an octogenarian, **the higher perioperative stroke risk of transfemoral stenting** must be weighed against the cardiac risk of endarterectomy.

**A. Higher stroke risk with endarterectomy** — Procedural stroke is generally more frequent with transfemoral stenting in this age group. A calcified or tortuous arch increases technical difficulty.
**B. Lower stroke risk with stenting in octogenarians** — Age and unfavorable arch anatomy can increase embolic risk during catheter passage.
**C. Higher stroke risk with transfemoral stenting** — Embolization from the arch or carotid plaque can cause a cerebral infarction. Cardiac comorbidity alone cannot settle the choice of procedure.
**D. Lower infarction risk with endarterectomy** — Myocardial infarction occurs more often with surgery in the comparison. The clinician must weigh cardiac and neurologic risks separately.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1214, carotid interventions and complications.

q: A 79-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease reports new rest pain after bypass surgery. Before attributing it to neuropathic pain and choosing an analgesic, which vascular mechanism should be assessed?
o: Increased arterial inflow to the painful tissue
Decreased arterial inflow to the painful tissue
Increased oxygen delivery to muscles at rest
Decreased oxygen demand by muscles at rest
explanation:
Ischemic rest pain develops when perfusion cannot meet tissue needs even without exertion. After bypass surgery, **assess for decreased arterial inflow**, including possible graft compromise, before treating the pain as neuropathic.

**A. Increased arterial inflow** — Successful revascularization should improve oxygen delivery. New pain warrants examination of graft and limb perfusion.
**B. Decreased arterial inflow** — Assess onset, temperature, color, pulses or Doppler signals, sensation and motor power. Sudden pain or new sensory or motor loss requires emergency vascular assessment.
**C. Increased oxygen delivery at rest** — Improved oxygen delivery would help relieve ischemic pain. It cannot account for ongoing arterial oxygen deprivation.
**D. Decreased resting oxygen demand** — Lower demand generally relieves exertional claudication. Pain persisting at rest raises concern that supply has fallen further.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1210–1212, lower-extremity ischemia.

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease is having his hypertension treatment reviewed. How should the treatment goal be set according to Hazzard?
o: Apply a uniform age-based target despite differences in function and comorbidity
Use a single blood pressure reading as the basis for diagnosis and treatment
Individualize the target for comorbidity, risk, and quality of life
Pursue the lowest achievable pressure despite treatment-related postural symptoms
explanation:
The treatment target balances prevention of stroke and cardiac events against harms such as orthostasis and kidney injury. **Individualize this man's target using cardiovascular and renal risk, function, treatment tolerance and quality of life.**

**A. Uniform age-based target** — Two people of the same age can differ considerably in albuminuria, vascular risk, frailty and upright pressure.
**B. Use one reading** — Confirm the usual pressure from standardized repeated measurements or out-of-office readings before planning long-term therapy.
**C. Individualize the target** — Diabetes and kidney disease increase vascular risk, while renal function, potassium and standing pressure influence what treatment he can tolerate.
**D. Pursue the lowest pressure despite symptoms** — Symptomatic postural hypotension can limit intensification. A standing-pressure goal may be more appropriate.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1222–1223.

q: An 84-year-old woman taking hydrochlorothiazide develops postural dizziness and weight loss after poor intake. Clinical assessment confirms volume depletion. There is no congestion or evidence of adrenal disease. Which approach is appropriate?
o: Replenish volume, stop the diuretic, and reassess its continuing indication
Increase the diuretic, reduce sodium intake, and monitor the postural dizziness
Restrict fluid and sodium intake, continue the diuretic, and monitor body weight
Start mineralocorticoid replacement, continue the diuretic, and monitor symptoms
explanation:
Poor intake and continued thiazide use can cause volume depletion and orthostatic symptoms. **Restore volume, stop the diuretic temporarily and reassess its indication.**

**A. Replenish volume, stop the diuretic, and reassess its continuing indication.** This corrects the deficit and removes an ongoing cause while electrolytes and renal function are reviewed.
**B. Increase the diuretic, reduce sodium intake, and monitor the postural dizziness.** More diuresis and less sodium can deepen the volume deficit.
**C. Restrict fluid and sodium intake, continue the diuretic, and monitor body weight.** Further restriction while continuing the diuretic can worsen postural hypotension.
**D. Start mineralocorticoid replacement, continue the diuretic, and monitor symptoms.** There is no evidence of mineralocorticoid deficiency to justify replacement, and the diuretic remains a reversible cause.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 589.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS

q: A 79-year-old man with heart failure has pulmonary congestion and edema. A loop diuretic is being considered. What is the principal expected benefit described by Hazzard?
o: Improved survival through an established reduction in mortality
Correction of potassium levels through increased urinary output
Relief of pulmonary congestion, edema, and associated dyspnea
Prevention of kidney injury through sustained intravascular hypovolemia
explanation:
Loop diuretics increase urinary sodium and water loss and lower elevated filling pressures. **Their principal benefit is relief of pulmonary congestion, dyspnea and peripheral edema**.

**A. Established survival benefit** Loop diuretics relieve fluid overload, but a survival benefit has not been established.
**B. Correct potassium by increasing urine output** Loop treatment can increase urinary potassium loss, requiring monitoring and sometimes replacement.
**C. Relieve congestion** Reduced lung and systemic venous congestion can improve breathing and mobility.
**D. Protect kidneys through hypovolemia** Excessive depletion reduces perfusion and can cause prerenal azotemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1182.

q: An 81-year-old woman attends a routine visit without acute symptoms or evidence of acute target-organ injury. A single blood pressure measurement after walking to the clinic is higher than usual. What should be done before diagnosing sustained hypertension and changing treatment?
o: Base the diagnosis on the first elevated office measurement.
Use diastolic pressure as the principal guide to cardiovascular risk.
Use seated readings to avoid the influence of changes in posture.
Repeat standardized blood pressure measurements and arrange out-of-office monitoring.
explanation:
Sustained hypertension refers to the patient's usual pressure. Walking, anxiety, cuff size and posture can alter a single office measurement. **Repeat the measurement after seated rest and confirm the pattern with standardized repeat visits or home or ambulatory monitoring.**

**A. Diagnose from the first reading** — A post-exertional reading in an asymptomatic patient can overestimate resting pressure.
**B. Use diastolic pressure as the principal risk guide** — In later life, systolic and pulse pressure carry substantial prognostic weight as the large arteries stiffen.
**C. Use seated readings to avoid posture** — A standardized seated reading is useful, but checking standing pressure can uncover a separate fall risk before treatment.
**D. Repeat and monitor outside the office** — Rest for at least five minutes with feet on the floor and an appropriate cuff. Home or 24-hour readings can uncover a white-coat elevation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1222.

q: An older man with hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction is being considered for a beta-blocker. Which consideration supports its use according to Hazzard?
o: Secondary prevention after a previous myocardial infarction
Its role as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension
Its role in reducing peripheral vascular resistance
Its role in preventing adverse metabolic effects
explanation:
Beta blockers slow heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. **A previous myocardial infarction is the listed cardiac reason to consider a beta blocker**, particularly after a recent infarct, with angina or with impaired systolic function.

**A. Secondary prevention after infarction** — The cardiac history supplies an indication beyond pressure lowering. Duration depends on time since infarction, ventricular function and ongoing indications.
**B. Monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension** — In older adults without a compelling cardiac indication, a thiazide-type diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB or long-acting calcium-channel blocker is usually a better initial choice.
**C. Reduced peripheral vascular resistance** — Traditional beta blockers may increase peripheral resistance. Their cardiac effects explain their use here.
**D. Prevent adverse metabolic effects** — Beta blockade can adversely affect glucose handling and blunt adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225–1226, Table 79-4. AHA/ACC Chronic Coronary Disease Guideline (2023), beta-blocker recommendations.

q: An 85-year-old nursing-home resident with advanced Parkinson disease, dysphagia, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and complete dependence for daily activities has persistently elevated blood pressure. His representative asks about treatment. Before selecting a drug, which approach follows Hazzard for a person with high comorbidity burden and limited life expectancy?
o: Choose a treatment target from age without discussing patient goals
Apply the community-living target before considering comorbidity burden
Individualize the treatment decision through clinical judgment and informed discussion
Select the drug formulation before considering adverse effects and quality of life
explanation:
Blood-pressure treatment prevents future vascular events, while orthostasis, pill burden and swallowing difficulties affect the patient now. **Discuss likely benefits, harms and goals with his representative before choosing a target or a formulation.**

**A. Set the target from age alone** — Advanced Parkinson disease, recurrent aspiration and dependence materially change the burden of treatment and the time available to benefit.
**B. Apply the community-living target first** — Nursing-home residents and people with an expected survival under three years were excluded from SPRINT. Its intensive target cannot simply be carried over.
**C. Individualize through informed discussion** — Establish what outcomes matter, assess prognosis and upright symptoms, and weigh prevention against comfort and feasibility.
**D. Choose a formulation first** — Dysphagia matters when implementing a plan. A liquid formulation cannot decide whether treatment advances his goals.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1223. Williamson et al., JAMA 2016, doi:10.1001/jama.2016.7050.

q: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and mild frailty walks with a walker and covers 5.2 meters in 8 seconds. Her baseline blood pressure is 148/82 on amlodipine 5 mg daily. In a trial she is assigned to an intensive systolic blood pressure target below 120 mm Hg. After amlodipine titration and addition of lisinopril, her blood pressure is 118/68 seated and 114/66 standing. She feels well and reports more energy. Which interpretation of the SPRINT evidence supports continuing her tolerated regimen with monitoring?
o: Benefits persisted in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed
Benefits diminished in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed
Injurious falls increased in participants assigned to intensive treatment
Quality of life declined in participants assigned to intensive treatment
explanation:
SPRINT compared systolic targets below 120 and below 140 mm Hg in selected high-risk adults. **Cardiovascular benefit persisted among enrolled older participants with frailty or slow gait**. An asymptomatic standing systolic pressure of 114 supports continuing this tolerated regimen with monitoring.

**A. Benefit persisted with frailty or slow gait** — Neither characteristic showed a clear interaction with treatment benefit in the ambulatory group aged 75 or older. This woman resembles that group.
**B. Benefit diminished with frailty or slow gait** — Slower gait alone did not identify a subgroup that lost the benefit. Monitor her own function and symptoms over time.
**C. Injurious falls increased** — The intensive group had no excess of injurious falls, although hypotension, electrolyte disturbances and acute kidney injury remain relevant during treatment.
**D. Quality of life declined** — Participants reported similar health-related quality of life across groups. Her individual improvement is compatible with tolerability.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1223. Williamson et al., JAMA 2016, doi:10.1001/jama.2016.7050.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1223, SPRINT

q: Chlorthalidone is being considered for hypertension in an older patient. How does Hazzard describe it in comparison with hydrochlorothiazide?
o: Lower potency and a shorter half-life
Greater potency and a longer half-life
Greater potency and a shorter half-life
Lower potency and a longer half-life
explanation:
Chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide both promote sodium excretion. Their milligram doses and duration of action differ. **Chlorthalidone has greater potency and a longer half-life.**

**A. Lower potency, shorter half-life** — This understates both the dose effect and persistence of chlorthalidone.
**B. Greater potency, longer half-life** — A smaller dose can produce comparable pressure lowering, and a dose persists longer. Follow potassium and sodium, particularly after a change.
**C. Greater potency, shorter half-life** — The first comparison fits, but faster elimination would imply the opposite of chlorthalidone's longer half-life.
**D. Lower potency, longer half-life** — It lasts longer, but a need for more milligrams for the same response would imply lower potency. The comparison goes the other way.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1225.

q: A 73-year-old woman with hypertension takes a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for joint pain. What is the role of reviewing this medication in her blood pressure evaluation?
o: Identifying a medication contributing to elevated blood pressure
Identifying a medication providing an antihypertensive effect
Identifying a medication replacing repeated blood pressure measurements
Identifying a medication making standing blood pressure measurement unnecessary
explanation:
Medication-induced hypertension is a potentially reversible contributor to poor control. NSAIDs can promote sodium retention and raise blood pressure. **Review the NSAID as a possible cause of elevated readings.**

**A. Identify a pressure-raising medication** — Ask about regular and over-the-counter use and the timing of the pressure rise. COX-2 inhibitors can also contribute.
**B. Identify an antihypertensive effect** — NSAIDs are analgesic and anti-inflammatory. They may worsen pressure control and blunt the response to some antihypertensives.
**C. Replace repeated measurements** — Medication review identifies a contributor. Repeat measurements still establish the patient's pressure pattern.
**D. Omit standing measurements** — Identifying an NSAID does not address upright symptoms or the risk of a treatment-related pressure drop.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1222.

q: A 78-year-old man has recovered from pneumonia. Repeated clinic and home blood pressure readings are around 170/90 mm Hg, without orthostatic hypotension. He has untreated stage 2 hypertension and no coronary disease or heart failure. Combination treatment is planned. Which initial regimen best fits the Hazzard approach?
o: A thiazide plus an ACE inhibitor, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a beta-blocker, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a centrally acting drug, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a direct vasodilator, starting low and titrating gradually
explanation:
Combination therapy lowers pressure through complementary mechanisms. With repeated clinic and home readings near 170/90 after recovery, **start low doses of a thiazide and an ACE inhibitor and titrate with monitoring**.

**A. Thiazide plus ACE inhibitor** — Sodium excretion and renin–angiotensin blockade complement each other. Check standing pressure, creatinine, sodium and potassium.
**B. Thiazide plus beta blocker** — A beta blocker can be useful after infarction or with certain forms of heart failure. Neither indication is present here.
**C. Thiazide plus centrally acting drug** — Drugs such as clonidine can cause sedation and postural symptoms, which makes them a poor routine initial partner.
**D. Thiazide plus direct vasodilator** — Direct vasodilation can cause marked postural hypotension. Reserve such agents for a more specific indication.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1224–1225.

q: An 82-year-old woman with dementia sometimes refuses tablets. After the team adjusts medication administration, she willingly accepts oral treatment. Persistent hypertension requires treatment; a thiazide previously caused hyponatremia, and there is no cardiac indication for a beta-blocker. Renal function and potassium are normal. Which class is the most appropriate initial choice among these options according to Hazzard?
o: A centrally acting antihypertensive such as clonidine
An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril
A beta-blocker such as metoprolol
A direct vasodilator such as hydralazine
explanation:
ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation and lower vascular resistance. **Lisinopril is a suitable initial option** now that she willingly takes an oral medicine, the thiazide caused hyponatremia, and baseline renal function and potassium are normal.

**A. Centrally acting clonidine** — Sedation and postural symptoms can complicate dementia care. Missed doses may also lead to rebound hypertension.
**B. Lisinopril** — Begin at a low dose and recheck standing pressure, creatinine and potassium after initiation. Cough can limit tolerance.
**C. Metoprolol** — A beta blocker lacks a compelling cardiac indication in this vignette and can cause bradycardia or fatigue.
**D. Hydralazine** — A direct vasodilator can cause marked hypotension and complicate a simple daily regimen. It is a poor initial choice here.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225–1226, Table 79-4.

q: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, prediabetes, and BPH takes chlorthalidone 25 mg daily and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. His blood pressure is 146/84. He reports dizziness on standing quickly and nocturia four to five times nightly that disrupts sleep. Glucose is 118, potassium 3.4, and creatinine 1.1. When reviewing possible thiazide adverse effects, which strategy follows the principles described in Hazzard?
o: Increase the thiazide dose to reduce its metabolic adverse effects
Maintain the thiazide dose because urinary frequency is unrelated to this class
Maintain the thiazide dose because hypokalemia is unrelated to this class
Reduce thiazide and add an ACE inhibitor for BP control
explanation:
Thiazides increase urinary sodium and potassium losses. Frequency, low potassium and worsening glucose tolerance can limit the dose. **Reduce chlorthalidone and use an ACE inhibitor if additional pressure control is needed**, after checking the symptomatic standing pressure.

**A. Increase chlorthalidone** — Greater exposure can aggravate potassium loss, urinary symptoms and orthostasis.
**B. Continue because frequency is unrelated** — Diuresis can add to nocturia from prostatic disease. Ask about dose timing and assess the contribution of each cause.
**C. Continue because low potassium is unrelated** — Potassium of 3.4 is consistent with thiazide-related loss and warrants follow-up.
**D. Reduce thiazide, add an ACE inhibitor** — Lower thiazide exposure addresses potential adverse effects while the second class can maintain pressure control. Review tamsulosin as another contributor to dizziness and recheck potassium and creatinine.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1223, 1225–1226, Tables 79-3 and 79-4.

q: A 77-year-old woman presents after a fall and reports a month of dizziness on standing. She takes amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, and lisinopril 20 mg each morning. Blood pressure is 138/78 supine and 108/68 after three minutes standing; pulse rises from 68 to 74. Potassium is 3.3 and creatinine 1.2. During medication review, which option both removes the thiazide exposure associated with potassium loss and provides potassium replacement?
o: Move all three antihypertensives to bedtime without changing the prescribed drugs
Stop hydrochlorothiazide and provide potassium replacement with repeat monitoring
Reduce all three antihypertensive doses without providing potassium replacement
Replace lisinopril with an ARB while continuing the other prescribed drugs
explanation:
A 30 mm Hg systolic fall on standing with dizziness is symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Hydrochlorothiazide can contribute through volume and potassium losses. **Stop hydrochlorothiazide, replace potassium and recheck standing pressure, renal function and electrolytes.**

**A. Move all drugs to bedtime** — Changing the clock leaves the thiazide exposure and potassium loss in place and may aggravate nocturia.
**B. Stop the thiazide and replace potassium** — This removes the likely ongoing loss and addresses potassium of 3.3. Monitor replacement, especially while she takes lisinopril.
**C. Lower all doses without replacement** — She would remain exposed to the thiazide, and the plan gives no potassium replacement.
**D. Exchange lisinopril for an ARB** — The switch leaves the potassium-wasting drug in place and fails to correct the measured deficit.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1222–1223, 1225–1226, Table 79-4.

q: An 81-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and mild cognitive impairment has increasing confusion over two weeks. His family reports good medication adherence. He takes metformin, amlodipine, losartan, and recently added trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection, now on day five of seven. Potassium is 5.8, creatinine 1.9 (baseline 1.3), glucose 142, and blood pressure 128/76. Which medication-review plan best addresses the drug interaction relevant to his laboratory findings?
o: Add an oral potassium binder and complete the planned antibiotic course.
Stop metformin and amlodipine and continue the planned antibiotic course.
Stop trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and reassess the need for further antibiotic treatment.
Give intravenous calcium gluconate and arrange repeat potassium and creatinine measurements.
explanation:
Trimethoprim can raise potassium. The risk is greater with an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan and impaired kidney function.

**Stop trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and reassess the infection and any further antibiotic need.** Potassium of 5.8 with rising creatinine also warrants prompt clinical assessment.

**A. Add a potassium binder.** Lowering potassium while automatically completing the course leaves the interacting drugs together.
**B. Stop metformin and amlodipine.** Neither change interrupts the trimethoprim–losartan combination implicated in hyperkalemia.
**C. Stop the antibiotic and reassess.** This removes the recent interacting exposure and allows further treatment to be matched to the infection.
**D. Give calcium and repeat tests.** Calcium can stabilize the myocardium when indicated in acute hyperkalemia. This plan does not remove the interacting medication.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, p. 2068.

q: A 79-year-old woman with hypertension has maintained blood pressure below her individual target on stable treatment after successful lifestyle changes. Which approach to reducing treatment does Hazzard describe?
o: Consider maintaining the current dose as routine after lifestyle success
Consider reducing medication without follow-up of the withdrawal period
Consider reducing or withdrawing medication with planned monitoring
Consider increasing medication to maintain the gains from lifestyle changes
explanation:
Weight loss, exercise and lower sodium intake can reduce the medication needed to maintain control. **A supervised dose reduction or withdrawal with planned blood-pressure monitoring is reasonable** when readings have remained below target.

**A. Keep the original dose routinely** — The need for a particular dose can change after sustained lifestyle improvements. Reassessment may avoid excessive lowering.
**B. Reduce without follow-up** — Pressure can rise again after withdrawal, even when readings were stable before the change.
**C. Reduce or withdraw with monitoring** — Check home measurements, symptoms and follow-up readings, and reinstate treatment if pressure rises above the individual goal.
**D. Increase medication** — Pressure already lies below target. More medication increases the chance of hypotension without a demonstrated need.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1224.

q: A 78-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 35% predicted) presents with acute dyspnea and confusion. His daughter reports two days of memory difficulty and failure to recognize her this morning. His home medications include tiotropium, budesonide/formoterol, and lorazepam 0.5 mg three times daily, recently started for anxiety. Arterial blood gases show pH 7.32, pCO2 58, and pO2 65 on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Chest radiography shows hyperinflation without infiltrates, and examination reveals asterixis. Medication review focuses on a possible benzodiazepine contribution. Which effect described by Hazzard is relevant?
o: Increased ventilatory control and increased aspiration risk
Decreased ventilatory control and increased aspiration risk
Decreased ventilatory control and decreased aspiration risk
Increased ventilatory control and decreased aspiration risk
explanation:
Ventilatory control drives the response to a rising CO₂ level. A sedative can blunt that response and impair protective airway reflexes.
**Lorazepam can decrease ventilatory control and increase aspiration risk.**

**A. Increased drive and increased aspiration.** The aspiration concern is plausible, but a benzodiazepine depresses rather than stimulates ventilatory drive.
**B. Decreased drive and increased aspiration.** New sedation can aggravate CO₂ retention and impair airway protection. The respiratory acidosis also requires direct assessment and treatment.
**C. Decreased drive and decreased aspiration.** The direction of the aspiration effect is reversed.
**D. Increased drive and decreased aspiration.** Neither effect describes the respiratory risks of adding lorazepam in this setting.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1247.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A patient with delirium is found to be volume depleted while taking furosemide. There is no congestion, and the team identifies overdiuresis as a contributor. Which approach addresses the identified problem?
o: Increase the diuretic and prescribe a sedative as needed
Adjust the diuretic and correct volume depletion with monitoring
Maintain the diuretic dose and add a sedating medication
Increase the diuretic and restrict fluids to prevent congestion
explanation:
Volume depletion can precipitate delirium. Diuretic treatment should reflect current volume status as well as the diagnosis for which it was originally prescribed.
**Reduce or hold the contributing diuretic as appropriate, replace the deficit cautiously and monitor for response or congestion.**

**A. Increase the diuretic and prescribe a sedative as needed.** More diuresis worsens the identified volume loss, while a sedative does not treat it.
**B. Adjust the diuretic and correct volume depletion with monitoring.** Adjusting both the drug and fluid balance addresses the mechanism with follow-up of volume status.
**C. Maintain the diuretic dose and add a sedating medication.** The original dose can perpetuate losses despite treatment of agitation.
**D. Increase the diuretic and restrict fluids to prevent congestion.** Increasing diuresis and restricting fluid both drive volume in the wrong direction here.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 882, 885, 888, Table 58-5

q: A 75-year-old man with COPD remains limited when walking by dyspnea and fatigue despite optimized pharmacologic therapy. How should pulmonary rehabilitation be approached?
o: Wait for lung function to improve before starting exercise within rehabilitation
Reduce physical activity as a way to improve endurance over time
Refer for pulmonary rehabilitation combining exercise, education and behavior change
Defer rehabilitation because of his age and continue monitoring walking ability
explanation:
Breathlessness leads some patients to avoid walking. Inactivity then weakens leg muscles, making the same distance still more tiring.
**Refer for pulmonary rehabilitation combining tailored exercise, education and behavior change.**

**A. Wait for better lung function.** Functional benefits can occur despite persistent airflow obstruction.
**B. Reduce activity.** Avoidance reinforces deconditioning and further limits endurance.
**C. Combine training and self-management.** Supervised progression, pacing and a home exercise plan can improve walking tolerance and confidence.
**D. Defer because of age.** A program can be adapted for balance, weakness and comorbidity in an older participant.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1257–1258.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: An 84-year-old nursing-home resident with severe COPD, moderate vascular dementia (MMSE 18), and stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) presents with acute dyspnea. He is uncomfortable but follows simple commands. His MOLST specifies no intubation but permits bilevel positive airway pressure. Arterial blood gases show pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mm Hg, and PaO2 58 mm Hg; chest radiography shows no infiltrate. His son asks about comfort-focused care. Which initial ventilatory approach is supported by the source and the stated treatment preferences?
o: Favor oxygen therapy without ventilatory support for the respiratory acidosis
Favor bilevel noninvasive ventilation after assessing for relevant contraindications
Favor withholding ventilatory support because the directive declines intubation
Favor endotracheal intubation to address the hypercapnic respiratory failure
explanation:
The acidemia and markedly elevated PaCO₂ indicate acute ventilatory failure. Bilevel support through a mask can relieve the respiratory muscles and is explicitly permitted in this treatment plan.
**Assess airway protection and mask tolerance, then offer a monitored trial of bilevel noninvasive ventilation if appropriate.**

**A. Give oxygen alone.** Oxygen can correct the low PaO₂, but it does not provide the inspiratory assistance needed for CO₂ clearance.
**B. Offer bilevel ventilation.** Following simple commands supports a trial. Reassess comfort, alertness, gas exchange and the patient's goals with the family.
**C. Withhold all ventilatory support.** The directive distinguishes intubation from bilevel mask ventilation and permits the latter.
**D. Intubate.** This would cross his stated treatment limit.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1257, 1262.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A woman with COPD uses albuterol frequently and remains symptomatic. After evaluation of the poor symptom control, a long-acting bronchodilator is being considered. How does Hazzard's drug table distinguish SABA from LABA therapy?
o: SABA for regular maintenance and LABA for rescue when symptoms occur
Both SABA and LABA for rescue treatment when symptoms occur
SABA for rescue when needed and LABA for ongoing maintenance treatment
Both SABA and LABA for regular maintenance between episodes of dyspnea
explanation:
Bronchodilators relax airway smooth muscle. A rescue drug needs a prompt effect during symptoms, while a maintenance drug provides sustained control between episodes.
**Use short-acting albuterol for rescue and a long-acting bronchodilator for maintenance.**

**A. SABA for maintenance, LABA for rescue.** This reverses their usual roles in this COPD regimen.
**B. Both for rescue.** As-needed use of both would omit the scheduled long-acting component chosen for persistent symptoms.
**C. SABA for rescue, LABA for maintenance.** Frequent albuterol use warrants review of technique, adherence and the maintenance regimen.
**D. Both for scheduled maintenance.** Albuterol should remain available for sudden breathlessness.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1248–1249, Table 81-10.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: An 81-year-old man with severe COPD on continuous oxygen at 2 L/min and mild cognitive impairment develops worsening confusion over three days, poor sleep, and hallucinations. He recently finished antibiotics for an exacerbation. He takes tiotropium, budesonide/formoterol, a prednisone taper currently at 20 mg, and temazepam 15 mg nightly, started one week ago. Which action addresses the newly introduced benzodiazepine exposure during the delirium evaluation?
o: Increase the daily prednisone dose
Review stopping temazepam treatment
Start nightly quetiapine treatment
Request cranial computed tomography
explanation:
A newly introduced benzodiazepine can cause sedation or worsen delirium in an older person with limited respiratory reserve. Assess recent drugs alongside oxygenation and the COPD course.
**Review stopping temazepam, accounting for exposure duration and withdrawal risk.**

**A. Increase the daily prednisone dose.** Increasing prednisone does not remove the new sedative exposure and corticosteroids can themselves affect cognition.
**B. Review stopping temazepam treatment.** Reviewing temazepam directly addresses the new benzodiazepine and permits reassessment of attention and breathing.
**C. Start nightly quetiapine treatment.** Adding quetiapine increases central drug exposure without evaluating the hypnotic.
**D. Request cranial computed tomography.** Imaging may be indicated by particular findings but cannot address the temazepam exposure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 882–883, 885, 889

q: A 76-year-old woman with COPD has an FEV1 of 45% predicted, sarcopenia with a grip strength of 14 kg, and increasing difficulty bathing independently despite optimized bronchodilator therapy. She has lost 8 lb over 6 months; BMI is 19.2 and albumin is 3.1 g/dL. She asks about prognosis and hospice. Which assessment combines nutritional status, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, and exercise capacity to inform the prognosis discussion?
o: Calculate the multidimensional BODE index
Measure her six-minute walking distance
Repeat spirometry to reassess airflow limitation
Perform a standardized depression screening assessment
explanation:
Airflow obstruction alone gives an incomplete prognosis. Walking ability, nutritional reserve and the patient's experience of dyspnea contribute independent information.
**Calculate the BODE index using body mass index, airflow obstruction, dyspnea and exercise capacity.**

**A. BODE index.** Combine BMI, FEV₁, a dyspnea scale and six-minute walking distance. Use the result alongside her functional losses and goals.
**B. Six-minute walking distance.** This measures exercise capacity, one of the four components.
**C. Repeat spirometry.** FEV₁ measures airflow obstruction but misses exercise tolerance, nutritional status and perceived breathlessness.
**D. Depression screening.** Mood deserves assessment but a depression scale does not measure the four requested domains.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1245–1246.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: An 85-year-old man with COPD and chronic kidney disease is hospitalized with pneumonia. He develops delirium with agitation that threatens essential treatment despite nonpharmacologic measures. After assessing risks, the team decides to use haloperidol. Which initial approach matches Hazzard?
o: Start with a high dose and titrate until the patient is deeply sedated
Start with a high dose and continue it until the pneumonia resolves
Start low and reassess, aiming for an awake, manageable patient
Start with a low dose and continue it routinely after the delirium resolves
explanation:
Haloperidol is used selectively when dangerous agitation persists despite environmental and medical management. Titrate according to response and adverse effects.
**Start low, reassess before redosing and aim for a patient who is awake enough to accept safe care.**

**A. Start with a high dose and titrate until the patient is deeply sedated.** A high dose and deep sedation compromise monitoring and increase harm.
**B. Start with a high dose and continue it until the pneumonia resolves.** Sedative need follows behavior and safety, not the duration of pneumonia.
**C. Start low and reassess, aiming for an awake, manageable patient.** Repeated examination allows a cautious dose to achieve the immediate goal.
**D. Start with a low dose and continue it routinely after the delirium resolves.** Reassess and taper promptly once the indication resolves.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 889

q: A 77-year-old woman with moderate COPD and frailty has lost 15 lb unintentionally, reports exhaustion, and has a grip strength of 15 kg. She has temporal wasting and reduced breath sounds, uses tiotropium and as-needed albuterol, and has had progressive breathlessness for two weeks. She is unable to climb to her bedroom and sleeps in a recliner; her daughter is considering nursing-home placement. After evaluation of her recent deterioration and stabilization of her respiratory illness, which rehabilitation plan directly addresses exercise limitation and nutritional needs?
o: Provide dietary counseling while substituting rest for exercise training
Combine pulmonary rehabilitation with individualized assessment of nutritional needs
Provide inhaler education while deferring physical reconditioning
Provide nutritional supplements while deferring supervised exercise training
explanation:
After a COPD deterioration has been evaluated and stabilized, exercise limitation and weight loss require distinct parts of the rehabilitation plan. **Offer pulmonary rehabilitation and assess her individual nutritional needs.**

**A. Dietary counseling with rest** Counsel about her intake, but prolonged rest perpetuates deconditioning and leaves stair-climbing limitation untreated.
**B. Pulmonary rehabilitation with nutritional assessment** Tailored exercise training can improve exertional capacity and dyspnea. Reviewing the weight loss and intake addresses the risk of further muscle loss.
**C. Inhaler education without reconditioning** Good inhaler technique supports disease control. Education alone cannot train the muscles required for walking and climbing.
**D. Supplements with deferred exercise** Supplements may help if food intake falls short. They cannot provide the physiological training effect of supervised exercise.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 736–737. ATS pulmonary rehabilitation guideline, doi:10.1164/rccm.202306-1066ST.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A patient with COPD develops respiratory depression after an opioid overdose. Alongside respiratory support, treatment is needed to reverse the opioid effect. What is the role of naloxone here?
o: Reversal of the opioid effect during an overdose
Long-term medication treatment of opioid use disorder
Enhancement of the opioid effect for pain relief
Replacement of the opioid for continuing pain treatment
explanation:
Naloxone reverses opioid suppression of respiratory drive. COPD limits respiratory reserve, so this patient needs **prompt opioid reversal alongside ventilatory support**.

**A. Reverse the overdose.** By blocking mu-opioid receptors, naloxone can restore spontaneous breathing while assisted ventilation maintains gas exchange.
**B. Treat opioid use disorder long term.** Buprenorphine or methadone can suppress withdrawal and craving over time. Naloxone’s action is brief.
**C. Enhance pain relief.** Opioid receptor blockade can reduce analgesia as it reverses respiratory depression.
**D. Replace the opioid for pain.** Naloxone supplies no analgesia. Reassess the pain regimen once breathing has stabilized.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 326.
ref: Hazzard Ch 23 — SUBSTANCE USE AND DISORDERS

q: במשפחתו של מטופל עם דמנציה נשקל מעבר מהזנה בזונדה להזנה דרך PEG. מה יש להסביר על ההשוואה בין שתי דרכי ההזנה לפי המלצות הוועדה הארצית?
o: PEG הוכח כמפחית אספירציות ומשפר הישרדות בהשוואה לזונדה
זונדה הוכחה כמפחיתה אספירציות ומשפרת הישרדות בהשוואה ל-PEG
לא הוכח יתרון באספירציות או בהישרדות לאחת משתי השיטות
בחירת דרך ההזנה נקבעת לפי גיל המטופל ולא לפי מצבו הרפואי
explanation:
**בהשוואת PEG לזונדה בדמנציה לא הוכחה עדיפות בהישרדות או במניעת שאיפות.** בוחנים בנפרד נוחות, סיבוכים, משך הזנה צפוי והעדפות.

**א. יתרון מוכח ל־PEG.** יתרון טכני אפשרי בהזנה ממושכת אינו הוכחה לשיפור בשני התוצאים.
**ב. יתרון מוכח לזונדה.** המחקרים אינם מדגימים יתרון כזה לצינור דרך האף.
**ג. אין יתרון מוכח בתוצאים אלה.** זהו הגבול של הראיות שעמדו בפני הוועדה.
**ד. גיל לבדו.** הבחירה תלויה במצב הקליני ובמטרות המטופל.

אסמכתא · משרד הבריאות, המלצות הוועדה הארצית בעניין הזנה בחולים עם קיהיון, עמ׳ 4–5.
ref: משרד הבריאות, המלצות מותב הוועדה הארצית לחוק החולה הנוטה למות: PEG לחולה עם קיהיון שהוא נוטה למות
