q: At discharge, a patient with COPD reports being unable to keep taking inhalers because of their cost. What should the adherence assessment include, according to Hazzard?
o: Assess motivation while treating inhaler cost as unrelated to adherence.
Change the treatment before assessing the ability to use the selected devices.
Add inhaler devices before assessing the complexity of the existing regimen.
Assess cost, regimen complexity, and the ability to use inhalers.
explanation:
An inhaler can only deliver its intended dose when the patient can obtain it, prepare it and use it correctly. A discharge prescription can fail at any of these steps.
**Review cost, regimen complexity and the patient's ability to use each device.**

**A. Assess motivation alone.** Unaffordable refills can interrupt treatment even when the patient understands its purpose.
**B. Change medication first.** Observe a return demonstration and determine what the patient can actually obtain before changing the regimen.
**C. Add more devices.** Extra devices may require different techniques and increase expense or confusion.
**D. Assess practical barriers together.** Ask about refill costs, review each inhaler and use teach-back to identify a feasible regimen.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1255.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: An older woman with atrial fibrillation develops a slower heart rate after rapid beta-blocker dose escalation. Which drug effect explains why its contribution should be considered?
o: Slowing of atrioventricular nodal conduction
Acceleration of atrioventricular nodal conduction
Improvement of conduction during rapid dose escalation
Enhancement of the baroreceptor reflex during dose escalation
explanation:
Beta blockers reduce sympathetic stimulation of the AV node. **Slower AV nodal conduction reduces the ventricular rate in AF**, and a rapid dose increase can overshoot the intended effect.

**A. Slowing of AV conduction** — Fewer atrial impulses pass to the ventricles, explaining the lower pulse and possible bradycardia.
**B. Acceleration of AV conduction** — Faster transmission would tend to increase, not lower, the ventricular response.
**C. Improved conduction on escalation** — Higher doses may impair conduction enough to cause symptomatic block.
**D. Enhanced baroreceptor reflex** — Beta blockade can blunt compensatory responses. Reflex enhancement does not explain the new bradycardia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1201, Rate Control.

q: חולה בישראל הוגדר כחולה הנוטה למות וסובל מקוצר נשימה קשה. הוא מבקש הקלה בסבלו. איזה עיקרון תואם את סעיף 23 לחוק החולה הנוטה למות?
o: להימנע מטיפול מקל בשל הסיכון הסביר הנלווה לחיי החולה
לתת טיפול המכוון לגרימת מוות לשם הקלה על סבל החולה
לתת טיפול מקל לפי רצונו גם בסיכון סביר לחייו
להפסיק טיפול רציף אף שההפסקה עלולה להביא למות החולה
explanation:
טיפול מקל נועד להקל כאב וסבל גופני, נפשי או חברתי. סעיף 23 לחוק החולה הנוטה למות מחייב לפעול ככל האפשר להקלת סבלו של המטופל, בכפוף לרצונו ובהתאם לעקרונות טיפול מקל ראוי.
**יש לתת טיפול להקלת קוצר הנשימה בהתאם לרצונו, גם אם כרוך בכך סיכון סביר לחייו.**

**א. הימנעות בגלל הסיכון** סיכון סביר הנלווה לטיפול מקל ראוי אינו סיבה לשלול את הטיפול.
**ב. טיפול שמטרתו גרימת מוות** סעיף 19 אוסר פעולה המכוונת להמית, גם אם מבקשים להקל על הסבל.
**ג. הקלת סבל בהתאם לרצון** מקלים על קוצר הנשימה בטיפול מידתי ומעריכים את התגובה ואת תופעות הלוואי.
**ד. הפסקת טיפול רציף** הפסקה העלולה להביא למות החולה כפופה לאיסור שבסעיף 21. סעיף 23 עוסק במתן טיפול מקל.

אסמכתא · חוק החולה הנוטה למות, התשס״ו–2005, סעיפים 19, 21 ו־23(א).
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 84-year-old man is hospitalized with a COPD exacerbation, acute hypercarbia, and respiratory acidosis. He is conscious, cooperative, able to protect his airway, and hemodynamically stable. There is no contraindication to a face mask. What is the role of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation in this setting?
o: To defer ventilatory support while awaiting the response to medical treatment.
To support respiratory muscles while medical treatment improves airflow.
To replace bronchodilator treatment with ventilatory support through a mask.
To provide oxygen as sufficient respiratory support despite the respiratory acidosis.
explanation:
Hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis means the respiratory muscles cannot clear CO₂ adequately. Mask ventilation assists the next breath while drugs address the underlying obstruction.
**Use noninvasive positive pressure ventilation to support the respiratory muscles during medical treatment.**

**A. Wait for medical treatment alone.** In a suitable patient with acidotic hypercapnia, early ventilatory support reduces the need for intubation.
**B. Unload the respiratory muscles.** His alertness, stable circulation and ability to protect his airway make mask treatment feasible.
**C. Replace bronchodilators.** Pressure support assists ventilation. It does not reverse bronchoconstriction by itself.
**D. Give oxygen as the only support.** Correcting hypoxemia can leave inadequate ventilation and acidemia unresolved.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1257.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A 79-year-old woman with COPD, diabetes, and mild cognitive impairment lives alone. She uses her albuterol inhaler “when I remember” and reports difficulty with inhaler technique. Her daughter finds expired inhalers and reports two hospitalizations for exacerbations in six months. FEV1 is 48% predicted. Her medications are as-needed albuterol MDI, daily tiotropium HandiHaler, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Which intervention addresses her difficulty delivering inhaled bronchodilators?
o: Increase the number of handheld-inhaler doses while retaining the existing delivery technique.
Add oral roflumilast in place of adapting bronchodilator delivery to her practical difficulties.
Use nebulized bronchodilators and arrange the help needed for preparation and cleaning.
Use oral theophylline as the preferred response to difficulty operating handheld inhalers.
explanation:
Preparing and coordinating a handheld inhaler require memory, dexterity and an adequate inhalation. Escalating a prescribed dose achieves little if the drug never reaches the airways.
**Use nebulized bronchodilators and arrange reliable help with setup, administration and cleaning.**

**A. Increase handheld doses.** Repeating a poorly executed maneuver can reproduce the same delivery failure.
**B. Substitute roflumilast.** This oral exacerbation-prevention drug has specific indications and does not replace delivery of her inhaled bronchodilators.
**C. Adapt delivery and support.** A nebulizer reduces the coordination demand. Her living situation makes it important to establish who will prepare and clean it.
**D. Prefer theophylline.** Its narrow therapeutic range and interactions make it a poor workaround for an unusable device.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1248, Figure 81-2, and p. 1255.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1248, 1254–1255

q: An 81-year-old nursing-home resident with severe COPD, dementia, and recurrent aspiration becomes poorly responsive after starting oral morphine for dyspnea. He has marked respiratory slowing, hypoxemia, and hypercapnic respiratory acidosis. His directive requests DNR status but continuation of medical treatment. Which approach addresses a reversible drug effect while recognizing the severely impaired consciousness?
o: Give naloxone while preparing to provide invasive airway support
Increase oxygen delivery and observe for recovery of consciousness
Begin noninvasive ventilation and observe for recovery of consciousness
Provide comfort measures and forgo reversal of the opioid effect
explanation:
Opioids can suppress the respiratory drive, causing slow breathing, carbon dioxide retention and then impaired consciousness. Naloxone reverses the opioid effect, but ventilation can be needed before it works.
**Support breathing immediately and give naloxone. Prepare for intubation if he cannot protect his airway or adequate ventilation cannot be maintained.**

**A. Naloxone and airway preparation** This treats a reversible cause while allowing immediate assisted ventilation and escalation if needed. His DNR order addresses resuscitation at arrest, and he requested ongoing medical treatment.
**B. Oxygen and observation** Oxygen can improve saturation while ventilation remains inadequate and carbon dioxide continues to rise.
**C. Noninvasive ventilation and observation** Poor responsiveness and recurrent aspiration raise concern that he cannot protect his airway. Observation also delays opioid reversal.
**D. Comfort care alone** He has a potentially reversible drug effect and has asked to continue medical treatment. DNR status alone does not justify withholding that treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 326. American Heart Association, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines, Part 10, opioid overdose.
ref: Hazzard Ch 7 — DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: A 77-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 55%), hypertension, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m2) is reviewed after an exacerbation treated with prednisone 40 mg for 5 days. He remains breathless when dressing and can no longer shop independently. He takes tiotropium, as-needed albuterol, amlodipine 10 mg, and lisinopril 20 mg. Blood pressure is 128/76 and room-air oxygen saturation is 93%. Alongside review of his drug treatment, which pulmonary rehabilitation approach is supported by Hazzard?
o: Offer pulmonary rehabilitation for dyspnea and exercise limitation
Defer pulmonary rehabilitation because patients over 70 benefit less
Defer pulmonary rehabilitation because comorbidity prevents benefit
Offer pulmonary rehabilitation to promote rest and reduce activity
explanation:
A person can remain unable to dress or shop after an exacerbation even with moderate airflow obstruction. Rehabilitation targets these activities through exercise and self-management.
**Offer pulmonary rehabilitation for his continuing breathlessness and functional limitation.**

**A. Refer on the basis of his limitation.** Tailor endurance and strength training to his baseline and identify dressing or shopping as outcomes he can track.
**B. Exclude him by age.** Age above 70 is not a reason to withhold an individualized program.
**C. Exclude him for comorbidity.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease guide assessment and exercise planning; they do not automatically prevent benefit.
**D. Promote rest.** The program uses monitored, progressive activity to reverse deconditioning.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1257–1258.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A hospitalized woman develops delirium after a medication change. Evaluation identifies a drug that could be contributing to confusion. Which approach addresses the medication-related cause?
o: Consider stopping, replacing, or reducing the potentially harmful medication
Consider continuing the medication and using sedation to treat the cause
Consider continuing the medication and using physical restraint to treat the cause
Consider continuing the medication and changing the room to treat the cause
explanation:
A plausible medication cause warrants reassessment of indication, dose and alternatives. Drugs with withdrawal potential require a planned taper.
**Stop, substitute or reduce the potentially harmful drug as clinically appropriate.**

**A. Consider stopping, replacing, or reducing the potentially harmful medication.** All three strategies can reduce the relevant exposure depending on necessity and withdrawal risk.
**B. Consider continuing the medication and using sedation to treat the cause.** Sedation can mask symptoms while the drug continues to act.
**C. Consider continuing the medication and using physical restraint to treat the cause.** A restraint does nothing to change the adverse drug effect and can worsen agitation.
**D. Consider continuing the medication and changing the room to treat the cause.** Changing rooms does not correct drug exposure and may add disorientation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 885, 887, Figure 58-2

q: A 75-year-old man with stable COPD receives optimal inhaled treatment. Two resting room-air measurements show PaO2 58 mm Hg; PaCO2 is 52 mm Hg and pH is normal. He has cor pulmonale with edema and no recent exacerbation. Which recommendation follows the long-term oxygen indications and survival evidence in Hazzard?
o: Daily long-term oxygen for resting hypoxemia with cor pulmonale
Nocturnal ventilation because its survival benefit is better established in stable COPD
Exertional oxygen because the resting oxygen value is above daily-treatment eligibility
Nocturnal oxygen because daily-treatment eligibility requires a lower resting oxygen value
explanation:
Long-term oxygen improves survival in appropriately selected patients with severe resting hypoxemia. Cor pulmonale is evidence that chronic hypoxemia is already affecting the right heart.
**Prescribe daily long-term oxygen for the repeated PaO₂ of 58 mm Hg with cor pulmonale.**

**A. Daily long-term oxygen.** The qualifying range extends to PaO₂ at or below 59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension or specified erythrocytosis. Prescribe at least 16 hours daily.
**B. Nocturnal ventilation instead.** Stable compensated hypercapnia may prompt separate assessment for ventilatory support. It does not displace this oxygen indication.
**C. Exertional oxygen only.** His repeated abnormal measurements were taken at rest, and cor pulmonale changes the qualifying threshold.
**D. Nocturnal oxygen only.** A sleep-only prescription would leave his qualifying daytime hypoxemia untreated.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1256–1257, Table 81-11.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A woman with COPD remains limited by dyspnea despite optimized pharmacologic therapy. Which nonpharmacologic intervention is appropriate now according to the COPD chapter?
o: Reduce physical activity and avoid exercise training until her respiratory symptoms resolve
Prescribe home oxygen for her activity limitation despite the absence of oxygen desaturation
Postpone exercise training until pulmonary function has returned to the normal range
Refer for pulmonary rehabilitation combining exercise training, education, and behavior change
explanation:
Pulmonary rehabilitation teaches patients to remain active despite chronic airflow limitation. It combines supervised conditioning, education and changes in everyday activity.
**Refer now because dyspnea persists despite optimized medication.**

**A. Avoid activity until dyspnea resolves.** Waiting can deepen deconditioning and further reduce the distance she can walk.
**B. Prescribe home oxygen for limitation alone.** Oxygen eligibility depends on measured hypoxemia and the circumstances in which it occurs.
**C. Wait for normal lung function.** Rehabilitation can improve symptoms and endurance in people with persistent, even severe, obstruction.
**D. Refer for comprehensive rehabilitation.** An initial assessment allows exercise intensity and self-management goals to be adapted to what she needs to do at home.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1257–1258.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: חולה בישראל הוגדר כחולה הנוטה למות שאינו בעל כשרות. אשתו וילדיו חלוקים לגבי רצונותיו הקודמים, וטרם נאספו נתונים ומסמכים רלוונטיים. מהי חובת הרופא בשלב בירור הרצון?
o: להכריע לפי עמדת רוב בני המשפחה המשתתפים בפגישה
לאסוף מידע ומסמכים על רצונו במאמץ סביר
לקבוע שאין רצון ידוע משום שהמשפחה חלוקה בדעתה
לאמץ את עמדת בן המשפחה המבקש טיפול נרחב יותר
explanation:
אי־הסכמה במשפחה אינה מבטלת את החובה לחפש מידע על רצונו של החולה. מגבשים את ההחלטה לפי מסלול ההכרעה שבחוק. **לאסוף מידע ומסמכים על רצונו במאמץ סביר**.

**א. להכריע לפי עמדת רוב בני המשפחה המשתתפים בפגישה.** רוב במשפחה אינו קובע את רצונו.
**ב. לאסוף מידע ומסמכים על רצונו במאמץ סביר.** המאמץ כולל חיפוש מסמכים והקשבה לעדות על דבריו.
**ג. לקבוע שאין רצון ידוע משום שהמשפחה חלוקה בדעתה.** מחלוקת בין קרובים אינה מוכיחה שאין רצון שאפשר לברר.
**ד. לאמץ את עמדת בן המשפחה המבקש טיפול נרחב יותר.** העדפת טיפול נרחב אינה מעניקה לבן המשפחה סמכות יתר.

אסמכתא · חוק החולה הנוטה למות, סעיף 9, עמ׳ 7.

q: An older adult has suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression. Naloxone is considered during emergency treatment. What is its purpose?
o: To reverse the effects of the opioid overdose
To preserve the opioid effect to prevent withdrawal
To reduce opioid craving during maintenance treatment
To provide a long-acting opioid substitute for pain
explanation:
Opioid overdose can slow breathing until ventilation becomes inadequate. In an older adult with suspected overdose, **naloxone reverses that respiratory depression** while the team supports breathing.

**A. Reverse opioid effects.** Naloxone rapidly competes with the opioid at its receptors. Judge the response by the rate and depth of spontaneous breathing.
**B. Preserve opioid effects.** Continued receptor activation sustains hypoventilation. Reversal can precipitate withdrawal in a physically dependent patient.
**C. Reduce craving.** Methadone and buprenorphine can control craving during maintenance treatment. A rescue dose of naloxone has no sustained effect on craving.
**D. Provide a long-acting substitute.** An opioid agonist used for pain can prolong respiratory suppression during overdose.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 326.
ref: Hazzard Ch 23 — SUBSTANCE USE AND DISORDERS

q: A 76-year-old man with persistent pain and kidney impairment is being considered for opioid treatment after assessment of benefits and risks. Which initiation and follow-up strategy is described in Hazzard?
o: Start extended-release treatment at a high dose and assess response later
Start immediate-release treatment at a high dose and escalate rapidly for pain
Start immediate-release treatment at a low effective dose with close early follow-up
Start extended-release treatment at a fixed dose and review tolerability when pain worsens
explanation:
A trial of opioid analgesia is easiest to adjust when initial exposure is brief and small. **Use a low effective dose of an appropriate immediate-release preparation with close early follow-up.**

**A. Start extended-release treatment at a high dose and assess response later** High-dose extended-release treatment increases risk before tolerance or benefit is known.
**B. Start immediate-release treatment at a high dose and escalate rapidly for pain** A shorter-acting formulation does not make a high starting dose or rapid escalation safe.
**C. Start immediate-release treatment at a low effective dose with close early follow-up** Renal impairment influences drug selection and dose. Review function, comfort, sedation and breathing early.
**D. Start extended-release treatment at a fixed dose and review tolerability when pain worsens** Waiting for worsening pain misses toxicity, and a fixed long-acting dose is difficult to adjust promptly.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1060–1061, Table 68-6.

q: בת 83 עם דמנציה מתקדמת הוגדרה כחולה הנוטה למות. יש קושי בבליעה, אך הערכה רב־מקצועית קבעה שניתן לספק את צורכי המזון והנוזלים דרך הפה בעזרת התאמות וסיוע. לפי המלצות המותב הארצי, איזו דרך הזנה מועדפת במצב זה?
o: מעבר להזנה בזונדה כפתרון קבוע
המשך הזנה דרך הפה עם התאמות
מעבר להזנה דרך PEG כבר בשלב זה
מעבר למתן נוזלים דרך הווריד
explanation:
הערכת בליעה ותזונה מאפשרת לבחור דרך הזנה שנותנת מענה לצרכים ושומרת על ההנאה וההשתתפות באכילה במידת האפשר. **המשך הזנה דרך הפה עם התאמות**.

**א. מעבר להזנה בזונדה כפתרון קבוע.** זונדה קבועה אינה נחוצה אם האכילה הפומית מספקת.
**ב. המשך הזנה דרך הפה עם התאמות.** ממשיכים דרך הפה עם התאמת מרקם, תנוחה וסיוע.
**ג. מעבר להזנה דרך PEG כבר בשלב זה.** PEG כרוך בפעולה פולשנית בלי תועלת נוספת שהודגמה במקרה.
**ד. מעבר למתן נוזלים דרך הווריד.** נוזלים תוך־ורידיים אינם מענה תזונתי מתאים כשהאכילה אפשרית.

אסמכתא · משרד הבריאות, המלצות מותב הוועדה הארצית לחוק החולה הנוטה למות בנושא PEG לחולה עם קיהיון שהוא נוטה למות, עמ׳ 5–6.
ref: משרד הבריאות, המלצות מותב הוועדה הארצית לחוק החולה הנוטה למות: PEG לחולה עם קיהיון שהוא נוטה למות

q: A 77-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 45%), coronary disease, and diabetes has had four admissions for COPD exacerbations in eight months. Between admissions he needs help with basic ADLs from his older wife, who is exhausted. Creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min by Cockcroft–Gault. He takes 14 medications, including warfarin requiring frequent INR testing, and says, “I am tired of the struggle.” Which referral plan explicitly integrates symptom management, discussion of care goals, and support for the family?
o: Home-health referral centered on medication administration and INR checks
Adult-day-program referral centered on activities and caregiver respite
Palliative-care review of symptoms, goals, and caregiver needs
Care-management referral centered on appointments and service coordination
explanation:
Repeated COPD admissions can leave breathlessness, treatment burden and family exhaustion between crises. Palliative care brings those needs into the same clinical discussion.
**Request a palliative-care review of symptoms, goals and support for his wife.**

**A. Home-health medication visits** These visits can make medication and INR monitoring easier, but their stated focus omits goals and broader symptom needs.
**B. Adult day program** Activities and respite may help his wife. They do not provide the integrated clinical review requested.
**C. Palliative consultation** The team can assess breathlessness, ask what he means by being tired of the struggle and plan practical family support.
**D. Appointment coordination** Organizing visits helps access. It needs to be paired with symptom management and decisions about future treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1045, 1047, 1049.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A patient with COPD uses albuterol frequently. Which pair of adverse effects of short-acting beta-2 agonists is listed in Hazzard?
o: Slower heart rate and increased serum potassium
Faster heart rate and decreased serum potassium
Slower heart rate and decreased serum potassium
Faster heart rate and increased serum potassium
explanation:
Albuterol is a short-acting β₂ agonist. Systemic adrenergic effects can accelerate the heart rate, while β₂ stimulation shifts potassium into cells.
**Frequent doses can cause tachycardia and lower serum potassium.**

**A. Slower pulse and higher potassium.** Both changes run in the opposite direction to the expected drug effects.
**B. Faster pulse and lower potassium.** Palpitations, tremor and hypokalemia are especially relevant with frequent dosing or susceptibility to arrhythmia.
**C. Slower pulse and lower potassium.** The potassium change fits; bradycardia is not the characteristic pulse response.
**D. Faster pulse and higher potassium.** The pulse change fits, but intracellular potassium uptake lowers the serum concentration.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1249, Table 81-10.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: A 79-year-old woman with COPD and osteoporosis needs systemic corticosteroids for a moderate to severe exacerbation. How should exposure-related harm be limited while preserving beneficial treatment, according to Hazzard?
o: Extend the duration of treatment courses to reduce steroid adverse effects
Use a conservative dose and duration suited to the exacerbation
Withhold treatment because clinical benefit has not been demonstrated
Increase the dose to reduce delirium and muscle weakness
explanation:
Systemic corticosteroids can improve recovery during a moderate or severe COPD exacerbation. Older adults are also vulnerable to delirium, muscle weakness and cumulative bone harm.
**Choose a conservative dose and duration appropriate to the exacerbation.**

**A. Extend treatment.** Additional days increase cumulative systemic exposure.
**B. Limit exposure while treating the flare.** In hospitalized patients, a five-day course of oral prednisone 40 mg/day performed as well as a longer conventional regimen.
**C. Withhold treatment because benefit is absent.** Established benefit in moderate or severe episodes supports treating when indicated, with attention to her osteoporosis.
**D. Increase the dose.** Higher doses increase adverse effects. Delirium becomes a particular concern above 60 mg/day of prednisone.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1261.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

q: An 81-year-old man with advanced COPD has refractory dyspnea despite optimal treatment of the underlying disease. An opioid is being considered for palliation. Which potential benefit and cognitive risk are described by Hazzard?
o: Relief of dyspnea with a risk of reduced mental functioning
Relief of dyspnea with an expected improvement in mental functioning
Worsening dyspnea with a risk of reduced mental functioning
Worsening dyspnea with an expected improvement in mental functioning
explanation:
An opioid may reduce the sensation of otherwise refractory breathlessness. **Potential relief must be balanced against reduced mental functioning**, especially when alertness matters to the patient.

**A. Relief with cognitive risk.** Ask whether the breathing benefit is worth any impairment in alertness.
**B. Relief and cognitive improvement.** Improved cognition is not an expected opioid effect.
**C. Worse breathlessness and poorer cognition.** Cognitive risk is real but the therapeutic aim and potential effect are relief of air hunger.
**D. Worse breathlessness and better cognition.** Neither direction represents the anticipated benefit-risk discussion.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 69 — MANAGEMENT OF COMMON NONPAIN SYMPTOMS

q: An older patient with diabetes and chronic kidney disease takes metformin and has an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 32 mL/min/1.73 m². Which monitoring principle is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Review renal function and dose in relation to reduced renal clearance
Increase the metformin dose to compensate for reduced clearance through the kidneys
Stop metformin and change to insulin on the basis of this value
Continue the dose and monitor glucose in place of assessing renal clearance
explanation:
Metformin exposure rises when kidney clearance falls. An eGFR near the lower limit requires monitoring both the trajectory and the dose.

**At a stable eGFR of 32, review renal function and dose.** This value lies just above the absolute contraindication below 30, and an acute illness could change the decision.

**A. Review dose and filtration.** Rechecking kidney function helps prevent accumulation as renal reserve declines.
**B. Increase the dose.** Reduced clearance raises exposure, so increasing the dose moves in the wrong direction.
**C. Automatically stop and substitute insulin.** The given value alone does not cross the stated contraindication threshold.
**D. Follow glucose instead of renal function.** Glucose measures treatment effect. It cannot tell whether metformin is accumulating.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp1576–1577, Table 99-11.

q: An older woman with advanced kidney disease develops unexplained behavioral changes and cognitive impairment. What possibility should be considered according to Hazzard?
o: These changes may support a gastrointestinal presentation rather than uremia
These changes may indicate improved adaptation to declining renal clearance
These changes may represent uremia and warrant assessment in context
These changes may favor dementia before assessing the renal contribution
explanation:
Uremia is the clinical effect of advanced loss of renal clearance. In an older patient, **unexplained behavioral change or cognitive impairment can be part of uremia** and should be assessed alongside other causes of delirium.

**A. A gastrointestinal presentation explains the behavior** — Anorexia, nausea and vomiting may accompany uremia, but they do not account for or exclude its cognitive manifestations.
**B. The changes indicate successful adaptation** — Declining cognition or function can signal symptomatic kidney failure. Improvement in adaptation would not explain a new decline.
**C. Assess for a uremic contribution** — Compare the patient with baseline and evaluate kidney function, medications and intercurrent illness. The symptoms are compatible with uremia, without being diagnostic by themselves.
**D. Attribute the change to dementia first** — Establish the time course and assess reversible contributors. A new change can reflect delirium even in a patient who already has dementia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1291, 1295, Indications for Dialysis and Cognitive Impairment.

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease requests treatment for joint pain. Which prescribing principle is emphasized in Hazzard’s chapter on the aging kidney?
o: Prefer NSAIDs as a means of preserving the patient’s residual kidney function
Choose medication doses without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
Avoid potential renal toxins and adjust renally excreted medication dosing
Choose dosing intervals without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
explanation:
In CKD, **avoid nephrotoxic exposures and adapt renally cleared medicines to kidney function**. Check changes in renal function, interacting drugs and whether a dose or interval adjustment is needed.

**A. Prefer NSAIDs for renal preservation.** Systemic NSAIDs can impair renal perfusion and worsen kidney function.
**B. Ignore renal excretion when dosing.** Accumulation can cause toxicity, especially with predominantly renally cleared drugs.
**C. Avoid toxins and adjust doses.** This addresses both further kidney injury and excessive drug exposure.
**D. Ignore renal excretion when setting intervals.** Lengthening the interval is one valid adjustment for some drugs.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 82, p. 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older woman with reduced renal clearance is taking a medication excreted by the kidney. Which principle should guide a safety review of the prescription?
o: Consider increasing the dose to compensate for reduced kidney function.
Consider adjusting the dose amount and the frequency of administration.
Consider shortening dose intervals to compensate for reduced renal clearance.
Consider adjusting for the clinical response while disregarding renal clearance.
explanation:
Reduced renal clearance prolongs exposure to a renally eliminated drug. **Reconsider both the dose and the dosing interval** to prevent accumulation while maintaining benefit.

**A. Increase the dose.** More drug per dose raises exposure when elimination is already slow.
**B. Adjust dose and frequency.** A lower dose, longer interval or both may be appropriate depending on the drug and measured renal function.
**C. Shorten the interval.** Closer doses allow even less time for clearance between administrations.
**D. Use response alone.** Toxicity may develop before a clinical change signals excessive exposure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 303, 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: A 77-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and moderate mitral stenosis needs anticoagulation for stroke prevention. Which treatment accords with the Hazzard definition of valvular atrial fibrillation?
o: Use warfarin for stroke prevention
Use apixaban for stroke prevention
Use rivaroxaban for stroke prevention
Use dabigatran for stroke prevention
explanation:
Moderate or severe mitral stenosis creates a high-risk setting for atrial thrombosis when AF develops. **Use warfarin**, with INR monitoring and a usual target range of 2–3 for this indication.

**A. Warfarin** — A vitamin K antagonist is the recommended anticoagulant in AF with mitral stenosis of this severity.
**B. Apixaban** — This direct factor Xa inhibitor is suitable for many other patients with AF, but moderate mitral stenosis changes the choice.
**C. Rivaroxaban** — A different factor Xa inhibitor does not overcome the mitral stenosis restriction.
**D. Dabigatran** — Direct thrombin inhibition is also outside the recommended treatment in this setting.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1203, Table 77-8. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline, §6.8.5.

q: דיירת בית אבות בת 83 עם דמנציה מתקדמת ו-CKD שלב 3B (eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73m²) אוכלת בצורה לקויה במשך שבועות. הצוות מדווח שהיא מצניעה אוכל בפה ואיבדה 8% ממשקל גופה. פגישות משפחה מאשרות מטרות טיפול ממוקדות נוחות. בדיקות מעבדה מראות albumin 2.9 g/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. מהי ההתערבות המתאימה ביותר?
o: התחלת megestrol acetate 400 mg ביום
הנחת PEG tube לתמיכה תזונתית
יישום תוכנית האכלה ידנית מסייעת
התחלת דיאטה כלייתית עם הגבלת חלבון
explanation:
בדמנציה מתקדמת דיספגיה יכולה להתבטא בהשארת מזון בפה ובירידה במשקל. בודקים גורמים הניתנים לתיקון, נעזרים בהערכת בליעה ומתאימים את העזרה בארוחה למטרה שהוגדרה.
**האכלה ידנית מסייעת מאפשרת להציע מזון בכמויות ובקצב שהמטופלת יכולה לשאת.**

**א. מגסטרול** ממריצי תיאבון לא הוכיחו שיפור בתוצאות החשובות למטופלים עם דמנציה מתקדמת ואינם מטפלים בהפרעת הבליעה.
**ב. התקנת PEG** בדמנציה מתקדמת לא הודגם שיפור בהישרדות או במניעת אספירציה, והצינור עשוי להוסיף נטל.
**ג. האכלה ידנית** מתאימים מרקם, קצב ותנוחה, ומפסיקים או משנים את הגישה כשמופיעים שיעול או מצוקה.
**ד. הגבלת חלבון** הגבלה נוספת מקשה על צריכת מזון במטופלת שכבר יורדת במשקל ואינה פותרת את בעיית הבליעה.

אסמכתא · Hazzard 8e, עמ׳ 1048. משרד הבריאות, המלצות המותב בנושא PEG ודמנציה, עמ׳ 5–6.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An older woman using diphenhydramine nightly for sleep reports worsening constipation and memory concerns. Which medication-review action addresses the risks described in Beers 2023?
o: Continue diphenhydramine because hypnotic use reduces its anticholinergic effects
Avoid diphenhydramine because hypnotic use adds anticholinergic adverse effects
Increase diphenhydramine because hypnotic use protects against cognitive effects
Substitute doxylamine because hypnotic use avoids anticholinergic adverse effects
explanation:
Diphenhydramine blocks muscarinic signaling regardless of why it is taken. Constipation and cognitive complaints are relevant adverse effects in an older person taking it nightly.

**Avoid routine diphenhydramine for sleep.** Its limited sustained hypnotic benefit does not offset the anticholinergic concern in this patient.

**A. Continue because use for sleep reduces effects.** The indication does not change its pharmacology or protect the bowel and brain.
**B. Avoid because of anticholinergic effects.** Removing the nightly exposure addresses potential medication contributors to both reported symptoms.
**C. Increase for cognitive protection.** Greater exposure can worsen confusion and constipation.
**D. Substitute doxylamine.** This sleep aid is also a strongly anticholinergic first-generation antihistamine.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, p. 2057.

q: An 80-year-old man with renal failure and severe hyperkalemia develops a conduction abnormality on ECG. Which treatment provides immediate myocardial protection by stabilizing the cell membrane while potassium-lowering treatment is also planned?
o: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Administer insulin by the intravenous route
Administer an intravenous loop diuretic
Administer an oral ion-exchange resin
explanation:
Severe hyperkalemia with ECG conduction changes requires **intravenous calcium for immediate myocardial protection**. Calcium does not lower potassium, so start potassium-shifting and removal measures as appropriate.

**A. IV calcium gluconate.** It rapidly antagonizes the membrane effects of potassium. Monitor the ECG and reassess the response.
**B. IV insulin.** With glucose management, it shifts potassium intracellularly but does not replace calcium for immediate membrane stabilization.
**C. IV loop diuretic.** It can increase urinary potassium loss if renal function and urine output permit.
**D. Oral ion-exchange resin.** Its effect is too slow to protect against an imminent arrhythmia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271. UK Kidney Association, Management of Hyperkalaemia in Adults, 2026.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older woman requires treatment for a complicated urinary tract infection. In Hazzard Table 106-6, which of the following is identified as an oral option for empiric treatment, subject to local resistance and adverse-effect considerations?
o: Ciprofloxacin.
Nitrofurantoin.
Fosfomycin.
Amoxicillin/clavulanate.
explanation:
A complicated UTI can involve tissue beyond the bladder, so an oral agent must reach adequate systemic and renal tissue levels. **Ciprofloxacin is an empirical oral option when local susceptibility and patient risks permit.**

**A. Ciprofloxacin.** It reaches renal tissue. Recent cultures, local resistance and fluoroquinolone adverse effects influence whether it is appropriate.
**B. Nitrofurantoin.** Nitrofurantoin concentrates in bladder urine and gives inadequate renal tissue levels for pyelonephritis.
**C. Fosfomycin.** The usual oral fosfomycin regimen is intended for bladder infection and gives inadequate tissue exposure here.
**D. Amoxicillin/clavulanate.** Amoxicillin/clavulanate can have a role when an isolate is susceptible. It is not the empirical oral choice specified in this comparison.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1709.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · 1689, 1709

q: An older man with chronic pain takes tramadol and another serotonin-reuptake inhibitor. Which additional action of tramadol explains the warning about this combination?
o: Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of cholinergic transmission
Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of serotonin reuptake
Opioid receptor agonism with blockade of dopamine receptors
Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of histamine release
explanation:
Tramadol has both opioid and monoaminergic actions. **Opioid receptor agonism plus serotonin-reuptake inhibition** explains why another serotonergic drug can increase toxicity.

**A. Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of cholinergic transmission** Anticholinergic activity does not explain this interaction.
**B. Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of serotonin reuptake** The combined effect on serotonin raises concern for serotonin toxicity. Tramadol also deserves caution in patients with seizures.
**C. Opioid receptor agonism with blockade of dopamine receptors** Dopamine receptor blockade is not the relevant action of tramadol.
**D. Opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of histamine release** Histamine release does not explain the risk from a serotonin-reuptake inhibitor.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Table 68-6, p. 1061.

q: A woman with Alzheimer disease has dangerous aggression despite assessment of reversible causes and nonpharmacologic treatment. After a risk-benefit assessment, an antipsychotic trial is chosen. Which prescribing principle follows Hazzard?
o: Start at a high dose and reduce it after behavior is controlled
Start at a low dose and titrate to the minimum effective dose
Start several medications together to shorten the adjustment period
Start a long-acting injection without a coexisting psychotic disorder
explanation:
An antipsychotic trial in dementia is a trial against a specific target such as harmful aggression. Dose-related adverse effects can offset a reduction in symptoms.

**Start low and titrate toward the minimum effective dose.**

**A. High initial dose** Early high exposure increases sedation, orthostasis and motor adverse effects.
**B. Minimum effective dose** Gradual titration permits comparison of target behavior with emerging harm.
**C. Several drugs together** Starting more than one obscures which drug changed behavior or caused toxicity.
**D. Long-acting injection** For dementia-related behavior alone it precludes prompt dose adjustment and withdrawal.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 927, Tables 60-7 and 60-8
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: An older woman receiving long-term corticosteroids for an inflammatory condition develops muscle weakness and wasting. Which pair of effects of glucocorticoid excess is described by Hazzard?
o: Muscle breakdown and increased bone resorption
Muscle building and increased bone resorption
Muscle breakdown and increased bone formation
Muscle building and increased bone formation
explanation:
Chronic glucocorticoid excess is catabolic. **It breaks down skeletal muscle and promotes bone loss, including increased resorption.**

**A. Muscle breakdown and increased resorption** — Muscle wasting explains the weakness. Loss of bone strength increases the risk of low-trauma fracture.
**B. Muscle building and increased resorption** — The bone effect fits, but excess glucocorticoids cause loss of proximal muscle.
**C. Muscle breakdown and increased formation** — The muscle effect fits, but glucocorticoids impair bone formation over time.
**D. Muscle building and increased formation** — Both tissues lose structural reserve with prolonged excess.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 769, 1530.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: When reassessing anticoagulation for a patient older than 75 years with atrial fibrillation, which statement about bleeding risk agrees with Hazzard?
o: Full-dose dabigatran is associated with a reduced risk of gastrointestinal bleeding
Apixaban has a lower risk of major bleeding than warfarin
Direct oral anticoagulants increase intracranial bleeding risk compared with warfarin
Warfarin carries a low risk of unintentional overdose in older patients
explanation:
Major bleeding, intracranial bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are distinct outcomes. **Apixaban has a lower major-bleeding risk than warfarin in older adults with eligible AF.**

**A. Full-dose dabigatran lowers GI bleeding** — Full-dose dabigatran is associated with more gastrointestinal bleeding in older patients.
**B. Apixaban lowers major bleeding** — This advantage is relevant when choosing among agents for an older adult with an indication for stroke prevention.
**C. Direct anticoagulants increase intracranial bleeding** — Trials found less intracranial bleeding with direct anticoagulants than with warfarin.
**D. Unintentional warfarin overdose is uncommon** — Its narrow therapeutic range and sensitivity to interacting medications, diet and illness make excess exposure a concern.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1202 and 1204–1205, Table 77-9.

q: מטופלת עם מחלת כליות כרונית מסוגלת להבין את מצבה ולהחליט, ואין מצב חירום או חריג חוקי. מוצעת לה דיאליזה ובתה תומכת בטיפול. מה נדרש לפני התחלתו?
o: הסכמת הבת לאחר מסירת המידע הרפואי למשפחה
אישור הצוות לאחר הערכת התועלת הצפויה מהטיפול
הסכמת קרוב משפחה לאחר שיחה עם הרופא המטפל
הסכמת המטופלת לאחר מסירת המידע הדרוש להחלטה
explanation:
**נדרשת הסכמה מדעת של המטופלת עצמה** לאחר הסבר על הדיאליזה, הסיכויים, הסיכונים והחלופות הרלוונטיות.

**א. הסכמת הבת.** הבת יכולה לתמוך לפי רצון האם אך אינה מחליטה במקומה.
**ב. אישור הצוות.** התוויה רפואית אינה תחליף להסכמה.
**ג. הסכמה של קרוב.** אין לכך סמכות במקום מטופלת שמסוגלת להחליט.
**ד. בחירת המטופלת לאחר הסבר.** זהו היישום של דרישת ההסכמה מדעת בהיעדר חריג.

אסמכתא · חוק זכויות החולה, סעיף 13.

q: A 76-year-old man with stage 3b chronic kidney disease (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m²) and diabetes has asymptomatic bacteriuria with 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli discovered during preoperative evaluation for cataract surgery. Urinalysis shows 10–20 WBC per high-power field and no nitrites. He has no dysuria, urgency, or fever. Which management approach fits Hazzard?
o: Start ciprofloxacin to eradicate the urinary bacteria
Start nitrofurantoin to eradicate the urinary bacteria
Withhold antibiotics for the asymptomatic bacteriuria
Delay cataract surgery until the urinary bacteria are eradicated
explanation:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria before nonurologic surgery is not an indication for antibiotic treatment. **Withhold antibiotics before cataract surgery** in this man without urinary symptoms or systemic illness.

**A. Ciprofloxacin.** Eradicating a urine isolate has no demonstrated perioperative benefit in this setting.
**B. Nitrofurantoin.** There is no symptomatic cystitis to treat. Pyuria does not change that.
**C. Withhold antibiotics.** The exception for selected urologic procedures involving mucosal trauma does not apply to cataract surgery.
**D. Delay surgery.** A sterile urine culture is not a prerequisite for this nonurologic procedure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1702.

q: A 78-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has persistent constipation during opioid treatment despite nonpharmacologic measures and lactulose. Fecal impaction and obstruction have been excluded. Which treatment alternative is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Switch to polyethylene glycol as an osmotic laxative
Switch to regular magnesium hydroxide as a laxative
Switch to docusate as the maintenance stool softener
Switch to regular phosphate enemas as maintenance treatment
explanation:
When lactulose is insufficient and obstruction has been excluded, PEG offers another osmotic approach. Kidney impairment limits the use of saline laxatives.
**Switch to polyethylene glycol and titrate to comfortable evacuation.**

**A. PEG.** It retains water in the lumen and can be more effective than lactulose.
**B. Regular magnesium hydroxide.** Impaired renal clearance raises the risk of hypermagnesemia.
**C. Maintenance docusate.** It has little laxative activity and does not reliably relieve difficult evacuation.
**D. Regular phosphate enemas.** Absorbed phosphate can cause serious electrolyte disturbances in renal impairment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376–1378.

q: An 82-year-old woman with dementia has persistent liquid fecal soiling after a period of constipation. Rectal examination finds impacted hard stool. Which interpretation best fits the source?
o: The soiling argues for liquid stool production without a retained-stool mechanism
The soiling argues for a bowel disorder in which rectal emptying is unhelpful
The soiling is consistent with overflow associated with retained rectal stool
The soiling is consistent with a condition that needs containment before assessment
explanation:
A distended rectum containing impacted feces can permit liquid stool to escape around the mass. Cognitive impairment may prevent the patient from describing the antecedent constipation.
**The soiling represents overflow around retained rectal stool.**

**A. Liquid production alone.** This overlooks the firm impaction demonstrated on examination.
**B. Rectal emptying unhelpful.** Sustained emptying is central to treating overflow.
**C. Overflow from retention.** The combination of hard stool in the vault and watery soiling fits this mechanism.
**D. Containment first.** Pads can protect skin but leave the impaction untreated.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1361–1364.

q: Lubiprostone is being considered for a patient with Parkinson disease and chronic constipation after evaluation and unsuccessful conventional treatment. By which mechanism does it promote bowel movements?
o: Increasing intestinal fluid absorption through chloride channels
Reducing intestinal fluid secretion through chloride channels
Activating chloride channels to increase intestinal secretion
Blocking chloride channels to reduce stool water content
explanation:
Lubiprostone is a locally acting intestinal secretagogue. It increases the fluid available to soften stool and aid its passage.
**Activation of epithelial chloride channels increases intestinal fluid secretion.**

**A. Increased absorption.** Removing water from the lumen would tend to harden stool.
**B. Reduced secretion.** This reverses the effect of lubiprostone.
**C. Activated chloride channels.** Chloride enters the lumen and water follows.
**D. Channel blockade.** Blocking these secretory channels would oppose the desired increase in stool water.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1377.

q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has moderate dementia, heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35%, stage 4 chronic kidney disease with eGFR 22, and type 2 diabetes. She cannot report her medications. Staff report hard stools every 4 to 5 days despite senna 8.6 mg daily. Her abdomen is soft without masses. Which proposed addition accords with Hazzard's efficacy and renal-safety discussion?
o: Magnesium hydroxide for long-term constipation treatment
Polyethylene glycol for ongoing constipation
Phosphate enemas for regular constipation treatment
Docusate sodium for effective constipation treatment
explanation:
Hard, infrequent stools despite a stimulant suggest a need to improve stool hydration. Advanced kidney disease narrows the safe options, and heart failure matters when choosing a preparation and fluid volume.
**Add polyethylene glycol for ongoing constipation after checking for retained stool.**

**A. Magnesium hydroxide.** Long-term use in advanced kidney disease can cause magnesium accumulation.
**B. PEG.** An osmotic laxative can improve consistency when senna alone is insufficient. Monitor response and avoid excessive loose stool.
**C. Regular phosphate enemas.** Renal disease increases the risk of dangerous hyperphosphatemia.
**D. Docusate.** Many residents receive it, but its demonstrated laxative effect is small.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376, 1378, Table 87-11.

q: A 79-year-old man with constipation undergoes a review of medications with anticholinergic activity. How does that activity contribute to constipation?
o: Reduced gut smooth-muscle contractility through muscarinic blockade
Increased gut smooth-muscle contractility through muscarinic blockade
Reduced gut smooth-muscle contractility through muscarinic stimulation
Increased gut smooth-muscle contractility through muscarinic stimulation
explanation:
Acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors helps gastrointestinal smooth muscle contract. Anticholinergic drugs interfere with this excitatory signal.
**Muscarinic blockade reduces gut smooth-muscle contractility.**

**A. Reduced contraction with blockade.** Less effective propulsion prolongs transit and leaves more time to absorb water.
**B. Increased contraction with blockade.** Blocking this signal impairs contraction.
**C. Reduced contraction with stimulation.** The constipating drug blocks the receptor.
**D. Increased contraction with stimulation.** That is closer to normal cholinergic activity and does not explain constipation from blockade.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1358.

q: An older woman at high risk of constipation remains symptomatic despite lifestyle measures and appropriate trials of milder laxatives. Which treatment is supported for regular use in this refractory setting?
o: Docusate sodium as maintenance treatment for refractory constipation
Polyethylene glycol as maintenance treatment for refractory constipation
Magnesium citrate as maintenance treatment for refractory constipation
Soapsuds enemas as maintenance treatment for refractory constipation
explanation:
A high-risk patient with persistent symptoms needs a regimen that keeps stool soft enough to pass regularly. PEG is an effective osmotic laxative when milder measures fail.
**Use PEG regularly and titrate to effect.**

**A. Docusate.** Limited effect on stool passage makes it a poor maintenance choice for refractory symptoms.
**B. PEG.** Water retained in the lumen softens stool. Adjust the dose if loose stools or soiling develop.
**C. Magnesium citrate.** Rapid catharsis carries risks of dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.
**D. Soapsuds enemas.** Repeated administration can damage rectal mucosa.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376, 1378.

q: An independently mobile 81-year-old man has mild to moderate chronic constipation despite lifestyle changes. He drinks adequate fluids, has no suspected fecal impaction or obstruction, and has not tried laxatives. Which initial treatment fits the Hazzard stepwise approach?
o: Start daily oral docusate and review the bowel response
Start psyllium with fluids and review the bowel response
Start oral magnesium citrate and review the bowel response
Start daily enema treatment and review the bowel response
explanation:
Bulk-forming fiber increases stool volume and provides a stimulus to propulsion. It suits an ambulant person with mild or moderate constipation who can drink enough fluid.
**Start psyllium with adequate fluid and reassess.**

**A. Docusate.** It has less effect on stool consistency and frequency than psyllium.
**B. Psyllium.** Gradual introduction improves tolerance. Review for bloating and whether defecation becomes easier.
**C. Magnesium citrate.** A potent saline cathartic is excessive for uncomplicated initial treatment.
**D. Daily enemas.** There is no current impaction or outlet disorder to justify a regular rectal regimen.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1375, 1378, Table 87-11.

q: A 77-year-old woman has ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalamine 800 mg three times daily. Over 3 months, she has developed straining and a bowel movement every 4 days. She also takes weekly alendronate and vitamin D, and recently started amitriptyline 10 mg for peripheral neuropathy. There is no abdominal tenderness. Which mechanism explains the constipating effect of an anticholinergic medication?
o: Enhanced smooth-muscle contraction through muscarinic stimulation
Reduced smooth-muscle contraction through antimuscarinic activity
Increased stool water through chloride-channel activation
Increased propulsive activity through serotonin-receptor stimulation
explanation:
Amitriptyline blocks muscarinic receptors in the gut. Reduced cholinergic input makes contractions less effective and can worsen pre-existing difficulty passing stool.
**The constipating mechanism is reduced smooth-muscle contraction through antimuscarinic activity.**

**A. Muscarinic stimulation.** This would facilitate contraction. Amitriptyline antagonizes the receptor.
**B. Antimuscarinic inhibition.** A new anticholinergic drug is a plausible reversible contributor to the change in bowel habit.
**C. Chloride-channel activation.** Secretagogues use this mechanism to increase stool water.
**D. Serotonin-receptor stimulation.** A prokinetic such as prucalopride increases propulsion through serotonin receptors.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1358–1359.

q: An older man with constipation has a large, hard mass of impacted stool in the rectum on examination. Which treatment sequence accords with Hazzard?
o: Administer an enema first, then perform manual evacuation
Insert a suppository first, then perform manual evacuation
Wait for an oral softener before evacuating the rectum
Perform manual evacuation before further rectal treatment
explanation:
The location and consistency of retained stool determine how to clear it. A large hard plug that can be felt in the rectum needs direct removal.
**Manually evacuate the rectal mass before further rectal treatment.**

**A. Enema first.** A nozzle can traumatize the rectum when forced past a hard plug.
**B. Suppository first.** A suppository cannot efficiently dislodge a large solid mass.
**C. Wait for an oral softener.** This delays immediate relief and may leave stool accumulating proximally.
**D. Manual evacuation first.** Gentle removal opens the outlet. Reassess the vault and select further clearance as needed.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376, 1378, Table 87-11.

q: A 73-year-old woman hospitalized with a heart failure exacerbation receives intravenous furosemide 40 mg twice daily. She has had no bowel movement since admission four days ago. Her home polyethylene glycol 17 g daily was omitted. She also takes lisinopril, carvedilol, and spironolactone and eats regular meals. Potassium is 3.8, magnesium 1.9, and creatinine 1.2. Which description correctly explains the action of polyethylene glycol if it is restarted?
o: It increases intraluminal fluid through an osmotic effect
It decreases intraluminal fluid through increased water absorption
It produces evacuation through local stimulation by a rectal suppository
It requires bacterial conversion into acetic acid and other short-chain fatty acids
explanation:
PEG is a poorly absorbed osmotic polymer. It can soften stool without bacterial fermentation or direct contact with the rectal mucosa.
**PEG increases fluid in the bowel lumen by osmosis.**

**A. Increased luminal fluid.** Water remains with the stool and facilitates passage.
**B. Increased water absorption.** This would dry the stool and worsen constipation.
**C. Local rectal stimulation.** A suppository works locally. Oral PEG acts throughout the bowel lumen.
**D. Conversion to short-chain fatty acids.** Bacterial fermentation characterizes lactulose.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1373, 1376.

q: An 80-year-old man receiving morphine for metastatic prostate cancer has constipation despite laxative treatment. The team is considering a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist. Which mechanism explains this drug class’s role in refractory opioid-related constipation?
o: Stimulate peripheral opioid receptors to counter opioid-related constipation
Block peripheral opioid receptors to counter opioid-related constipation
Stimulate peripheral opioid receptors to lower anal sphincter tone
Block peripheral opioid receptors to increase anal sphincter tone
explanation:
Morphine activates gut mu receptors, slowing propulsion, increasing water absorption and raising anal sphincter tone. A peripheral antagonist counters these bowel effects when laxatives have been inadequate.
**Block peripheral mu-opioid receptors.**

**A. Stimulate gut receptors.** Further stimulation would reinforce opioid-induced constipation.
**B. Block gut receptors.** Peripheral antagonism targets the bowel while generally preserving central analgesia.
**C. Stimulate to lower sphincter tone.** Opioid stimulation tends to increase anal sphincter tone.
**D. Block to increase sphincter tone.** Raising outlet resistance would make defecation harder.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1377–1378.

q: An 88-year-old woman continues to strain with bowel movements despite docusate. She is at high risk of constipation complications, and milder alternatives have failed. Impaction and obstruction have been excluded. Which change accords with Hazzard?
o: Continue docusate and progressively increase its maintenance dose
Change to oral polyethylene glycol for ongoing constipation
Change to regular magnesium salts for ongoing constipation
Add regular soapsuds enemas to the constipation regimen
explanation:
Docusate softens stool poorly in clinical trials and does not improve colonic propulsion. A high-risk patient who remains symptomatic needs a more effective maintenance regimen.
**Change to oral PEG and titrate to comfortable stools.**

**A. Escalate docusate.** Even at substantial doses its laxative effect is slight.
**B. Use PEG.** Luminal water retention can relieve straining once mechanical obstruction and impaction have been excluded.
**C. Regular magnesium salts.** Rapid catharsis can cause fluid loss or magnesium toxicity, especially with impaired clearance.
**D. Regular soapsuds enemas.** Repeated use risks mucosal injury and does not suit routine maintenance.

**B. Repeated phosphate enemas.** The plug remains, and absorbed phosphate presents an additional hazard in renal impairment.
**C. Regular magnesium hydroxide.** An oral maintenance regimen cannot relieve the plug promptly and magnesium can accumulate.

**Assess obstruction and tailor clearance to its location, severity and the patient’s comfort goals.**

**A. Assess and select treatment.** The findings guide whether specialist evaluation, distal treatment or an oral regimen is appropriate.
**B. Give oral laxatives first.** Oral purging can worsen distension when obstruction is suspected.
**C. Prioritize glycerin suppositories.** A local rectal agent alone will not clear extensive proximal loading.
**D. Exclude constipation from the rectal examination.** The radiograph already shows stool beyond the examining finger.

q: A 76-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes prednisone 7.5 mg daily. Three weeks after starting amitriptyline 25 mg for peripheral neuropathy, she develops hard stools every four to five days with straining. She also takes methotrexate, folic acid, and omeprazole. Examination shows mild abdominal distension and stool in the rectal vault. Which strategy addresses a possible anticholinergic medication contribution while considering an alternative for neuropathic pain?
o: Review replacing amitriptyline with gabapentin for treatment of neuropathic pain
Review adding docusate sodium 100 mg twice daily while retaining amitriptyline
Review adding bisacodyl 5 mg orally each day while retaining amitriptyline
Review adding regularly scheduled glycerin suppositories while retaining amitriptyline
explanation:
Amitriptyline blocks muscarinic receptors and can slow intestinal transit even at analgesic doses. **Review withdrawal or replacement of the tricyclic while treating the constipation already present.**

**A. Review replacing amitriptyline with gabapentin for treatment of neuropathic pain** Gabapentin is a possible alternative for neuropathic pain. Adjust for kidney function and monitor dizziness and gait.
**B. Review adding docusate sodium 100 mg twice daily while retaining amitriptyline** A stool softener leaves the new anticholinergic exposure in place.
**C. Review adding bisacodyl 5 mg orally each day while retaining amitriptyline** A stimulant can help bowel evacuation but does not remove the medication contribution.
**D. Review adding regularly scheduled glycerin suppositories while retaining amitriptyline** Rectal treatment can address retained stool without preventing further slowing from amitriptyline.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1063–1065, Table 68-8.

q: An older woman with constipation and abdominal distension has an empty rectum on examination. An abdominal radiograph shows fecal loading in the ascending and transverse colon without acute obstruction. What treatment implication does this finding have?
o: It supports reducing laxatives and providing education about bowel habits
It supports directing evacuation primarily toward stool retained in the rectum
It supports concluding that constipation is absent despite her symptoms
It supports changing the laxative type or increasing its dose
explanation:
The distribution of retained stool helps distinguish slow transit from a rectal evacuation problem. Stool in the ascending and transverse colon can remain beyond the reach of a digital examination.
**Review and change the laxative type or increase its dose for persistent proximal loading.**

**A. Reduce laxatives.** This would suit a patient without retention who misinterprets a normal pattern, not demonstrated proximal loading.
**B. Focus evacuation on the rectum.** There is no rectal mass for local treatment to remove.
**C. Conclude constipation is absent.** The proximal stool burden explains the negative rectal examination.
**D. Adjust the laxative regimen.** After excluding acute obstruction, target slow colonic passage and monitor symptoms and stool output.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1364–1365, Table 87-6.

q: A 72-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic cancer started sustained-release morphine 30 mg twice daily for pain. Two weeks later, pain is controlled, but he has had no bowel movement for six days despite docusate 200 mg twice daily. Examination shows mild abdominal distention and a moderate amount of stool in the rectal vault. His goals include maintaining quality of life and activity. Which change is supported for treating his opioid-related constipation?
o: Add senna as an active stimulant laxative
Continue docusate as the principal maintenance laxative
Add magnesium citrate as the regular maintenance laxative
Use soapsuds enemas as the regular bowel regimen
explanation:
Morphine slows gut propulsion and can cause constipation even when analgesia is satisfactory. Docusate alone has little laxative effect.
**Add senna, an active stimulant laxative, after assessing the retained stool.**

**A. Senna.** Its propulsive effect addresses opioid-related slowing and can help preserve comfort while analgesia continues.
**B. Docusate as principal treatment.** The current regimen has failed, and simply softening stool does little to correct slow propulsion.
**C. Magnesium citrate.** Rapid catharsis and fluid loss make it a poor regular regimen for an older patient.
**D. Regular soapsuds enemas.** Repeated rectal irrigation can irritate the mucosa and is unnecessarily burdensome for maintenance.

q: An 80-year-old woman with limited mobility cannot safely reach the toilet at night. Constipation treatment and medication review are already underway. Which environmental intervention directly addresses toilet access?
o: Use a bedpan in bed for bowel movements
Provide an accessible commode and help with transfers
Restrict toilet access to predetermined staff-care times
Use a distant toilet without a way to call for assistance
explanation:
An urge to defecate is of little help if a person cannot safely reach a toilet. Postponing evacuation because of the environment can compound retention.
**Provide a safely accessible commode and help with transfers.**

**A. Use a bedpan.** A supported seated posture better facilitates defecation and comfort when attainable.
**B. Accessible commode and assistance.** This reduces the distance and transfer barrier. Provide privacy and a way to call for help.
**C. Restrict access to staff schedules.** The resident needs a way to respond to the urge outside scheduled care times.
**D. Distant toilet without assistance.** This maintains the barrier and increases the risk of an unsafe transfer or fall.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1371, Table 87-8.

q: A 91-year-old man with advanced Parkinson disease, dysphagia requiring a pureed diet, and recurrent aspiration pneumonia has severe constipation. He takes carbidopa/levodopa, pramipexole, and lansoprazole. He spends an hour straining on the toilet. Examination shows normal anal tone but impaired coordination of pelvic floor relaxation. Lactulose, suppositories, and enemas have not helped. His creatinine clearance is 35 mL/min. Which intervention directly targets the pelvic floor coordination problem?
o: Use lubiprostone to provide sensory and muscular retraining of the pelvic floor.
Refer for pelvic floor biofeedback after assessing his ability to participate.
Use repeated tap-water enemas to retrain coordinated pelvic floor relaxation.
Arrange colostomy before assessing participation in a pelvic floor retraining program.
explanation:
Dyssynergic defecation occurs when the pelvic floor fails to relax during a push. Biofeedback provides information about muscle activity so the patient can practice the correct sequence.
**Assess his ability to participate and refer for pelvic floor biofeedback when feasible.**

**A. Lubiprostone.** It increases intestinal secretion and can soften stool. It does not retrain pelvic muscles.
**B. Biofeedback.** The training targets coordinated propulsion and outlet relaxation. Parkinson-related functional or cognitive limitations can affect feasibility.
**C. Repeated enemas.** These may empty stool but do not teach voluntary relaxation.
**D. Colostomy first.** Surgery is a last resort after assessment and appropriate conservative treatment.

q: An 82-year-old woman with CKD and constipation asks about magnesium citrate. Which safety consideration matches Hazzard?
o: Normal serum creatinine prevents magnesium accumulation during treatment
Rapid cathartic action reduces fluid losses during treatment
Magnesium laxatives carry risks of toxicity and fluid losses
Long-term magnesium use is particularly appropriate in kidney disease
explanation:
Magnesium salts produce osmotic catharsis. Rapid water loss and absorption of magnesium can both pose problems in an older adult, particularly with kidney disease.
**Magnesium cathartics can cause fluid loss and magnesium toxicity.**

**A. Normal creatinine guarantees safety.** Toxicity can occur even when creatinine appears normal.
**B. Rapid action limits loss.** A brisk cathartic response can increase dehydration and incontinence.
**C. Toxicity and fluid loss.** Reduced clearance increases the danger from absorbed magnesium, and citrate is especially potent.
**D. Long-term use in CKD.** Renal impairment is a reason to avoid regular magnesium-based treatment.

q: A 78-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer (PSA 156 ng/mL) is being considered for docetaxel. He lives alone, has difficulty managing finances, and has fallen twice in the past month. BMI is 19.2 kg/m². He takes tamsulosin, amlodipine, and trazodone for sleep. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 35 mL/min). Which assessment best addresses the aging-related vulnerabilities relevant to chemotherapy planning?
o: Base the vulnerability assessment on tumor burden and PSA concentration
Perform a comprehensive geriatric assessment before selecting the treatment plan
Base the vulnerability assessment on routine oncologic performance status
Perform an age-based assessment using chronological age as the main measure
explanation:
Difficulty managing finances, recent falls and a low BMI warrant assessment before docetaxel. Ask about food intake and available help because he lives alone. **Perform a comprehensive geriatric assessment before settling on the treatment plan.**

**A. Tumor burden and PSA** — These findings characterize the cancer. They cannot tell whether he can manage medicines or get help after a fall.
**B. Comprehensive geriatric assessment** — Examine daily function, cognition, mobility, nutrition, medications, comorbidities and social support alongside anemia and renal impairment.
**C. Routine performance status** — A global rating can overlook instrumental dependence and the effects of sedating medicines.
**D. Chronological age** — Being 78 gives no reliable estimate of his individual reserve or the support he needs during chemotherapy.

q: An 81-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer is admitted with delirium after her first cyclophosphamide-based chemotherapy cycle. Her daughter reports poor intake and slowing over the preceding week. Vital signs are stable. Sodium is 128 mEq/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.9, WBC 2.8 K/microliter, and Mini-Cog 1/5. For future care planning, which use of comprehensive geriatric assessment matches the multidisciplinary intervention reported to reduce chemotherapy toxicity?
o: Forward the assessment results without implementing interventions
Use routine oncology performance status in place of assessment
Review the assessment and implement tailored team interventions
Use routine history and physical examination in place of assessment
explanation:
Delirium during chemotherapy calls for evaluation of precipitants such as poor intake, hyponatremia and worsening renal function. **For later cycles, have the team review the geriatric assessment and implement targeted care.**

**A. Forward the report alone** — In GAIN the usual-care oncologist received the assessment without the structured team's intervention.
**B. Use routine performance status** — Overall activity does not resolve the patient's cognitive, nutritional or medication-related needs.
**C. Implement tailored team interventions** — Reassess cognition after the acute delirium, address intake and medicines, and coordinate support. This is how assessment can change care.
**D. Use history and examination alone** — They remain essential to acute care but lack the structured multidomain assessment and implementation tested for subsequent treatment.

Reference · GAIN, JAMA Oncology 2021, Intervention Delivery (PMID 34591080) · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1387–1388.

q: An older woman takes gabapentin and has a creatinine clearance of 42 mL/min. Which treatment adjustment matches the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Increase the dose to compensate for impaired kidney function
Reduce the dose because of central nervous system adverse effects
Maintain the dose and substitute liver-function monitoring for renal adjustment
Maintain the dose and substitute blood-count monitoring for renal adjustment
explanation:
The kidneys eliminate gabapentin, so reduced filtration can prolong exposure and cause central adverse effects.

**Reduce gabapentin at a creatinine clearance of 42 mL/min.** This falls below the 60 mL/min renal dosing threshold.

**A. Increase for renal impairment.** Slower elimination favors accumulation with a higher dose.
**B. Reduce for CNS effects.** Adjusting the regimen downward helps limit drowsiness, confusion, and other central effects.
**C. Use liver tests instead.** Liver tests do not measure the renal elimination problem or prevent drug accumulation.
**D. Use blood counts instead.** Checking for hematologic changes cannot replace renal dose adjustment.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, p. 2073.

q: An 84-year-old woman with colon cancer is three days after hemicolectomy. She pulls out her Foley catheter and becomes agitated when staff try to replace it. CAM findings include acute onset, inattention, and disorganized thinking. She takes donepezil 10 mg for mild dementia; electrolytes are normal and hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL. Review confirms no ongoing indication for the catheter. Which step addresses this source of immobilization?
o: Replace the catheter and add wrist restraints during care
Retain catheter use while increasing the donepezil dose
Leave out the catheter and monitor a voiding trial
Retain catheter use while starting intramuscular haloperidol
explanation:
A bladder catheter can immobilize a patient and become a focus of distress. A medically unnecessary catheter offers no benefit that balances these risks.
**Leave the catheter out and monitor whether she voids adequately.**

**A. Replace the catheter and add wrist restraints during care.** Replacing the tether and adding restraints combines two recognized precipitants.
**B. Retain catheter use while increasing the donepezil dose.** Increasing donepezil does not relieve the discomfort or restriction from the catheter.
**C. Leave out the catheter and monitor a voiding trial.** A monitored voiding trial permits mobility and identifies retention if it develops.
**D. Retain catheter use while starting intramuscular haloperidol.** Haloperidol suppresses behavior without addressing an unnecessary device.

q: A 76-year-old man meets the Fried operational criteria for exhaustion and slow walking. Which additional finding belongs to the phenotype and could complete three criteria?
o: Multimorbidity measured with a comorbidity index
Unintentional weight loss meeting the Fried criterion
Low albumin measured in a blood sample
Low hemoglobin measured in a blood sample
explanation:
The Fried phenotype counts qualifying findings across five domains. **Unintentional weight loss would supply a third component alongside exhaustion and slow walking.**

**A. Multimorbidity score** — A burden-of-disease index counts diagnoses. It does not measure one of the five physical components.
**B. Qualifying unintentional weight loss** — For the original CHS measure, ask whether more than 10 lb was lost unintentionally in the preceding year.
**C. Low serum albumin** — This may prompt evaluation for nutritional or inflammatory illness. It cannot be added to the Fried score.
**D. Low hemoglobin** — Anemia may help explain exhaustion and deserves investigation. Hemoglobin is not scored separately.

q: A woman cannot meet her nutritional needs by eating, but her gastrointestinal tract is suitable for feeding. Which potential advantage of enteral rather than parenteral nutrition is described in Hazzard?
o: Less preservation of gastrointestinal function and a lower risk of hyperglycemia
Greater preservation of gastrointestinal function and a higher risk of hyperglycemia
Less preservation of gastrointestinal function and a higher risk of hyperglycemia
Greater preservation of gastrointestinal function and a lower risk of hyperglycemia
explanation:
Enteral nutrition uses the gastrointestinal tract, whereas parenteral nutrition supplies nutrients intravenously. **A functioning gut favors enteral feeding, which supports gastrointestinal function and carries a lower hyperglycemia risk.**

**A. Less gut preservation and less hyperglycemia** — The glucose comparison points in the right direction, but enteral feeding helps preserve gut function.
**B. More gut preservation and more hyperglycemia** — Gut preservation fits. Intravenous glucose delivery generally poses the greater hyperglycemia concern.
**C. Less gut preservation and more hyperglycemia** — Both comparisons run counter to the potential benefits of enteral feeding.
**D. More gut preservation and less hyperglycemia** — This pair explains part of the preference when the gut is usable. Glucose monitoring still matters.
