q: בת 73, מגיעה למיון עם קוצר נשימה, החמרה במצבה בחודש האחרון, ירידה תפקודית, וסחרחורת במאמץ מינימאלי מזה כשבוע. אשפוזים חוזרים בחצי שנה האחרונה עקב החמרת אי. ספיקת לב רקע: • מחלת לב איסכמית – ניתוח מעקפים לפני כ- 10 שנים, צנתור אחרון במהלך אשפוזה הקודם עם התערבות למעקפים ופתיחתם • מחלת כלי דם היקפיים • סוכרת מטופלת במשתנים במינונים מקסימאליים, SACUBITRIL/VALSARTAN (ENTRESTO) במינון מקסימאלי וב- SGLT2. בבדיקה - לחץ דם 125/80, דופק 105, נשימות 24. מעבדה - BUN 23, קריאטינין 1.5 בהחמרה מבסיס. אק"ג - סינוס טכיקרדיה ללא הפרעת הולכה. אקוקרדיוגרפיה - חדר שמאל מורחב עם מקטע פליטה 20%, ואי ספיקה מיטראלית קלה. מה מהבאים יכול לשפר את איכות חייה ויאריך אותם ?
o: השתלת קוצב – Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT)
מכשיר תומך בחדר שמאל - Left ventricular assisted device (LVAD)
תיקון מסתם מיטראלי – Mitral Clip
אין מה שיכול לשפר את מצבה, מומלץ להעבירה לטיפול פליאטיבי בלבד.
explanation:
A durable LVAD supports forward flow in severe refractory systolic failure. **Refer this patient for advanced-HF assessment for an LVAD**, which can improve quality of life and survival in selected candidates.

**A. CRT** The ECG has no conduction delay. Markedly reduced EF alone does not predict benefit from resynchronization.
**B. LVAD** Repeated admissions, severe limitation and EF 20% despite substantial treatment support assessment. Vascular disease, renal function, frailty and her wishes influence suitability.
**C. MitraClip** Her mitral regurgitation is mild. Edge-to-edge repair targets selected patients with significant regurgitation despite therapy.
**D. Palliative care alone** Palliative care belongs alongside device evaluation and may become the preferred path. The vignette does not rule out advanced treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1184, 1189–1190.

q: בן 83 סובל מהידרדרות תפקודית וקוגניטיבית בשנה האחרונה. הוא הולך לאט מאוד, סובל מנפילות חוזרות, סובל מפחד מפני נפילות, ירד במשקל 7 ק"ג בשנה האחרונה, מרגיש עייפות כל הזמן, וגם עולה חשד למחלת אלצהיימר בחומרה בינונית. לפי הקריטריונים של FRIED כיצד ניתן להגדיר את החולה?
o: PREFRAIL
FRAIL
VERY FRAIL
COGNITIVE FRAIL
explanation:
The Fried physical phenotype classifies a person as robust, prefrail or frail by counting five features. **He meets the frail category if the 7-kg loss was unintentional and his slow gait and exhaustion meet the phenotype criteria.**

**A. Prefrail** — One or two components indicate prefrailty. Zero indicates a robust phenotype. If the 7-kg weight loss was unintentional, it provides a third feature alongside slowness and exhaustion. Confirm that history before assigning the category clinically.
**B. Frail** — Slowness, qualifying unintentional weight loss and exhaustion meet the threshold. Recurrent falls need a separate assessment.
**C. Very frail** — This is not an additional Fried phenotype category. The model distinguishes robust, intermediate and frail.
**D. Cognitive frailty** — This separate construct requires physical frailty and mild cognitive impairment after dementia has been excluded. Suspected moderate Alzheimer dementia calls for diagnostic clarification.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 619–620, Table 42-2, and p. 627. Fried et al., J Gerontol A 2001, PMID 11253156.
Key note: The stem omits whether the weight loss was intentional. If only slowness and exhaustion qualify, the classification is prefrail. Falls, fear of falling and cognitive decline cannot substitute for a third Fried component.

q: בת 84 מטופלת במחלקה שיקומית לאחר שבר בצוואר הירך. לאחר חודש של שיקום היא. הולכת עם הליכון בהשגחה בלבד בתחום החדר ומתוכננת להשתחרר למחלקה סיעודית. מה תפקיד הריפוי בעיסוק בשיקום שלה?
o: שליחת צוות לביקור לבדיקת התאמת המסגרת לתפקודה
הערכה קוגניטיבית בשאלה של התאמתה למחלקה לתשושי נפש
שיפור ADL – אכילה, הלבשת פלג גוף עליון, טיפוח
במצב זה אין תועלת בריפוי בעיסוק
explanation:
Occupational therapy helps a patient recover or adapt everyday self-care tasks. Moving to a nursing facility changes the setting where she will use those skills, while the ability to eat, dress and groom herself still matters.

**Train eating, upper-body dressing and grooming. Gains in these activities preserve autonomy and reduce the amount of help she will need each day.**

**A. Visit to assess the facility.** Environmental assessment can be valuable when specific barriers need to be addressed. It does not replace direct training of the patient’s self-care skills.
**B. Cognitive assessment for a dementia unit.** Assess cognition when it affects performance or placement. No new cognitive or behavioral problem here makes classification the immediate therapy goal.
**C. Improve eating, dressing and grooming.** These are concrete activities the therapist can observe, adapt and practice with her before transfer.
**D. No role for occupational therapy.** A continuing need for nursing care can coexist with meaningful gains in selected daily activities.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 823, Table 55-4.
referenceNote: Printed IMA citation retained; checked explanation source: Hazzard 8e · p. 823.

q: מה מהבאים מהווה גורם לאוסטיאופורוזיס שניוני?
o: היפרתירואידיזם
מין – אישה
קורס של 5 ימים של PREDNISONE 30 mg
סוכרת שאינה תלויה באינסולין
explanation:
Secondary osteoporosis is bone loss attributable to an underlying disease or drug. **Hyperthyroidism accelerates bone turnover and is a recognized endocrine cause of secondary osteoporosis.**

**A. Hyperthyroidism** Excess thyroid hormone increases remodeling and can produce net bone loss. TSH and thyroxine help identify it.
**B. Female sex** Sex is a background risk factor for primary osteoporosis. It is not a secondary endocrine disorder.
**C. Five days of prednisone** Long-term or repeated glucocorticoid exposure can cause important bone loss. A single five-day course is a poor fit for the chronic exposure described in this comparison.
**D. Non–insulin-dependent diabetes** Type 2 diabetes can increase fracture risk even when DXA looks reassuring. In hyperthyroidism, accelerated remodeling causes net bone loss; diabetes-related fragility can coexist with normal or high measured bone density.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 768–769, Table 51-3. Malaysian Ministry of Health, Management of Osteoporosis 2022, Table 2-1, p. 28.
Key note: Hazzard Table 51-3 names hyperthyroidism. The Malaysian guideline explicitly lists both thyrotoxicosis and type 2 diabetes among secondary causes, so the diabetes option is also clinically defensible.

q: בן 73, עם ציון מינימנטל של 23, איזה מהבאים מחשיד לדמנציה אחרת שאיננה אלצהיימר ?
o: ירידה של 3 נקודות במינימנטל בשנה
המטופל לא מסוגל לכתוב הודעות בטלפון הנייד בשנה האחרונה
הפרעות בשנת ה- REM
קושי בשליפת מילים
explanation:
**REM sleep behavior disorder**, particularly repeated dream enactment, raises suspicion for a synucleinopathy such as DLB in an older adult with dementia. Ask what actually happens during sleep.

**A. Three MMSE points lost annually.** A decline of this magnitude can occur in Alzheimer disease and is not specific for another etiology.
**B. New difficulty texting.** Loss of a previously mastered instrumental activity can occur with Alzheimer disease or other dementias.
**C. REM sleep disturbance.** Dream enactment from loss of normal REM atonia is the discriminating pattern. Ordinary insomnia is nonspecific.
**D. Word-finding difficulty.** Difficulty retrieving words is common in Alzheimer disease.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 900, 981 and 984.

q: מה מהבאים לא מוכר כסיבוך של האכלת צינור?
o: עצירות
תמותה
דלקת ריאות
ירידה במשקל
explanation:
Enteral feeding supplies nutrition through a tube but can cause gastrointestinal or respiratory complications. It also does not guarantee weight maintenance or survival in a frail patient.

**None of these outcomes can be reliably excluded as a complication.** Constipation is a recognized gastrointestinal problem, and weight loss, aspiration pneumonia and death have been reported among tube-fed patients with pressure injuries.

**A. Constipation.** Enteral nutrition can be accompanied by constipation. Review hydration, fiber intake, medications and bowel function.
**B. Death.** Severe complications of tube feeding can contribute to death. A death in a tube-fed patient requires clinical attribution because underlying illness also influences survival.
**C. Pneumonia.** Aspiration of refluxed feed or secretions can cause pneumonia despite tube access.
**D. Weight loss.** A feeding tube cannot guarantee delivery or absorption of prescribed calories. Weight loss is specifically reported in this clinical population.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 692. ESPEN guideline on home enteral nutrition, monitoring and complications, 2020.
Key note: All four responses received credit. Hazzard lists weight loss, aspiration pneumonia and death, and ESPEN also recognizes constipation. Each can occur with tube feeding.
keySource: IMA 2025-Jun Subspecialty official answer key after appeals, Q97
label: All answers accepted after appeal

q: מה לא גורם הפיך לאי שליטה על סוגר השתן?
o: מחלת עורקים פריפרית (PVD)
וגיניטיס אטרופית (Vaginitis Atrophic)
היפרקלצמיה
אי ספיקת לב עם בצקת פריפרית
explanation:
Reversible incontinence triggers include local irritation and excess urine production. **Peripheral arterial disease is the exception among these four choices.**

**A. Peripheral arterial disease** — Peripheral arterial insufficiency is not the listed venous-edema mechanism that increases nocturnal urine output.
**B. Atrophic vaginitis** — Atrophic vaginitis or urethritis can produce irritative symptoms and leakage.
**C. Hypercalcemia** — Hypercalcemia can cause polyuria, increasing the burden on bladder storage and toileting.
**D. Heart failure with dependent edema** — Fluid mobilized from dependent edema can increase nighttime urine production in heart failure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch. 47, pp. 701–702, Table 47-3.

q: איזה מהבאים לא מעלה סיכון ל- Deep Vein Thrombosis?
o: טיפול ב- TAMOXIFEN
תסמונת נפרוטית
סרטן לבלב
טיפול תרופתי ב- ESCITALOPRAM ( CIPRALEX)
explanation:
Deep venous thrombosis risk rises in acquired prothrombotic states and with certain medications. **Escitalopram is the exception among these established risk factors**.

**A. Tamoxifen.** This selective estrogen receptor modulator increases venous thromboembolism risk.
**B. Nephrotic syndrome.** Loss of anticoagulant proteins and other coagulation changes promote thrombosis.
**C. Pancreatic cancer.** It is a particularly thrombogenic malignancy.
**D. Escitalopram.** It lacks the characteristic prothrombotic associations of the other three exposures.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1390, 1515.

explanationSource.status: Page-backed supplemental explanation; original IMA bibliography retained. Partial support; review note retained.

q: בן 75 אחרי שבר בצוואר הירך עם כאב נוירופטי ומצב רוח ירוד. ברקע מטופל ב- LEVETIRACETAM (KEPRRA) על רקע מחלה פרכוסית. סובל מזיהום בפצע הניתוחי. איזה מהתרופות הבאות לא תעלה את הסיכון לפרכוסים?
o: TRAMADOL (TRAMADEX)
CIPROFLOXACIN (CIPRO)
BUPROPION (WELLBUTRIN)
PREGABALIN (LYRICA)
explanation:
Drugs that lower the seizure threshold can provoke breakthrough seizures despite antiseizure treatment. For this man taking levetiracetam, **pregabalin** treats neuropathic pain and is also used as an adjunct for focal seizures.

**A. Tramadol.** This analgesic can provoke seizures even at therapeutic doses. A history of epilepsy increases concern.
**B. Ciprofloxacin.** This fluoroquinolone can cause central nervous system excitation and seizures. Impaired renal clearance can increase exposure.
**C. Bupropion.** Its dose-related seizure risk makes it contraindicated in someone with an established seizure disorder, despite the depressive symptoms.
**D. Pregabalin.** It binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release. Adjust for kidney function and watch for dizziness during hip-fracture recovery.

Reference · Harrison 21e, p. 3311, Table 425-5, and Hazzard 8e, pp. 1063–1064.

q: An older inpatient has an acute, fluctuating change in mental status. Which additional findings satisfy the CAM algorithm for delirium?
o: Inattention with disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Disorganized thinking with preserved attention and normal consciousness
Altered consciousness with preserved attention and organized thinking
Inattention with organized thinking and normal consciousness
explanation:
CAM requires an acute or fluctuating change and inattention. The remaining requirement can be met by disorganized thought or a change in arousal.
**With the acute change already present, identify inattention plus either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness.**

**A. Inattention with disorganized thinking or altered consciousness.** This combination completes all required parts of CAM.
**B. Disorganized thinking with preserved attention and normal consciousness.** Disorganized thought cannot substitute for the essential attentional disturbance.
**C. Altered consciousness with preserved attention and organized thinking.** Altered arousal also cannot substitute for impaired attention.
**D. Inattention with organized thinking and normal consciousness.** Inattention alone does not complete the algorithm when thought organization and consciousness are both normal.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 880

q: An older inpatient develops delirium after several psychoactive medications are added. Which interpretation best explains why these drugs need review?
o: Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.
Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.
Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.
Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.
explanation:
Centrally acting medicines can directly alter attention, and multiple drugs create opportunities for drug–drug and drug–disease interactions. Medication exposure is often modifiable.
**Reconcile the new psychoactive drugs and assess their individual and combined effects.**

**A. Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.** Removing or reducing unnecessary exposure can address a remediable precipitant.
**B. Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.** Drug effects are often among the more readily corrected contributors to delirium.
**C. Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.** Additional drugs increase exposure and interaction risk. They do not reliably offset one another.
**D. Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.** Direct effects and interactions both matter, even when a single drug has been added.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 882

q: What acute-onset timeframe distinguishes delirium from dementia's insidious course?
o: Up to a year
Hours to days
Weeks to months
A month or more
explanation:
When comparing delirium with dementia, establish the interval over which attention and cognition first changed. Duration of residual symptoms is a separate question.
**Delirium typically begins over hours to days.**

**A. Up to a year.** Cognitive effects can persist for many months, but that describes follow-up rather than usual onset.
**B. Hours to days.** A change developing within hours or a few days strongly favors an acute syndrome.
**C. Weeks to months.** An insidious change in memory and everyday function over weeks or months favors a chronic cognitive disorder. Sudden new inattention demands an acute assessment.
**D. A month or more.** Symptoms may persist a month after illness. That is not the typical interval over which delirium starts.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 883, 886, Table 58-4

q: On the 4AT screening tool, what score suggests possible delirium?
o: A total score of 1
A total score of 0
A total score of 2
A score of 4 or more
explanation:
The 4AT is a four-item bedside screen for possible delirium. Its total ranges from zero to twelve and must be interpreted with the clinical history.
**A total of four or more suggests possible delirium and prompts clinical assessment.**

**A. A total score of 1.** One is below the delirium screening threshold.
**B. A total score of 0.** Zero does not meet the positive threshold. A single test cannot exclude intermittent symptoms.
**C. A total score of 2.** Two is likewise below the delirium threshold and can reflect cognitive impairment.
**D. A score of 4 or more.** Four or more warrants further assessment for an acute, fluctuating change and its cause.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 884, Table 58-3

q: An older patient develops delirium. Which finding specifically supports brain imaging during the diagnostic evaluation?
o: Fever with clinical suspicion of meningitis
Concern for a subclinical seizure disorder
New focal neurologic findings on examination
A recent change in psychoactive medication
explanation:
Investigations for delirium should follow the bedside findings. Imaging looks for structural disease such as a stroke or subdural collection.
**A new focal neurologic deficit specifically supports brain imaging.**

**A. Fever with clinical suspicion of meningitis.** Suspected meningitis directs assessment toward cerebrospinal fluid when safe.
**B. Concern for a subclinical seizure disorder.** Concern about nonconvulsive seizures directs assessment toward EEG.
**C. New focal neurologic findings on examination.** A new focal sign suggests a structural intracranial process warranting CT or MRI.
**D. A recent change in psychoactive medication.** A change in psychoactive medication first calls for exposure review and directed assessment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 885

q: Which drug class remains the treatment of choice for delirium caused by seizures or alcohol/medication withdrawal, despite not being first-line for delirium generally?
o: Melatonin receptor agonists
Antipsychotics
Benzodiazepines
Alpha-2 agonists
explanation:
Sedatives may worsen ordinary delirium, but withdrawal and seizures have a different treatment mechanism. Benzodiazepines can control withdrawal-related excitation and seizure activity.
**A benzodiazepine treats ongoing seizure activity or delirium from alcohol or sedative-hypnotic withdrawal.** Establish the specific drug and withdrawal syndrome before choosing treatment.

**A. Melatonin receptor agonists.** Trials of melatonin agents in delirium have mixed results and they do not treat withdrawal seizures.
**B. Antipsychotics.** Antipsychotics may control selected dangerous behaviors but do not treat a withdrawal syndrome.
**C. Benzodiazepines.** Enhancing inhibitory GABA signaling can stop an active seizure and counter the hyperexcitability of alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Other withdrawal syndromes require their own treatment.
**D. Alpha-2 agonists.** Dexmedetomidine can be an ICU adjunct in resistant alcohol withdrawal but does not protect against withdrawal seizures. Clonidine or lofexidine can relieve autonomic symptoms of opioid withdrawal, a different syndrome.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 889. ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management, VI.13–14. ASAM National Practice Guideline for Opioid Use Disorder, 2020 focused update, Part 3.

q: What is the single most important, validated risk factor for Alzheimer disease?
o: Low educational attainment
Traumatic brain injury
Advancing chronological age
Habitual physical inactivity
explanation:
A risk factor can be strongly predictive without being modifiable. Both the incidence and the proportion of people living with Alzheimer disease rise sharply across successive older age groups.

**Advancing chronological age** has the strongest established association with Alzheimer risk across older adults.

**A. Less education.** Limited schooling is associated with higher risk, possibly through differences in cognitive reserve, but age has the stronger overall association.
**B. Traumatic brain injury.** A history of head injury can raise susceptibility, especially with severe or repeated injury. It is not the dominant predictor across older adults.
**C. Advancing age.** The steep age gradient applies across a broad range of backgrounds and exposures.
**D. Physical inactivity.** Inactivity is a modifiable midlife risk, useful for prevention counseling, but less important than age as an overall predictor.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 894, 896–897.

q: Hazzard links midlife physical inactivity and obesity to later Alzheimer disease. Which interpretation of their relationship is supported?
o: They are interrelated factors that each independently increase later AD risk
Inactivity affects AD risk through obesity without an independent association
Obesity affects AD risk through inactivity without an independent association
Their association is confined to vascular dementia rather than later AD
explanation:
Physical inactivity and obesity frequently coexist in midlife. An independent association means that the relationship of one exposure with later Alzheimer disease is not fully explained by the other.

**Each is independently associated with later Alzheimer risk, even though the two are interrelated.** Ask about both activity and weight when reviewing midlife exposures.

**A. Interrelated but independent.** Their co-occurrence leaves room for each to contribute separate information about later risk.
**B. Inactivity solely through obesity.** Lower activity can be associated with risk even after accounting for obesity.
**C. Obesity solely through inactivity.** Obesity likewise has an association beyond physical inactivity.
**D. Vascular dementia alone.** Midlife vascular and metabolic factors are associated with later Alzheimer disease as well as cerebrovascular disease.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 896.

q: Roughly what fraction of AD cases worldwide might be attributable to potentially modifiable risk factors?
o: About 78%
More than 95%
About one-third
About 1-5%
explanation:
A population-attributable fraction estimates how much disease in a population might be associated with particular exposures. It cannot predict how much one person's risk will fall after a lifestyle change.

**About one-third of Alzheimer cases worldwide** were estimated to be potentially attributable to modifiable risk factors.

**A. About 78%.** This percentage describes the share of familial Alzheimer mutations attributed to PSEN1, a different denominator.
**B. More than 95%.** This is the approximate share of Alzheimer cases with late onset. It does not measure modifiable exposures.
**C. About one-third.** This estimate concerns potentially modifiable factors across the worldwide population with Alzheimer disease.
**D. About 1% to 5%.** This describes the much smaller familial share of all Alzheimer cases.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 895–898.

q: Which gene accounts for the majority of familial (early-onset) AD mutations?
o: PSEN1
APP
PSEN2
MAPT
explanation:
Three principal autosomal dominant familial Alzheimer genes affect amyloid precursor protein or its processing. The frequency question concerns identified familial mutations, a small subset of all Alzheimer disease.

**PSEN1 accounts for the largest share, approximately 78%.** Its protein, presenilin-1, participates in the enzyme complex that cleaves amyloid precursor protein.

**A. PSEN1.** Pathogenic variants are the commonest of the three familial mutation groups.
**B. APP.** APP mutations account for a smaller share, about 18%, despite the central role of its protein in amyloid biology.
**C. PSEN2.** Presenilin-2 mutations account for a still smaller share, about 4%.
**D. MAPT.** Pathogenic variants in the tau gene are associated with familial frontotemporal dementia rather than this group of Alzheimer mutations.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 897–898, 990.

q: Hazzard reports discordance between a clinical Alzheimer dementia diagnosis and autopsy findings. In its discussion of the 2018 research framework, what is the implication for trials of disease-modifying treatment?
o: Select participants by symptoms alone because the clinical syndrome establishes the pathology
Select participants without biological characterization because pathology does not affect efficacy assessment
Select participants with biological confirmation to evaluate treatment in the intended disease
Select participants with non-AD cognitive syndromes because these establish the same biological diagnosis
explanation:
An Alzheimer-like cognitive syndrome can arise without the amyloid plaques and tau tangles a disease-modifying drug is intended to target. Autopsy studies found this mismatch in roughly 10% to 30% of people diagnosed clinically with Alzheimer dementia.

**Enroll participants with biological confirmation of the target disease.** Otherwise, including people who lack the target can dilute an apparent treatment effect or obscure its interpretation.

**A. Symptoms alone.** Typical memory loss identifies a clinical phenotype, but it cannot guarantee the underlying pathology.
**B. Omit biological characterization.** A drug directed at a particular disease process cannot be fairly evaluated if that process is absent in some participants.
**C. Confirm the biology.** Appropriate biomarkers align trial enrollment with the disease mechanism the drug is designed to affect.
**D. Assume other syndromes have the same pathology.** Other dementia syndromes may overlap clinically or have mixed pathology. Their labels cannot establish the same molecular target.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 908–909.

q: When counseling a family about symptomatic medication for Alzheimer disease, which statement best reflects the evidence described in Hazzard?
o: In mild cognitive impairment, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors delay progression to Alzheimer dementia.
In early Alzheimer disease, memantine has sufficient evidence to recommend routine treatment.
In established Alzheimer dementia, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are used for stability or slower decline.
In moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease, combined treatment produces better outcomes than either agent alone.
explanation:
Cholinesterase inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefits in established Alzheimer dementia. **Maintaining everyday abilities or slowing decline relative to the untreated course is a reasonable treatment goal**, with individual review for tolerability and meaningful function.

**A. Prevent conversion from MCI.** Cholinesterase inhibitors have not reliably delayed progression of MCI to Alzheimer dementia.
**B. Routine memantine for early disease.** Its established indication is moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia. Evidence does not support routine use in mild disease.
**C. Cholinesterase inhibitors for established dementia.** Discuss small average benefits rather than promising a noticeable improvement or a plateau in every patient.
**D. Combination is superior to either drug alone.** One moderate-to-severe trial found modest cognitive and ADL gains with memantine added to continued donepezil. DOMINO-AD found no significant added benefit over continued donepezil alone. Consistent superiority to both monotherapies has not been shown.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 911. Tariot et al., JAMA, 2004, PMID 14734594. DOMINO-AD, N Engl J Med, 2012, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1106668.

q: Which patient group matches the FDA-approved indication for memantine (Namenda) stated in Hazzard 8e?
o: Patients diagnosed with Alzheimer disease of any severity
Patients diagnosed with moderate to severe Alzheimer disease
Patients diagnosed with the mild cognitive impairment syndrome
Patients diagnosed with Alzheimer disease of mild severity
explanation:
Memantine reduces excessive NMDA receptor activity and is a symptomatic medication. The approved indication specifies Alzheimer dementia and a particular severity range.

**Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia** is the patient group matching that indication.

**A. Alzheimer disease at any severity.** This would extend the indication to mild disease and earlier biological stages.
**B. Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.** At this stage memantine can offer modest benefits in cognition, daily activities or behavior.
**C. Mild cognitive impairment.** MCI retains functional independence. Memantine has no established preventive indication for this syndrome.
**D. Mild Alzheimer disease.** Mild dementia falls earlier than the approved severity range for memantine.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 896, 911.

q: What is the most common initial clinical presentation of Alzheimer disease?
o: Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in executive function
Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in visuospatial abilities
Initial symptoms dominated by slowly progressive recent-event memory loss
Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in language abilities
explanation:
The usual first manifestation of Alzheimer disease is difficulty learning or retaining recent events. Relatives may notice repeated questions or forgotten conversations while older memories remain accessible.

**Slowly progressive recent-event memory loss** is the most common initial presentation.

**A. Executive dysfunction first.** Difficulty planning or judging can lead a less common nonamnestic presentation.
**B. Visuospatial impairment first.** An initial problem recognizing objects or navigating space is possible, but is less frequent than amnestic onset.
**C. Progressive recent-memory loss first.** Forgetting newly learned information over months or years gives the characteristic early history.
**D. Language impairment first.** Word-finding difficulty or a language-led syndrome can occur early in some patients, but it is not the usual first pattern.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 900–901.

q: According to Hazzard, how are neuropsychiatric symptoms in dementia associated with disease progression and caregiver burden?
o: Faster disease progression and greater caregiver burden
Faster disease progression and lower caregiver burden
Slower disease progression and greater caregiver burden
Slower disease progression and lower caregiver burden
explanation:
Neuropsychiatric symptoms affect patients and the people providing daily care. Frequent, distressing behavior can increase supervision needs and accompanies a less favorable clinical course.

**They are associated with faster disease progression and greater caregiver burden.**

**A. Faster progression, greater burden** Both associations match the clinical pattern.
**B. Faster progression, lower burden** Faster decline fits, but caregiving demands commonly increase.
**C. Slower progression, greater burden** Greater burden fits, but the observed disease course is faster.
**D. Slower progression, lower burden** Both directions are reversed.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 919
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: In a dementia patient with an acute or fluctuating change in behavior, what must be excluded before anything else?
o: Schizophrenia
Delirium
Generalized anxiety disorder
Major depressive disorder
explanation:
Delirium is an acute, usually fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness. Dementia increases vulnerability to delirium from infection, pain, a medication change or another medical stressor.

**Assess for delirium first when cognition or behavior changes acutely or fluctuates.**

**A. Schizophrenia** A new primary psychotic disorder does not readily explain waxing and waning attention.
**B. Delirium** An abrupt departure from baseline is the cue to identify and treat an underlying precipitant.
**C. Generalized anxiety** Anxiety can cause restlessness but does not usually cause fluctuating consciousness.
**D. Major depression** Depression can cause withdrawal or poor concentration, usually over a longer time course.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 922–923
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: An older adult with dementia develops irritability and anxiety. Which approach best reflects the presentation of depression in dementia described by Hazzard?
o: Include agitation, irritability, and anxiety in the assessment of depression in dementia.
Favor a separate psychiatric disorder when new depressive symptoms emerge during established dementia.
Use poor concentration and anhedonia as the principal features distinguishing depression from dementia.
Use the presentation in cognitively intact older adults as the main pattern for recognizing depression.
explanation:
Depression can be difficult to recognize in dementia because low motivation, impaired concentration and loss of interest overlap with the cognitive disorder. Affect and behavior may carry more diagnostic information than a verbal description of sadness.

**Ask about irritability, agitation and anxiety when evaluating a possible depressive syndrome.**

**A. Include behavioral manifestations** These symptoms can accompany depression in dementia and are worth exploring with a reliable informant.
**B. Favor a separate disorder automatically** Consider neurodegeneration, pain, medicines and a mood disorder together. New symptoms alone cannot distinguish them.
**C. Rely on concentration and anhedonia** Their overlap with dementia and apathy limits their discriminatory value.
**D. Use the cognitively intact pattern** Memory, language and awareness change how the patient expresses distress.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 923
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: The MIND at Home study found unmet care needs in nearly all community-dwelling dementia patients. Which care plan best follows the response Hazzard recommends?
o: Support safe surroundings, daily activities and physical and mental health
Support medical treatment while leaving home safety to a later crisis
Support physical care while setting aside meaningful daily activities
Support the patient directly while excluding the caregiver from planning
explanation:
The MIND at Home study found unmet needs extending beyond medical treatment to safety, meaningful activity, advance planning and caregiver support. A practical care plan covers the person's daily environment as well as illness.

**Support a safe home, meaningful activity and physical and mental health together.**

**A. Increase airway collapse** Pressure supports airway patency and works in the opposite direction.

**C. Keep the airway open** Elimination of obstructive events and snoring indicates effective pressure.
**D. Preserve events for comfort** Mask fit and comfort matter for adherence, but untreated obstruction defeats the purpose of titration.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 649.

q: Which symptom pattern best supports restless legs syndrome in an older adult with an urge to move the legs?
o: Symptoms improve with movement, worsen at rest, and tend to occur later in the day.
Symptoms worsen with movement, improve at rest, and tend to occur later in the day.
Symptoms improve with movement, worsen at rest, and are defined by early-day predominance.
Symptoms worsen with movement, improve at rest, and are defined by early-day predominance.
explanation:
Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically from the urge to move and its timing. **Symptoms begin or worsen at rest, improve with movement, and predominate later in the day.**

**A. Movement helps, rest worsens, later onset** All three features support RLS.
**B. Movement worsens, rest helps, later onset** The time of day fits, but both activity-related features are reversed.
**C. Movement helps, rest worsens, early predominance** The response to movement fits, but early-day predominance is atypical.
**D. Movement worsens, rest helps, early predominance** Neither the timing nor the response to activity fits the usual syndrome.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 651–652.

q: At what serum ferritin level should a patient with RLS start iron supplementation?
o: Start iron after ferritin rises above 300 mcg/L
Start iron when ferritin is below 75 mcg/L
Start iron for dopaminergic augmentation, without a ferritin-based trigger
Start iron after ferritin rises above 75 mcg/L
explanation:
Iron status affects RLS management even without overt anemia. **A ferritin below 75 micrograms per liter is an indication to consider iron replacement** in an adult with clinically significant RLS. Check transferrin saturation as well.

**A. Wait until above 300** A high ferritin is not the routine trigger for starting iron.
**B. Below 75** Low stores can contribute to symptoms. The clinical threshold is higher than that often used to identify overt iron deficiency.
**C. Augmentation alone** Earlier or spreading symptoms during dopaminergic therapy warrant medication review and iron studies. They do not replace iron assessment.
**D. Above 75 alone** Simply exceeding 75 is insufficient. With ferritin above this range, the full iron profile and route of therapy matter.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 652. AASM RLS and PLMD guideline (2025), good-practice statement.

Key note: Hazzard gives a ferritin below 75 micrograms per liter. Current adult AASM guidance includes exactly 75 and also considers transferrin saturation below 20 percent.

q: How many periodic limb movements in sleep (PLMS) per hour are required to diagnose PLMD?
o: At least 15 per hour
At least 4 per hour
At least 10 per hour
At least 90 per hour
explanation:
Periodic limb movements in sleep are counted by polysomnography. **The adult frequency threshold in current criteria is more than 15 movements per hour**, and PLMD also requires clinically meaningful disturbance that the movements explain after competing causes are excluded.

**A. At least 15 per hour** This is the closest offered choice. Even a higher index alone cannot diagnose PLMD without attributable symptoms.
**B. At least 4 per hour** Four consecutive movements define a series, not the adult hourly frequency threshold.
**C. At least 10 per hour** This is below the adult PLMD threshold.
**D. At least 90 per hour** Ninety seconds is an upper intermovement interval for scoring a series, not the required hourly index.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 651–652. AASM RLS and PLMD guideline (2025), diagnostic criteria in the introduction.

Key note: Hazzard uses at least 15 movements per hour. The AASM adult criterion is more than 15, so exactly 15 does not meet that frequency requirement.

q: Which drug is FDA-approved specifically for non–24-hour sleep-wake rhythm disorder?
o: Suvorexant
Zolpidem
Ramelteon
Tasimelteon
explanation:
In non-24-hour sleep–wake rhythm disorder, the biological clock fails to stay synchronized with the 24-hour day. **Tasimelteon** is a melatonin-receptor agonist approved for this indication in adults.

**A. Suvorexant** It blocks orexin receptors and is used for insomnia.
**B. Zolpidem** It is a GABAergic hypnotic for insomnia.
**C. Ramelteon** It is also a melatonin-receptor agonist, but its approved indication concerns sleep-onset insomnia.
**D. Tasimelteon** Its MT1 and MT2 receptor activity can help entrain the circadian rhythm.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 657, 659–660. FDA Hetlioz prescribing information, section 1.

q: How long must symptoms persist for insomnia to be classified as chronic rather than short-term?
o: More than 2 weeks
More than 6 weeks
More than 6 months
More than 3 months
explanation:
Chronic insomnia requires recurrent nighttime difficulty with daytime consequences despite adequate sleep opportunity. **Three months is the duration threshold**. Current diagnostic criteria also require symptoms at least three nights per week.

**A. More than two weeks** This duration can still represent short-term insomnia.
**B. More than six weeks** It remains below the chronic duration threshold.
**C. More than six months** A patient need not wait six months to meet chronic criteria.
**D. More than three months** Symptoms lasting longer than three months satisfy the duration requirement. A patient who has reached exactly three months can also qualify.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 657. VA/DoD insomnia and OSA guideline (2025), Appendix F, ICSD-3-TR chronic insomnia criteria.

Key note: The chapter says more than three months. ICSD-3-TR uses at least three months, including the three-month boundary.

q: What is the recommended first-line treatment for insomnia in all adults, including older patients?
o: CBT-I
Temazepam
Flurazepam
Zolpidem
explanation:
Chronic insomnia often persists through learned wakefulness in bed and worry about sleep. **CBT-I is the first-line treatment for adults, including older patients**, because it addresses these perpetuating factors and has durable benefit.

**A. CBT-I** It combines behavioral and cognitive methods such as stimulus control, sleep restriction and examining unhelpful beliefs.
**B. Temazepam** This benzodiazepine can impair psychomotor performance and increase falls.
**C. Flurazepam** Its prolonged action increases concern for next-day sedation in older patients.
**D. Zolpidem** Its short onset does not remove risks of confusion, complex sleep behaviors and falls.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 659–662.

q: An older adult has syncope attributed to symptomatic cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome. Which treatment does Hazzard identify as the treatment of choice?
o: Midodrine as used for the vasodepressor form of the syndrome
Catheter ablation as used for intrinsic cardiac tachyarrhythmias
Carotid sinus denervation before attempting the preferred therapy
Atrioventricular sequential pacing using a dual-chamber pacemaker
explanation:
In cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome, an exaggerated reflex can slow or pause the heart enough to cause syncope. **Dual-chamber atrioventricular sequential pacing** targets the documented cardioinhibitory mechanism, especially in older patients with severe recurrent unpredictable events.

**A. Midodrine** — Raising vascular tone targets a vasodepressor component. It does not directly prevent an asystolic pause.
**B. Catheter ablation for tachyarrhythmia** — This would address a rapid intrinsic rhythm. The dominant mechanism here is reflex bradycardia or asystole.
**C. Carotid sinus denervation** — Denervation has been considered in refractory cases and is not the initial device-based treatment.
**D. Dual-chamber pacing** — Maintaining rate and AV coordination can prevent the cardioinhibitory component. A coexisting fall in vascular resistance may still cause symptoms.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 675. European Society of Cardiology 2021 pacing guideline, §5.4.

q: During an Epley maneuver for posterior-canal BPPV, each position is held for approximately 10 to 15 seconds or until vertigo subsides. What is the intended mechanical effect?
o: Move particles from the utricle into the posterior semicircular canal
Move particles from the posterior semicircular canal into the cochlea
Move particles from the horizontal canal into the posterior semicircular canal
Move particles from the posterior semicircular canal into the utricle
explanation:
Posterior-canal BPPV results from displaced particles that move with gravity and spuriously stimulate the vestibular system. **The Epley maneuver guides the particles from the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle**.

**A. Utricle to posterior canal** — This is the direction in which free particles enter the canal and provoke symptoms.
**B. Posterior canal to cochlea** — The cochlea serves hearing and is not the destination of canalith repositioning.
**C. Horizontal canal to posterior canal** — This would transfer particles between canals. The maneuver described treats posterior-canal disease.
**D. Posterior canal to utricle** — Sequential changes in head position use gravity to clear the affected canal and reduce provoked vertigo and nystagmus.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 676, Figure 45-2.

q: An older ED patient has an acute change in attention but is quiet rather than agitated. Which approach best follows the chapter's discussion of delirium?
o: Use the absence of agitation to favor ordinary fatigue over a delirium assessment.
Rely on the treating clinician's impression because structured screens add little in this setting.
Use a structured delirium screen because hypoactive presentations are commonly underrecognized.
Regard the quiet presentation as evidence of a benign course without subsequent functional risk.
explanation:
Delirium can produce reduced activity and drowsiness as well as agitation. A new change in attention is important even in a quiet patient.
**Use a structured delirium screen and investigate the precipitant. Hypoactive delirium is common and easy to miss.**

**A. No agitation favors fatigue** Quiet behavior can be the motor presentation of delirium. New inattention warrants assessment of onset, fluctuation and arousal.
**B. Clinical impression is enough** Bedside impressions often miss hypoactive cases. A brief structured tool makes the relevant features explicit.
**C. Structured screening** A 4AT or bCAM helps organize the assessment, then collateral history and examination help identify the acute cause.
**D. Quiet behavior means a benign course** Delirium is associated with longer hospitalization and later functional and cognitive decline, even when disruptive behavior is absent.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 209–211.

q: Why might caregiver AD8 help when a highly educated patient passes brief performance testing?
o: It obtains a care-partner account of cognitive change from baseline
It measures current patient orientation through administration of the AMT4
It measures current patient performance through administration of the O3DY
It provides a definitive dementia diagnosis from the screening result
explanation:
A performance test measures what the patient can do at the bedside today. The caregiver AD8 instead asks a knowledgeable informant about change in the patient's usual thinking and everyday abilities over several years.
**Choose the care partner's account of decline from baseline. It can reveal change in someone who still performs well on a brief test.**

**A. Care-partner history** New difficulty with finances, appointments or familiar appliances can be apparent to someone who knows the person well. Two or more affirmative responses indicate high dementia risk.
**B. AMT4 orientation testing** Age, birth date, place and year are questions the patient answers. A highly educated patient may still answer them accurately despite meaningful change.
**C. Ottawa 3DY performance** The patient reports day, date and year and spells a word backward. This is another brief measure of current performance.
**D. Definitive diagnosis** An abnormal informant screen warrants further evaluation and safer discharge planning. A positive score alone cannot diagnose dementia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 212–213, Figure 15-3.

q: What follows uncertain confidence in a patient's ability to report abuse?
o: Record suspicion solely from the cognitive-screen result
Record no suspicion without further assessment
A physical assessment for findings suggesting abuse or neglect
Return to the initial cognitive assessment as the next step
explanation:
Senior Aid begins with a cognitive check and questions about help, threats, exploitation or harm. The examiner then judges how confidently the patient can report what has happened.
**When the history is unreliable or suspicion remains uncertain, perform the physical assessment and combine its findings with the history and observations.**

**A. Suspicion from cognition alone** An orientation error can limit the reliability of the account. It is not evidence that abuse occurred.
**B. No suspicion without further assessment** A person who cannot give a reliable account may still have experienced harm. Continue the assessment.
**C. Physical assessment** Look for patterned injuries or unusual bruising and for possible neglect, including dehydration, malnutrition or poorly controlled disease. Interpret findings in context.
**D. Repeat the cognitive assessment** Repeating the first step leaves the uncertainty about injury or neglect unresolved. The pathway proceeds to physical examination.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 213–214, Figure 15-4.

q: Why can serum creatinine underestimate perioperative renal vulnerability?
o: Reduced hepatic blood flow prolongs drug half-life
Prolonged use of indwelling devices increases infection risk
Reduced skeletal muscle lowers creatinine production despite diminished filtration
Reduced lower-esophageal sphincter tone increases reflux
explanation:
Serum creatinine reflects production by skeletal muscle as well as removal by the kidney. **Low muscle mass can hide diminished filtration by reducing creatinine production.**

**A. Lower hepatic flow** This can prolong the half-life of hepatically cleared drugs, but creatinine production primarily reflects muscle.
**B. Indwelling devices** A prolonged catheter can increase infection risk. It does not explain a deceptively modest creatinine concentration.
**C. Reduced muscle mass** When generation and filtration fall together, the serum concentration may rise little despite clinically important renal impairment.
**D. Lower esophageal sphincter tone** This favors reflux and aspiration. It does not determine the relationship between creatinine and filtration.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 27, pp. 375–376, Table 27-3 and Renal Complications.

q: Why might delaying surgery for optimization be harmful?
o: Emergency surgery may lower mortality compared with elective surgery
Anesthesia type may determine outcomes after baseline risk is controlled
Operator experience may predict 7-day mortality better than preoperative risk factors
A needed elective procedure may become a higher-risk emergency while waiting
explanation:
Preoperative optimization is intended to reduce an identifiable, modifiable risk. **Delay itself can cause harm if a needed elective procedure becomes an emergency.**

**A. Emergency surgery lowers mortality** Older adults undergoing emergency surgery experience particularly high complication and mortality rates.
**B. Anesthetic type determines the result** In the comparison described, spinal versus general anesthesia did not predict outcome after adjustment for baseline risk.
**C. Operator experience best predicts seven-day mortality** Preoperative risk factors predicted early mortality better than anesthesiologist experience or anesthesia duration.
**D. Progression while waiting** Consider the natural history of the surgical disease and the likely benefit of extra preparation before postponing an intervention.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 27, p. 376, Emergency Surgeries and Period of Risk.

q: Which perioperative care plan is supported by Hazzard’s discussion of postoperative risk?
o: Use the immediate postoperative period as the priority for complication surveillance.
Use the anesthetic technique as the primary basis for predicting postoperative outcomes.
Use the anesthetic duration as the primary basis for predicting seven-day mortality.
Use extended preoperative optimization as the priority over avoiding emergency surgery.
explanation:
Postoperative surveillance is most valuable when complications are most likely to appear. **Prioritize the immediate postoperative period and continue surveillance through early recovery.**

**A. Monitor closely immediately after surgery** Risk peaks soon after the operation. About half of adverse events occur within three weeks, so a good first day does not close the window.
**B. Predict outcomes from anesthetic technique** After accounting for preoperative risk factors, spinal versus general anesthesia did not predict outcomes in the comparison described.
**C. Predict seven-day mortality from anesthetic duration** The patient's preoperative risk factors were better predictors of seven-day mortality.
**D. Prioritize extended optimization** Postponing a needed procedure can turn it into a higher-risk emergency. Time spent on optimization must have an expected benefit.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, ch. 27, p. 376, Period of Risk and Emergency Surgeries.

q: What distinguishes sarcopenia from an isolated finding of low muscle mass?
o: Defining sarcopenia through physical frailty rather than through muscle findings
Defining sarcopenia through reduced muscle mass without assessing muscle function
Defining sarcopenia through inflammatory cachexia rather than through muscle findings
Defining sarcopenia through muscle function as well as muscle mass
explanation:
An isolated low lean-mass measurement says little about a person's ability to generate force or move. **Sarcopenia assessment incorporates muscle function as well as consideration of muscle quantity.**

**A. Define through physical frailty** Frailty and sarcopenia overlap, especially through weakness and slowness. Their diagnostic criteria are distinct.
**B. Define through low mass alone** Low lean mass occurs with other conditions including malnutrition and predicts disability less well than functional measurements.
**C. Define through inflammatory cachexia** Disease-associated wasting can coexist with sarcopenia. Inflammation is not its defining measurement.
**D. Assess function as well as mass** Modern schemes emphasize grip strength or performance. The precise role of mass depends on the definition, with EWGSOP2 using quantity or quality for confirmation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 730–732, 735–736.

q: Why is a bedside BIA result less definitive than a direct measurement of muscle function?
o: It directly measures the SPPB balance and chair-stand components
It estimates mass using population- and device-specific equations and cutoffs
It directly measures gait speed
It directly measures grip strength
explanation:
Bioelectrical impedance analysis uses the body's electrical properties to estimate lean tissue. **Its estimate depends on the device, prediction equation and reference population.**

**A. BIA measures SPPB components** Standing balance and chair rises require observation of the patient performing those tasks. An impedance reading cannot supply these scores.
**B. Device- and population-specific estimates** The equations and thresholds vary. A borderline reading therefore needs interpretation alongside measured strength and physical performance.
**C. BIA measures gait speed** A timed walk over a measured distance gives gait speed. BIA provides a body-composition estimate.
**D. BIA measures grip strength** A dynamometer measures grip force. Electrical impedance does not test voluntary contraction.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 732, 735.

q: A person has low muscle mass, preserved gait/grip, and low food intake without a catabolic disease. Which diagnosis does this chapter prioritize?
o: Malnutrition
Physical frailty
Cachexia
Sarcopenia
explanation:
Low intake can reduce muscle quantity even while strength and gait remain preserved. **In this pattern, prioritize malnutrition and assess the nutritional deficit.**

**A. Malnutrition** Low muscle mass and reduced intake supply the relevant phenotypic and etiologic clues. Clarify the intake history, weight change and other nutritional findings.
**B. Physical frailty** Low mass is not itself a Fried criterion. Preserved grip and gait and the absence of other stated criteria leave physical frailty unsupported here.
**C. Cachexia** Severe wasting from cancer, infection or advanced organ disease would suggest excess catabolism. The history instead points to poor intake.
**D. Sarcopenia** Preserved measured function argues against making sarcopenia the primary diagnosis from low mass alone.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 736, Differential Diagnosis.

q: Hazzard notes that fracture risk approximately doubles for each 1-SD decrease in T-score, yet many hip fractures occur above the osteoporosis threshold. What is the appropriate implication for fracture assessment?
o: Defer fracture assessment until a fragility fracture has occurred
Reduce follow-up when BMD lies in the osteopenic range
Combine BMD with clinical factors to assess fracture risk
Focus fracture assessment on women in the postmenopausal period
explanation:
Each standard-deviation decrease in T-score roughly doubles fracture risk, but the threshold of −2.5 does not capture everyone who fractures. **Use BMD and clinical risk factors together.**

**A. Wait for a fragility fracture** Risk assessment can identify people likely to benefit from prevention before an initial fracture.
**B. Reduce follow-up for osteopenia** Many fractures occur above the osteoporosis threshold. Low bone mass with advanced age or a prior fracture can confer substantial risk.
**C. Combine BMD and clinical factors** Age, previous fractures, glucocorticoid exposure and falls help distinguish people with the same T-score but different probabilities of fracture.
**D. Focus on postmenopausal women** Aging men and people with secondary causes also sustain fragility fractures and need assessment when indicated.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 759, 769–771.

q: Why should high-dose bolus vitamin D (e.g., 500,000 IU/year or 60,000 IU/month) be avoided in older adults?
o: They increase falls, with a trend toward increased fractures
They are the same as the loading dose for frank vitamin D deficiency
They consistently reduce falls compared with daily dosing
They are the stated maintenance regimen for all older adults
explanation:
Large intermittent vitamin D doses have different effects from daily replacement or a short course for deficiency. **Very large intermittent doses such as 500,000 IU yearly or 60,000 IU monthly increased falls, with concern about an increase in fractures.**

**A. Increased falls** Yearly 500,000 IU increased both falls and fractures in older women at increased fracture risk. In adults aged 70 or older with a previous fall, 60,000 IU monthly led to more falls than 24,000 IU monthly.
**B. Same as deficiency loading** A time-limited course to correct documented deficiency has a different dose pattern and indication from repeated preventive megadoses.
**C. Consistent fall prevention** Trials of very large boluses showed the opposite direction of effect on falls.
**D. Universal maintenance** Maintenance uses an appropriate regular dose, adjusted to the individual and the indication. These boluses are not routine maintenance.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 772–773, nutrition and vitamin D. Sanders et al., JAMA 2010, PMID 20460620. Bischoff-Ferrari et al., JAMA Intern Med 2016, PMID 26747333.

q: Why does denosumab's benefit not persist after stopping, unlike bisphosphonates?
o: Denosumab maintains its antifracture effect above pretreatment levels indefinitely after withdrawal
Denosumab remains incorporated into bone after its scheduled dosing stops
Prior vertebral fracture protects against the increased fracture risk after withdrawal
Denosumab is not incorporated into bone during its course of treatment
explanation:
Denosumab blocks RANK ligand only while enough antibody remains active between doses. **It is not incorporated into bone, so resorption can resume rapidly when dosing stops.**

**A. Indefinite fracture protection** As the pharmacologic effect wanes, fracture protection can be lost and vertebral fractures may occur.
**B. Incorporation into bone** Skeletal retention is characteristic of bisphosphonates. Denosumab is a circulating antibody.
**C. Protection from a prior vertebral fracture** A previous vertebral fracture increases the risk of further vertebral fractures after withdrawal.
**D. No incorporation during treatment** Without a skeletal reservoir, a treatment holiday is inappropriate. Arrange follow-on antiresorptive treatment if denosumab must be stopped.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 773, 776 · BHOF Clinician’s Guide, discontinuation of denosumab.

q: An older adult with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis asks how conservative treatment and joint replacement fit together. Which account follows Hazzard?
o: Medication modifies disease progression, while nonpharmacologic treatment is directed toward relief of symptoms.
Joint replacement precedes conservative treatment, which is introduced afterward for persistent symptomatic disease.
Conservative therapies target symptoms, with joint replacement considered when these treatments have failed.
Disease-modifying medication is the next treatment step when conservative symptom management has failed.
explanation:
OA treatment aims to lessen pain and preserve the activities that matter to the patient. **Conservative treatment addresses symptoms and function, with replacement considered when disabling disease persists.**

**A. Medication modifies progression** — Available analgesic and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve pain. None has established disease-modifying efficacy in routine OA care.
**B. Replacement precedes conservative care** — Education, exercise and appropriate analgesia usually precede surgery.
**C. Conservative treatment, then possible replacement** — Continued pain and functional loss despite adequately tried approaches justify discussing surgery with a suitable patient.
**D. Disease-modifying medication next** — No approved OA drug has demonstrated the structural effect proposed here. Reassess goals, function and surgical options.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 779, 784, 788–789.

q: Hazzard describes many genetic risk loci for osteoarthritis. Which interpretation of these findings is supported by the chapter?
o: Individual effects are small, with structural and inflammatory genes implicated
Individual effects are large, with structural and inflammatory genes implicated
Cartilage-matrix genes are excluded from the proposed genetic contribution
Interleukin-related genes are excluded from the proposed genetic contribution
explanation:
Common OA reflects the combined effects of loading, injury, aging and many genetic variants. **Individual genetic associations are generally small and include both structural and inflammatory pathways.**

**A. Small effects in both pathways** — Type II collagen contributes to cartilage structure. Interleukin-related genes can influence inflammatory signalling.
**B. Large effects in both pathways** — Identifying many loci does not imply that each common variant strongly predicts an individual's disease.
**C. Cartilage-matrix genes excluded** — COL2A1, which encodes type II collagen, is one of the implicated structural genes.
**D. Interleukin genes excluded** — Variants involving several interleukin pathways have been implicated in susceptibility.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 780–781, Genetics and Pathophysiology.

q: What synovial fluid white blood cell count threshold distinguishes OA from inflammatory/infectious arthritis?
o: Both below and above 2000 cells/mm³ are classified as OA by this threshold
Neither below nor above 2000 cells/mm³ helps distinguish these conditions
Above 2000 cells/mm³ supports OA; below 2000 suggests inflammation or infection
Below 2000 cells/mm³ supports OA; above 2000 suggests inflammation or infection
explanation:
The synovial white-cell count helps distinguish a relatively quiet effusion from one that needs an inflammatory or infectious workup. **Below 2,000 cells per cubic millimeter supports OA, while above 2,000 suggests inflammation or infection.**

**A. Both ranges indicate OA** — A high count is atypical for uncomplicated OA, even if degenerative changes are present on imaging.
**B. Neither range helps** — The count changes the differential, although it cannot establish a specific diagnosis or safely exclude infection on its own.
**C. High supports OA and low suggests inflammation** — This reverses the usual relationship between inflammatory activity and the number of leukocytes in the fluid.
**D. Low supports OA and high suggests inflammation or infection** — Interpret the result alongside the examination, crystal microscopy and cultures when indicated.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 783, Laboratory studies.

q: Which physical-therapy plan best reflects the chapter's approach to advanced knee osteoarthritis?
o: Avoid strengthening and neuromuscular training because advanced disease limits their usefulness.
Individualize strengthening and neuromuscular training, home progression and assistive-device needs.
Prescribe a fixed exercise program without adjusting it to the patient's progress or function.
Focus on prescribing a cane or walker while omitting a strengthening and home exercise program.
explanation:
Advanced knee OA can cause weakness, poor control and avoidance of activity. **Individualize strengthening and neuromuscular training, progress exercises at home, and assess the need for a walking aid.**

**A. Avoid strengthening** — Advanced disease calls for adaptation. Gentle range-of-motion and isometric work can be tolerable starting points.
**B. Individualized training and device assessment** — The therapist can assess pain, strength and gait, start at an achievable level and teach a progression the patient can continue.
**C. Fixed exercise prescription** — A fixed schedule can exceed current capacity or stop challenging the patient as function improves.
**D. Walking aid alone** — An aid may unload the knee and improve stability, but it does not replace strengthening or a sustained movement program.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 784 and 787, Exercise and Assistive devices.

q: Why are topical NSAIDs and topical capsaicin not recommended for hip OA?
o: Topical NSAIDs routinely cause acute renal failure when used as instructed
Topical NSAIDs are ineffective for knee OA as well
The hip joint is too deep for effective topical treatment
Capsaicin has demonstrated no pain benefit at the knee
explanation:
Local preparations work best when the target joint lies near the skin. **The depth of the hip makes meaningful benefit from topical NSAIDs or capsaicin unlikely.**

**A. Routine kidney failure with topical NSAIDs** — Systemic exposure is generally lower with appropriate local use. Routine acute kidney failure is not the reason for the hip recommendation.
**B. Topical NSAIDs ineffective at the knee** — The knee is accessible and topical NSAIDs have demonstrated symptomatic benefit there.
**C. Hip too deep** — Drug applied to skin over the hip cannot reliably reach the deep joint at an effective concentration.
**D. No knee pain benefit from capsaicin** — Capsaicin has modest evidence for pain relief at the knee, although local burning can limit tolerability.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 785 and 787. ACR/Arthritis Foundation OA guideline, topical NSAIDs and capsaicin.

q: An older adult with hip osteoarthritis has stable CKD stage IV and an eGFR of 24 cc/min. An oral analgesic is being considered for a brief pain flare; there is no liver disease. Which approach best follows the chapter's renal-safety advice?
o: Use oral celecoxib for pain control and monitor kidney function closely.
Use oral ibuprofen with a proton-pump inhibitor and reassess pain control.
Use oral acetaminophen for a short course and reassess pain control.
Use low-dose oral ibuprofen intermittently and reassess kidney function during treatment.
explanation:
In stage IV CKD, even a brief course of a systemic NSAID can compromise renal function. **A short acetaminophen trial with reassessment is the most appropriate option listed.**

**A. Celecoxib with renal monitoring** — COX-2 selectivity can reduce some upper gastrointestinal toxicity. It does not prevent NSAID-related kidney injury.
**B. Ibuprofen plus a PPI** — A PPI offers upper gastrointestinal protection. It cannot preserve renal perfusion during NSAID exposure.
**C. Short-course acetaminophen** — This avoids the NSAID mechanism of renal injury. Check the total daily dose from all products and continue only if helpful.
**D. Intermittent low-dose ibuprofen** — Intermittent exposure and follow-up creatinine checks do not make oral ibuprofen a preferred choice at an eGFR of 24.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 787–788. 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 6. ACR/Arthritis Foundation OA guideline, acetaminophen.

q: Why can a patient with a fracture still walk?
o: A small percentage of fractures are nondisplaced or “hairline” fractures
Painless walking is the usual presentation of a displaced hip fracture
An unrecognized nondisplaced fracture tends to become stable during walking
Displaced fractures typically permit painless weight bearing after a fall
explanation:
With a nondisplaced fracture the bone ends retain their alignment. **Some patients with a hairline hip fracture can still bear weight and walk, usually with pain.**

**A. A nondisplaced or hairline fracture** — Preserved alignment explains why walking is possible despite injury. Persistent hip pain after trauma still warrants evaluation.
**B. Painless walking is usual with displacement** — Displaced fractures typically cause pain and an inability to bear weight.
**C. Walking stabilizes an unrecognized fracture** — A nondisplaced fracture can progress to displacement, which is a reason to diagnose it promptly.
**D. Displaced fractures permit painless weight bearing** — A painful shortened, externally rotated leg and difficulty bearing weight are the classic presentation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 794.

q: What imaging follows negative radiographs when fracture remains suspected?
o: Plain radiographs alone exclude a fracture
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
No further imaging after negative plain radiographs
Computed tomography
explanation:
An occult hip fracture may escape plain radiography. **Obtain MRI when a fall, persistent hip pain and examination findings still suggest fracture.**

**A. Plain films exclude fracture** — A nondisplaced fracture can leave little visible cortical change on the radiograph.
**B. Magnetic resonance imaging** — MRI can show the fracture and the adjacent bone marrow edema even when the radiograph appears normal.
**C. No further imaging** — Missing the injury permits continued loading and possible displacement.
**D. Computed tomography** — CT can detect some occult fractures. MRI is more sensitive and is the next study specified here.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 794.

q: Why is arthroplasty commonly used for displaced femoral-neck fractures?
o: Retinacular vascular injury increases the risk of nonunion and femoral-head osteonecrosis
Retinacular vessels lie away from the femoral neck and escape direct injury
Femoral-neck perfusion is plentiful and redundant, supporting healing after fracture fixation
Internal fixation is preferred because it restores the femoral-head blood supply
explanation:
The femoral head depends on small retinacular vessels that run closely against the neck. **A displaced neck fracture can disrupt these vessels, leading to nonunion or osteonecrosis.**

**A. Retinacular injury threatens union and head viability** — Replacement bypasses both the fracture's need to unite and the injured head's need for perfusion.

q: Does absence of a single terminal disease automatically exclude a frail patient from hospice?
o: No; prognosis rests on the severity and irreversibility of frailty and multimorbidity
No; certification of a terminal prognosis is optional when frailty is present
Yes; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction generally makes frail patients ineligible
Yes; frailty with multimorbidity is insufficient grounds for a terminal prognosis
explanation:
Severe irreversible frailty and several progressive diseases can together produce a terminal trajectory. US Medicare separates the principal diagnosis used on a claim from the patient's clinical eligibility for hospice.
**Assess whether the combined trajectory supports a prognosis of six months or less even without one dominant terminal disease.**

**A. Severity and irreversibility** Document functional course, contributing illnesses and the clinical basis for certification.
**B. Certification optional** Frailty does not waive the required physician certification.
**C. Billing restriction excludes patient** The restriction concerns reporting frailty, debility or adult failure to thrive as the principal diagnosis.

q: Why compare prognosis with time to benefit?
o: Short life expectancy tends to bring forward the benefit of preventive interventions
Preventive interventions generally spare frail patients the immediate harms associated with treatment
Life expectancy sometimes ends before preventive benefit develops, exposing patients to immediate harms
Prognosis is relevant to hospice selection but generally irrelevant to preventive treatment
explanation:
Time to benefit is the interval before an intervention is likely to produce the outcome the patient wants. Screening and tightly controlled preventive targets may take years to help, while their harms can occur immediately.
**If life expectancy is shorter than the time to benefit, the patient may experience treatment harm without living long enough to benefit.**

**A. Benefit comes sooner** A short prognosis does not accelerate the biological effect of prevention.
**B. Immediate harms are avoided** Testing, medication adverse effects and treatment burden can begin at once.
**C. Delayed benefit and immediate harm** Comparing these horizons helps choose interventions with a realistic chance of benefiting this patient.
**D. Relevant only to hospice** Prognosis also informs preventive care and decisions about treatment intensity.

q: In which direction is clinicians' survival estimate commonly biased?
o: Toward overestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
Clinical estimates are entirely uncorrelated with actual survival
Toward underestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
No systematic bias is described
explanation:
Clinical estimates of survival contain useful information but can be biased toward optimism. Combining the patient's illness trajectory, function and cognition with a relevant prognostic index can improve the estimate.
**Clinicians commonly overestimate survival, by a factor of three to five in the observations summarized here.**

**A. Overestimation** An estimate of months can exceed the actual survival by several fold. Communicate a range rather than applying a fixed correction to one patient.
**B. No correlation** Clinicians' estimates correlate with outcomes despite systematic error.
**C. Underestimation** This reverses the direction of the commonly observed bias.

q: Why does adequate control of acute postoperative pain matter for an older adult’s longer-term recovery?
o: Poorly controlled pain may protect against chronic pain by reducing mobility demands.
Poorly controlled pain may shorten admission by limiting excessive postoperative activity.
Appropriate pain control may help prevent chronic pain and pain-related mobility limitations.
Appropriate pain control may improve comfort while increasing the later risk of chronic pain.
explanation:
Acute postoperative pain affects the stress response and the ability to move. **Adequate analgesia can support mobilization and may reduce the risk of persistent pain.**

**A. Poorly controlled pain may protect against chronic pain by reducing mobility demands** Limiting mobility is an adverse consequence of uncontrolled pain.
**B. Poorly controlled pain may shorten admission by limiting excessive postoperative activity** Poor control is associated with longer admission and delayed recovery.
**C. Appropriate pain control may help prevent chronic pain and pain-related mobility limitations** Relieving pain enough to participate in recovery may reduce both immediate disability and later persistent pain.

q: Which mechanism defines neuropathic pain in Hazzard, rather than nociceptive pain?
o: Activation of pain receptors by local tissue inflammation
A lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory system
Activation of pain receptors by mechanical tissue distortion
Activation of pain receptors by tissue injury after trauma
explanation:
Pain can arise from injured tissues or from the sensory pathways themselves. **A lesion or disease of the somatosensory system defines neuropathic pain.**

**A. Activation of pain receptors by local tissue inflammation** Local inflammatory mediators activate nociceptors in tissue.
**B. A lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory system** Diabetic polyneuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia are examples of this mechanism.
**C. Activation of pain receptors by mechanical tissue distortion** Mechanical distortion stimulates tissue nociceptors.
**D. Activation of pain receptors by tissue injury after trauma** Trauma can activate nociceptors. It causes neuropathic pain when it also injures the somatosensory system.

One in three

This historical US measure counted Part D beneficiaries receiving at least one opioid prescription during 2016. **Approximately one in three beneficiaries received one.**

**A. A quarter** One quarter underestimates the proportion described.
**B. 7% to 10%** Seven to ten percent is well below the reported proportion.
**C. 60%** Sixty percent substantially overstates the proportion.

q: How does opioid-induced hyperalgesia present clinically, in contrast to opioid tolerance?
o: Improving pain with increasing opioid doses
Tolerance alone, with no increase in pain on dose escalation
Increased levels of pain with increased doses of opioids
Reduced sensitivity to painful stimuli
explanation:
When opioid analgesia appears to fail, check disease progression, tolerance and increased pain sensitivity. **Pain that becomes worse as the opioid dose rises suggests opioid-induced hyperalgesia.**

**A. Improving pain with increasing opioid doses** Improvement after escalation can occur when the previous dose has lost effect.
**B. Tolerance alone, with no increase in pain on dose escalation** Tolerance means a dose gives less relief. By itself it does not explain paradoxical worsening with repeated escalation.
**C. Increased levels of pain with increased doses of opioids** Increasing pain or allodynia outside the original region should prompt reassessment and consideration of a gradual reduction.
**D. Reduced sensitivity to painful stimuli** Hyperalgesia means greater sensitivity to painful stimuli.

q: A patient with facet-mediated pain obtains 80% pain relief after a diagnostic medial-branch nerve block. What is the clinical significance of this response?
o: It argues against the medial branch as a relevant target for a subsequent intervention.
It supports considering radiofrequency denervation of the medial branch for longer-lasting pain relief.
It supports vertebral augmentation as the next treatment for the facet-mediated pain.
It supports repeating diagnostic testing while ruling out a longer-lasting nerve procedure.
explanation:
A diagnostic medial branch block temporarily interrupts sensory input from a lumbar facet joint. **An 80% reduction in pain after the block supports considering medial branch radiofrequency denervation.**

**A. It argues against the medial branch as a relevant target for a subsequent intervention** Substantial temporary relief supports, rather than argues against, the targeted nerve.
**B. It supports considering radiofrequency denervation of the medial branch for longer-lasting pain relief** Radiofrequency treatment at the responsive branch can provide longer relief. Discuss symptoms, goals and procedural risks.
**C. It supports vertebral augmentation as the next treatment for the facet-mediated pain** Vertebral augmentation treats selected painful vertebral body fractures, not facet-mediated pain.
**D. It supports repeating diagnostic testing while ruling out a longer-lasting nerve procedure** Further diagnostic testing may depend on the clinical protocol. The observed relief does not rule out a longer-lasting procedure.
